Kronecker Delta Rule for Long Context Linear Attention

Anamaria-Roberta Hartl*1    Levente Zólyomi*1,2    Michael List1    Günter Klambauer1,2    Sebastian Böck2    Sepp Hochreiter1,2

1  Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) predominantly use the Transformer architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017; Touvron et al., 2023a; Qwen Team, 2023; OpenAI, 2025), whose softmax attention mechanism has computational costs that grow quadratically with context length, while its key–value cache grows linearly. Consequently, inference becomes increasingly costly as contexts grow. To reduce these costs, recent work has explored replacing softmax attention with linear attention mechanisms (Katharopoulos et al., 2020; Schlag et al., 2021), which can be traced back to the idea of fast weight programmers (Schmidhuber, 1992). Linear attention compresses the context into a fixed-size memory matrix that is updated as new tokens arrive, yielding linear computational complexity and a constant memory footprint. Recently, recurrent architectures based on associative memories (Kohonen, 1972; Anderson, 1972), including xLSTM (Beck et al., 2024), as well as related state-space and memory-based approaches such as Mamba (Gu and Dao, 2024; Dao and Gu, 2024; Lahoti et al., 2026), DeltaNet (Yang et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025; Kimi Team et al., 2025; Hatamizadeh et al., 2026), RWKV-5 and 6 (Peng et al., 2024), and other recent architectures (Sun et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025; Behrouz et al., 2025), have emerged as competitive alternatives to Transformers.

A crucial challenge for linear attention is controlling memory growth. If the memory of recurrent architectures grows without being bounded, its readout can become arbitrarily large, leading to numerical instabilities, particularly during learning. The original LSTM (Hochreiter, 1991; Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997) uses a bounded squashing function to control the exposed cell state, while its forget gate regulates the accumulation of information in memory. RWKV-5 and RWKV-6 (Peng et al., 2024) similarly control memory growth through a forget gate. Mamba architectures (Gu and Dao, 2024; Dao and Gu, 2024; Lahoti et al., 2026) also restrain memory growth through a forget mechanism derived from a stable state-space ordinary differential equation. However, forget-based memory control becomes increasingly restrictive for long contexts. To retain information over long time spans, forget gates must remain close to one; otherwise, information from the beginning of the context is progressively attenuated. xLSTM (Beck et al., 2024) addresses this limitation by allowing forget gates close to one and introducing normalizer and stabilizer states to control the scale of its matrix memory and readout. However, normalization based on ratios of potentially large quantities can itself lead to numerical difficulties and learning instabilities, particularly in larger xLSTM networks (Beck et al., 2025b). mLSTM’s numerical instabilities are illustrated by the stress test in Figure 2.

The DeltaNet family (Yang et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025; Kimi Team et al., 2025; Hatamizadeh et al., 2026) controls memory growth through Delta Rule updates, whose dynamics converge to a steady-state distribution with bounded memory ensuring stable learning dynamics. However, revising a stored value can perturb previously stored values, leading to unwanted memory interference for long sequences. We introduce KronLSTM, which, like (Gated) DeltaNet, provides bounded memory through a delta-style update, but uses the Kronecker Delta Rule. The Kronecker Delta Rule is less invasive: it modifies the memory only along a single direction in matrix space, reducing interference with previously stored associations. This targeted memory revision results in a less noisy gradient flow over time.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    (i) Kronecker Delta Rule is introduced as a new update rule for associative matrix memories, which corrects the scalar associations while having minimal interference with previously stored values.

  • •

    (ii) KronLSTM is introduced as a novel linear attention architecture based on the Kronecker Delta Rule equipped with a vector forget gate, a β\beta gate, and a target gate.

  • •

    (iii) Stability properties for the Kronecker Delta Rule are mathematically proved via bounds on the expected memory norm. These bounds ensure stable learning and proper gradient flow.

  • •

    (iv) Experiments empirically validate the strong performance of KronLSTM at long-context language modeling and retrieval tasks. KronLSTM performs strongly across language modeling, recall, and state tracking benchmarks.

2  KronLSTM

In Subsection 2.1, we introduce the Kronecker Delta Rule and analyze its memory dynamics, and
in Subsection 2.2, the Kronecker Delta Rule is embedded in the KronLSTM sequence-mixer block.

2.1  Kronecker Delta Rule

Linear attention update rules for matrix memory.

Linear attention (Katharopoulos et al., 2020) compresses the context into a matrix memory 𝑺\bm{S} that is updated per token and read out per query,

𝑺t+1=𝑺t+𝒗t​𝒌t⊤,𝒉t=𝑺t​𝒒t=∑i<t𝒗i​(𝒌i⊤​𝒒t),\bm{S}_{t+1}\;=\;\bm{S}_{t}\;+\;\bm{v}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top}\,,\qquad\bm{h}_{t}\;=\;\bm{S}_{t}\bm{q}_{t}\;=\;\sum_{i<t}\bm{v}_{i}\,\big(\bm{k}_{i}^{\top}\bm{q}_{t}\big)\,, (1)

with 𝑺t∈ℝdv×dk\bm{S}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}\times d_{k}}, keys 𝒌t\bm{k}_{t} and queries 𝒒t\bm{q}_{t} in ℝdk\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}}, and values 𝒗t\bm{v}_{t} in ℝdv\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}}. Therefore, 𝑺\bm{S} is an associative memory (Kohonen, 1972; Anderson, 1972) with a Hebbian rule, i.e.,  an outer product update rule. Modern linear attention architectures like xLSTM (Beck et al., 2024), Mamba (Gu and Dao, 2024; Dao and Gu, 2024; Lahoti et al., 2026), RWKV-5 and 6 (Peng et al., 2024) rely on these associative memories equipped with gates and transformations. The memory growth is controlled by a forget gate, which stabilizes the memory dynamics.

In contrast, the Delta Rule (Widrow and Hoff, 1960; Schlag et al., 2021) corrects the memory with the difference of the retrieval to the current value when writing into the memory

𝑺t+1=𝑺t−βt​(𝑺t​𝒌t−𝒗t)​𝒌t⊤=𝑺t​(𝑰−βt​𝒌t​𝒌t⊤)+βt​𝒗t​𝒌t⊤,\bm{S}_{t+1}\;=\;\bm{S}_{t}\;-\;\beta_{t}\big(\bm{S}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}-\bm{v}_{t}\big)\,\bm{k}_{t}^{\top}\;=\;\bm{S}_{t}\big(\bm{I}-\beta_{t}\,\bm{k}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top}\big)\;+\;\beta_{t}\,\bm{v}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top}, (2)

with step size βt\beta_{t}. Each step is gradient descent on 12​‖𝑺t​𝒌t−𝒗t‖2\tfrac{1}{2}\left\lVert\bm{S}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}-\bm{v}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}, and the transition 𝑰−βt​𝒌t​𝒌t⊤\bm{I}-\beta_{t}\bm{k}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top} is a generalized Householder matrix, which admits chunkwise-parallel training (Yang et al., 2024).

The two rules differ in how an association, once stored, is changed. The Hebbian write of (1) is additive, so the memory grows with the sequence and an earlier value can be buried by later writes but never revised. The delta rule (2) revises: it removes the value currently stored at 𝒌t\bm{k}_{t} before writing 𝒗t\bm{v}_{t}. The correction, however, proceeds along (𝑺t​𝒌t−𝒗t)​𝒌t⊤(\bm{S}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}-\bm{v}_{t})\bm{k}_{t}^{\top}, a direction determined by the current memory content, so values stored at keys that overlap with 𝒌t\bm{k}_{t} are affected as well. We aim at an error-correcting write that acts solely on the pair (𝒌t,𝒗t)(\bm{k}_{t},\bm{v}_{t}).

Kronecker Delta Rule.

Let 𝑺t∈ℝdv×dk\bm{S}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}\times d_{k}} be the memory matrix, 𝒌t∈ℝdk\bm{k}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}} and 𝒗t∈ℝdv\bm{v}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}} the key and value at step tt, ct∈ℝc_{t}\in\mathbb{R} a target and βt\beta_{t} a step size. The scalar 𝒗t⊤​𝑺t​𝒌t\bm{v}_{t}^{\top}\bm{S}_{t}\bm{k}_{t} measures how strongly the memory associates 𝒌t\bm{k}_{t} with 𝒗t\bm{v}_{t}. The Kronecker Delta Rule corrects this scalar towards the target along the outer product of the pair as follows

𝑺t+1=𝑺t−βt​(𝒗t⊤​𝑺t​𝒌t−ct)​𝒗t​𝒌t⊤=𝑺t−βt​(𝒗t⊤​𝑺t​𝒌t)​𝒗t​𝒌t⊤⏟erase+βt​ct​𝒗t​𝒌t⊤⏟write.\bm{S}_{t+1}\;=\;\bm{S}_{t}\;-\;\beta_{t}\big(\bm{v}_{t}^{\top}\bm{S}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}\,-\,c_{t}\big)\,\bm{v}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top}\;=\;\bm{S}_{t}\;-\;\underbrace{\beta_{t}\big(\bm{v}_{t}^{\top}\bm{S}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}\big)\,\bm{v}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top}}_{\text{erase}}\;+\;\underbrace{\beta_{t}\,c_{t}\,\bm{v}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top}}_{\text{write}}\,. (3)

In place of the dvd_{v}-dimensional residual 𝑺t​𝒌t−𝒗t\bm{S}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}-\bm{v}_{t} of the delta rule, a scalar is corrected, and the direction 𝒗t​𝒌t⊤\bm{v}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top} of the correction is determined by the input pair alone without utilizing the memory content. A target ct≡1c_{t}\equiv 1 stores each association with unit strength, while ct=0c_{t}=0 erases it. The target ctc_{t} may depend on the input, i.e., serves as a gate, so that what is written becomes input-dependent. The right-hand side of (3) separates the update into an erase and a write term, both scaled by βt\beta_{t}. Choosing the target c~t=ct/βt\tilde{c}_{t}=c_{t}/\beta_{t} removes the step size from the write, so that βt\beta_{t} alone determines how much of the stored association is erased and ctc_{t} alone how much is written. KronLSTM uses this form, with both quantities computed from the input as gates (Section 2.2).

Properties of the Kronecker Delta Rule.

(i) Error correction (see Appendix Property A2 and Property A6). An update is a step of gradient descent with step size βt\beta_{t} on 12​(𝒗t⊤​𝑺​𝒌t−ct)2\tfrac{1}{2}\big(\bm{v}_{t}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{k}_{t}-c_{t}\big)^{2}. Re-presenting the same pair gives 𝒗t⊤​𝑺t+1​𝒌t−ct=(𝒗t⊤​𝑺t​𝒌t−ct)​(1−βt​‖𝒂t‖2)\bm{v}_{t}^{\top}\bm{S}_{t+1}\bm{k}_{t}-c_{t}=\left(\bm{v}_{t}^{\top}\bm{S}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}-c_{t}\right)(1-\beta_{t}\left\lVert\bm{a}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}), so it contracts the error iff 0<βt<2/‖𝒂t‖20<\beta_{t}<2/\left\lVert\bm{a}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}, and the Newton step βt=1/‖𝒂t‖2\beta_{t}=1/\left\lVert\bm{a}_{t}\right\rVert^{2} meets the target in a single update; for ct=0c_{t}=0 this deletes the association. (ii) Delta Rule in vectorized form (see Appendix Property A7). With the Kronecker product 𝒂t=𝒌t⊗𝒗t=vec⁡(𝒗t​𝒌t⊤)\bm{a}_{t}=\bm{k}_{t}\otimes\bm{v}_{t}=\vecop(\bm{v}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top}) and the vectorized memory 𝒔=vec⁡(𝑺)\bm{s}=\vecop(\bm{S}), we have 𝒗t⊤​𝑺​𝒌t=𝒂t⊤​𝒔\bm{v}_{t}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{k}_{t}=\bm{a}_{t}^{\top}\bm{s} and ‖𝒂t‖2=‖𝒌t‖2​‖𝒗t‖2\left\lVert\bm{a}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}=\left\lVert\bm{k}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}\left\lVert\bm{v}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}, and (3) becomes

𝒔t+1=(𝑰−βt​𝒂t​𝒂t⊤)​𝒔t+βt​ct​𝒂t,\bm{s}_{t+1}\;=\;\big(\bm{I}-\beta_{t}\,\bm{a}_{t}\bm{a}_{t}^{\top}\big)\,\bm{s}_{t}\;+\;\beta_{t}\,c_{t}\,\bm{a}_{t}\,, (4)

the Widrow–Hoff Delta Rule (Widrow and Hoff, 1960) with input 𝒂t\bm{a}_{t} and target ctc_{t}, which gives the rule its name. The transition factor is a generalized Householder matrix that does not depend on ctc_{t}, so the chunkwise-parallel formulation of DeltaNet (Yang et al., 2024) applies with 𝒂t\bm{a}_{t} in place of 𝒌t\bm{k}_{t}, the target entering only the driving term. For βt​‖𝒂t‖2∈(1,2)\beta_{t}\left\lVert\bm{a}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}\in(1,2) the transition factor has a negative eigenvalue, the idea behind the state-tracking capabilities of Delta Rule models (Grazzi et al., 2025).

(iii) Interference (see Appendix Property A9). For any other stored pair (𝒌i,𝒗i)(\bm{k}_{i},\bm{v}_{i}), the update changes the association by

Δ⁡(𝒗i⊤​𝑺​𝒌i)=−βt​(𝒗t⊤​𝑺t​𝒌t−ct)​(𝒗i⊤​𝒗t)​(𝒌t⊤​𝒌i),\Delta\big(\bm{v}_{i}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{k}_{i}\big)\;=\;-\,\beta_{t}\,\big(\bm{v}_{t}^{\top}\bm{S}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}-c_{t}\big)\,\big(\bm{v}_{i}^{\top}\bm{v}_{t}\big)\big(\bm{k}_{t}^{\top}\bm{k}_{i}\big)\,, (5)

the product of value overlap and key overlap. Orthogonality in either factor protects a stored association, whereas the Hebbian and the Delta rule interference is controlled by key overlap alone.

(iv) Capacity (see Appendix Property A11). Each triple (𝒌t,𝒗t,ct)(\bm{k}_{t},\bm{v}_{t},c_{t}) imposes one linear constraint 𝒂t⊤​𝒔=ct\bm{a}_{t}^{\top}\bm{s}=c_{t} on the dk​dvd_{k}d_{v} entries of 𝑺\bm{S}, so up to dk​dvd_{k}d_{v} scalar associations can be stored exactly when the features {𝒂i}\{\bm{a}_{i}\} are linearly independent, against dkd_{k} value vectors for 𝑺​𝒌i=𝒗i\bm{S}\bm{k}_{i}=\bm{v}_{i}. In particular, a single key can hold several mutually orthogonal values, which the read-out 𝑺​𝒌\bm{S}\bm{k} returns as their sum. See Appendix A3 for more properties and more details on the above properties.

Convergence, steady state, and memory norm bounds.

We will present expected bounds on the memory norm, which in turn imply stable memory dynamics that obviate numerical instabilities. Memories grow with the length of the context and the number of vectors or associations to store; therefore long contexts are most relevant when analyzing memory stability. We model a long context as a stream of i.i.d. triples (𝒌t,𝒗t,ct)∼p(\bm{k}_{t},\bm{v}_{t},c_{t})\sim p with fixed step size β\beta and set

𝑨¯:=E⁡[𝒂​𝒂⊤]≻𝟎,𝒃¯:=E⁡[c​𝒂],𝒔LS:=𝑨¯−1​𝒃¯,ρ:=c−𝒂⊤​𝒔LS,κ:=β​maxi​‖𝒂i‖2,\bar{\bm{A}}:=\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\bm{a}\bm{a}^{\top}]\succ\bm{0},\quad\bar{\bm{b}}:=\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[c\,\bm{a}],\quad\bm{s}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}:=\bar{\bm{A}}^{-1}\bar{\bm{b}},\quad\rho:=c-\bm{a}^{\top}\bm{s}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}},\quad\kappa:=\beta\max_{i}\left\lVert\bm{a}_{i}\right\rVert^{2}, (6)

so 𝑺LS=argmin𝑺E⁡[(𝒗⊤​𝑺​𝒌−c)2]\bm{S}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}=\mathop{\mathrm{argmin}\,}_{\bm{S}}\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[(\bm{v}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{k}-c)^{2}] is the least-squares memory and ρ\rho the irreducible residual, with E⁡[ρ​𝒂]=𝟎\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\rho\,\bm{a}]=\bm{0}. Throughout, 0<β​‖𝒂i‖2<20<\beta\left\lVert\bm{a}_{i}\right\rVert^{2}<2, and qβ:=1−β⁡(2−κ)​λmin​(𝑨¯)q_{\beta}:=1-\beta(2-\kappa)\lambda_{\min}(\bar{\bm{A}}).

Theorem 1 (Unbiased mean and steady state).

The expected iterate obeys the exact recursion E⁡[𝐬t+1]=(𝐈−β​𝐀¯)​E​[𝐬t]+β​𝐛¯\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\bm{s}_{t+1}]=(\bm{I}-\beta\bar{\bm{A}})\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\bm{s}_{t}]+\beta\bar{\bm{b}}, whose unique fixed point is 𝐬LS\bm{s}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}, so ‖E⁡[𝐒t]−𝐒LS‖F≤rt​‖𝐒0−𝐒LS‖F\left\lVert\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\bm{S}_{t}]-\bm{S}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}\leq r^{t}\left\lVert\bm{S}_{0}-\bm{S}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}} with r=maxk⁡|1−β​λk​(𝐀¯)|<1r=\max_{k}{{\left|1-\beta\lambda_{k}(\bar{\bm{A}})\right|}}<1. Moreover the iterates form a time-homogeneous Markov chain on ℝdk​dv\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}d_{v}} whose kernel contracts on laws with finite second moment; by the standard theory of Markov chains on general state spaces (Meyn and Tweedie, 1993) it has a unique stationary distribution πβ\pi_{\beta}, the law of 𝐒t\bm{S}_{t} converges to it geometrically from any initialization, and the stationary mean is exactly Eπβ​[𝐒]=𝐒LS\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}_{\pi_{\beta}}[\bm{S}]=\bm{S}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}.

Theorem 1 combines Appendix Theorem A6 and Appendix Theorem A7 which have been proven in Appendix A3.

Theorem 2 (Memory norm bounds).

With λmin,λmax\lambda_{\min},\lambda_{\max} the extreme eigenvalues of 𝐀¯\bar{\bm{A}}, the least-squares memory is sandwiched by the explained target energy,

E⁡[c2]−E⁡[ρ2]λmax​(𝑨¯)≤‖𝑺LS‖F2≤E⁡[c2]−E⁡[ρ2]λmin​(𝑨¯),\frac{\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[c^{2}]-\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\rho^{2}]}{\lambda_{\max}(\bar{\bm{A}})}\;\;\leq\;\;\left\lVert\bm{S}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}\;\;\leq\;\;\frac{\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[c^{2}]-\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\rho^{2}]}{\lambda_{\min}(\bar{\bm{A}})}\,, (7)

and all its singular values obey the same upper bound; residual energy can only shrink it. In the non-expansive regime κ≤1\kappa\leq 1, the steady state and — started at 𝐒0=𝟎\bm{S}_{0}=\bm{0} — every iterate satisfies

Eπβ​[‖𝑺‖F2]≤E⁡[c2]λmin​(𝑨¯),E⁡[‖𝑺t‖F2]≤(1+qβt/2)2​E⁡[c2]λmin​(𝑨¯)≤4​E​[c2]λmin​(𝑨¯),\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}_{\pi_{\beta}}\big[\left\lVert\bm{S}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}\big]\;\leq\;\frac{\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[c^{2}]}{\lambda_{\min}(\bar{\bm{A}})}\,,\qquad\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[\left\lVert\bm{S}_{t}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}\big]\;\leq\;\Big(1+q_{\beta}^{\,t/2}\Big)^{2}\frac{\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[c^{2}]}{\lambda_{\min}(\bar{\bm{A}})}\;\leq\;\frac{4\,\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[c^{2}]}{\lambda_{\min}(\bar{\bm{A}})}\,, (8)

the transient factor decays geometrically from 44 to 11.

Theorem 2 combines Appendix Theorem A8, Appendix Theorem A9, and Appendix Theorem A10 which are proven in Appendix A3. From the first step onward, the expected memory of the rule is bounded by a constant determined by the data distribution alone. More details and theoretical results are given in Appendix A3.

2.2  The KronLSTM architecture

In modern deep learning architectures for sequence modeling, the matrix update rules are stabilized and enhanced with gating mechanisms. The mLSTM (Beck et al., 2024) places the Hebbian write (1) under a sigmoid forget gate and an exponential input gate, and Gated DeltaNet (Yang et al., 2025) decays the memory of (2) by a scalar before the correction,

𝑺t+1=ft​𝑺t+it​𝒗t​𝒌t⊤,𝑺t+1=ft​𝑺t​(𝑰−βt​𝒌t​𝒌t⊤)+βt​𝒗t​𝒌t⊤.\bm{S}_{t+1}\;=\;\mathrm{f}_{t}\,\bm{S}_{t}\;+\;\mathrm{i}_{t}\,\bm{v}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top}\,,\qquad\bm{S}_{t+1}\;=\;\mathrm{f}_{t}\,\bm{S}_{t}\,\big(\bm{I}-\beta_{t}\,\bm{k}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top}\big)\;+\;\beta_{t}\,\bm{v}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top}\,. (9)

Kimi Delta Attention (Kimi Team et al., 2025) makes the decay (key) channel-wise, and Gated DeltaNet-2 (Hatamizadeh et al., 2026) replaces the single βt\beta_{t} by separate channel-wise erase and write gates. KronLSTM proceeds in the same way: the step size βt\beta_{t} and the target ctc_{t} of (3) become gates computed from the input; a forget gate decays the memory, and the rule is embedded in the projections, short convolutions, normalizations, and output gate of a standard sequence-mixer layer. All quantities below are per head, with key and value dimensions dkd_{k} and dvd_{v}; we suppress the head index and write 𝒙t∈ℝd\bm{x}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} for the layer input at step tt.

KronLSTM update.

The forget gate is a diagonal matrix 𝑭t\bm{F}_{t} with diagonal entries in (0,1)(0,1). It acts on the key dimension and hence decays the memory from the right, 𝑺t​𝑭t\bm{S}_{t}\bm{F}_{t}, retaining each key direction separately. We use target c~t=ct/βt\tilde{c}_{t}=c_{t}/\beta_{t} to decouple erase and write. The erase term of (3) is evaluated on the decayed memory 𝑺t​𝑭t\bm{S}_{t}\bm{F}_{t}. We obtain

𝑺t+1=𝑺t​𝑭t⏟forget−βt​(𝒗t⊤​𝑺t​𝑭t​𝒌t)​𝒗t​𝒌t⊤⏟erase+ct​𝒗t​𝒌t⊤⏟write,\bm{S}_{t+1}\;=\;\underbrace{\bm{S}_{t}\bm{F}_{t}}_{\text{forget}}\;-\;\underbrace{\beta_{t}\big(\bm{v}_{t}^{\top}\bm{S}_{t}\bm{F}_{t}\,\bm{k}_{t}\big)\,\bm{v}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top}}_{\text{erase}}\;+\;\underbrace{c_{t}\,\bm{v}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top}}_{\text{write}}, (10)

so that forgetting, erasing, and writing are controlled by three separate gates, 𝑭t\bm{F}_{t}, βt\beta_{t} and ctc_{t}. The standard coupled and the unit-target variant ct≡1c_{t}\equiv 1 are compared in Appendix A6, Table A3.

Gates.

The erase gate βt\beta_{t} and the write gate ctc_{t} are per-head scalars obtained from linear projections of the input followed by a sigmoid,

βt=σ⁡(𝒘β⊤​𝒙t+bβ)∈(0,1),ct=σ⁡(𝒘c⊤​𝒙t+bc)∈(0,1),\beta_{t}=\sigma\big(\bm{w}_{\beta}^{\top}\bm{x}_{t}+b_{\beta}\big)\in(0,1),\qquad c_{t}=\sigma\big(\bm{w}_{\mathrm{c}}^{\top}\bm{x}_{t}+b_{\mathrm{c}}\big)\in(0,1), (11)

both bounded by construction. The diagonal vector 𝐟t\mathbf{f}_{t} of the forget gate 𝑭t=diag⁡(𝐟t)\bm{F}_{t}=\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{f}_{t}) is obtained by raising a sigmoid gate to a learned positive per-head power, following the parameterization of Mamba (Gu and Dao, 2024) and Gated DeltaNet-2 (Hatamizadeh et al., 2026)

𝐟t=𝝈​(−(𝒔f)t)a=(1−𝝈⁡((𝒔f)t))a,(𝒔f)t=𝑾f​𝒙t+𝒃f∈ℝdk,α=exp⁡(alog)∈ℝ>0,\mathbf{f}_{t}\;=\;\bm{\sigma}(-(\bm{s}_{\mathrm{f}})_{t})^{a}\;=\;\big(1-\bm{\sigma}((\bm{s}_{\mathrm{f}})_{t})\big)^{a},\ \ (\bm{s}_{\mathrm{f}})_{t}=\bm{W}_{\mathrm{f}}\bm{x}_{t}+\bm{b}_{\mathrm{f}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}},\ \ \alpha=\exp(a_{\log})\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}, (12)

where aloga_{\log} is a single learned scalar per head, broadcast over the dkd_{k} key dimensions, and the exponent is taken component-wise. The sigmoid sets retention separately for each key direction as a function of the input. At the same time, the exponent rescales the head’s retention horizon by 1/a1/a, so that heads can operate at widely different timescales without high pre-activations. Since aloga_{\log} is learned in log space, the baseline retention timescale spans orders of magnitude across heads, while within a head the per-direction variation comes entirely from the input. The read-out is gated by a sigmoid output gate 𝐨t=𝝈⁡(𝑾o​𝒙t+𝒃o)∈(0,1)dv\mathbf{o}_{t}=\bm{\sigma}(\bm{W}_{\mathrm{o}}\bm{x}_{t}+\bm{b}_{\mathrm{o}})\in(0,1)^{d_{v}}.

KronLSTM block.

Queries, keys, and values are linear projections of 𝒙t\bm{x}_{t}, each followed by a short causal depthwise convolution and a SiLU activation, and are then ℓ2\ell_{2}-normalized with 𝒒t,𝒌t∈ℝdk\bm{q}_{t},\bm{k}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}} and 𝒗t∈ℝdv\bm{v}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}}. The memory 𝑺t∈ℝdv×dk\bm{S}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}\times d_{k}} is updated by (10) and read with the query, 𝒉~t=𝑺t​𝒒t∈ℝdv\tilde{\bm{h}}_{t}=\bm{S}_{t}\bm{q}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}}. The read-out passes through the sigmoid output gate and a per-head RMSNorm, and the concatenated heads are mixed by the output projection,

𝒉t=𝑾out​RMSNorm​(𝐨t⊙𝒉~t).\bm{h}_{t}\;=\;\bm{W}_{\text{out}}\,\mathrm{RMSNorm}\big(\mathbf{o}_{t}\odot\tilde{\bm{h}}_{t}\big).

With ℓ2\ell_{2}-normalized keys and values and a sigmoid βt\beta_{t}, we have βt​‖𝒌t‖2​‖𝒗t‖2=βt<1\beta_{t}\left\lVert\bm{k}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}\left\lVert\bm{v}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}=\beta_{t}<1, so every update is non-expansive and the memory operates in the regime of Theorem 2; the forget gate, with entries below one, only contracts it further. The architecture of the KronLSTM block is shown in Figure 3. It carries no state besides the memories 𝑺t\bm{S}_{t} of its heads: there is no normalizer state and no stabilizer state as in the mLSTM. KronLSTM can serve as a drop-in replacement for the attention layer in a Transformer block, analogous to mLSTM and sLSTM in the xLSTM architecture.

3  Experimental Validation

We experimentally validate the KronLSTM architecture on different benchmarks with a focus on language modeling tasks. We compare KronLSTM with the following recurrent linear attention architectures: Gated DeltaNet (GDN) (Yang et al., 2025), Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) (Kimi Team et al., 2025), Mamba-3 (Lahoti et al., 2026), and Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN-2) (Hatamizadeh et al., 2026). Recent deployments of linear attention in frontier models follow two hybrid-setting paradigms: either interleave the linear layers with a small number of softmax attention layers (NVIDIA, 2025; Merrill et al., 2026; Kimi Team et al., 2025) or use sliding-window attention (SWA) instead (Cabannes et al., 2026; Hatamizadeh et al., 2026). The advantage of the latter is keeping the memory footprint constant with respect to the context length. Therefore, we evaluate every architecture in two settings: as a pure linear attention model, and as a hybrid with SWA layers. For the hybrid setting, we employ a window size of 2048 at a 5:15{:}1 ratio of linear attention to SWA layers. All models are pretrained on the FineWeb-Edu dataset using the Llama2 tokenizer (Touvron et al., 2023b).

We train at a context of 8k, motivated by previous works (Guo et al., 2026; Beck et al., 2025a; Beck et al., 2026), where the throughput advantage of linear attention compared to the softmax attention emerges from 8k context onward. We evaluate the models within and extrapolating outside their context length (Section 3.2). The experiments in the following sections show 1.5B parameter models trained on 100B tokens. In Appendix A6, we provide a set of experiments at 400M model size.

3.1  Language Modeling

We assess the performance of KronLSTM compared to leading linear attention variants on standard language modeling benchmarks, concretely on five commonsense reasoning tasks (HellaSwag (Zellers et al., 2019), PIQA (Bisk et al., 2020), ARC-easy and ARC-challenge (Clark et al., 2018), WinoGrande (Sakaguchi et al., 2021)) and on LAMBADA (Paperno et al., 2016), reporting accuracy on all six tasks, their average (Avg-6), and LAMBADA perplexity. Table 1 shows the results of both linear and hybrid models. Among all competitors, KronLSTM has the highest average accuracy over the six tasks and the lowest perplexity on LAMBADA. As a linear model, KronLSTM performs best on five out of six tasks and improves on average on the strongest competitor, KDA, by 1.6 accuracy points. The hybrid setting confirms KronLSTM’s performance advantage, leading on four of six tasks and achieving the lowest perplexity on LAMBADA. Hybrid models with sliding-window attention change the averages by at most about one accuracy point. While mLSTM, Mamba-3 and GDN-2 benefit most from adding SWA, GDN and KDA change only minimally; KronLSTM remains robust, leading among all configurations.

3.2  Retrieval Capabilities

On long-context tasks, the Kronecker Delta Rule should improve the most over previous update rules, as interference grows with context length. We assess the performance of KronLSTM on two benchmarks with different context lengths.

The first benchmark is the real-world recall suite of Arora et al. (2024) (SWDE, SQuAD, FDA, TriviaQA, NQ, DROP) for 2k context. Results are given in Table 2. KronLSTM has the best average accuracy, and it is the best method in three out of six tasks in both pure linear attention models and hybrid models. In general, hybrid models using SWA gain five to nine accuracy points.

The second benchmark is the RULER needle-in-a-haystack (NIAH) tasks (Hsieh et al., 2024) where models are evaluated at 4k, 8k and 16k context length, with 16k assessing the extrapolation capabilities of the models. Results are presented in Table 3. Among all linear attention models, KronLSTM is the best or second-best method across all sequence lengths, except for task S1. KronLSTM has the highest accuracy on S3 and MQ tasks across all sequence lengths. Among all hybrid models, KronLSTM achieves the highest accuracy (averaged over all lengths) on all tasks and has the highest accuracy at 16k on each task, confirming its strong long context capabilities. The improvement of KronLSTM over competitors like Gated DeltaNet is consistent with the interference analysis of Property A9. On S2 and S3, whose needles are unique sentences embedded in natural language text, KronLSTM outperforms GDN except for S2 at 16k. For hybrid models, KronLSTM outranks GDN-2 and Mamba-3 by 15.2 accuracy points on S2 at 4k. KronLSTM’s margin increases on MQ and MV with sequence length. On MQ, KronLSTM’s lead distance grows from 2.4 to 4.1 accuracy points when increasing the context from 4k to 16k. On MV, KronLSTM is 3.5 accuracy points behind the best method, GDN, for 4k context, while KronLSTM is the leading method for 8k and 16k, with a 1.1 and 3.8 accuracy point lead, respectively.

For longer contexts, the memory updates of GDN more frequently interfere with already stored content and perturb it, resulting in more degraded performance at 16k. In contrast, the Kronecker Delta Rule is less invasive and performs better at longer contexts. The exception is S1, where KronLSTM underperforms. S1 is the most artificial task with frequently repeated noise sentences, which is unrealistic for real-world text. We attribute the performance drop of the KronLSTM in this task to the residual accumulation for recurring keys. Hybrid models with SWA have a considerably smaller S1 accuracy, except KronLSTM. The hybrid models containing the baseline linear attention layers reach at most 51.8, 26.6, and 12.6 accuracy for 4k, 8k, and 16k context length, respectively. These accuracies closely match the fraction of the context covered by the attention window, indicating that the needle is primarily retrieved when it lies within the window, with Mamba-3 and mLSTM dropping to zero at 16k. The results suggest limited reliance on the recurrent architecture’s memory. KronLSTM exceeds these accuracies on average across all context lengths and achieves the best performance across all six tasks at 16k. Section 3.3 examines how these methods perform after context extension.

3.3  Long Context Extension

In applications, language models do not extrapolate to longer context but are trained on them, typically by continued pretraining at increased context length (Fu et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2024). This stage unlocks retrieval far beyond the original pretraining length (Fu et al., 2024). Linear attention models have no positional encoding to adapt; rather, they must learn to keep more associations over longer time spans. We therefore branch the 1.5B linear KronLSTM and GDN-2 runs at 75B tokens and train them for the remaining 25B tokens at a sequence length of 32k on a long-document mixture derived from ProLong-64K (Gao et al., 2024), so that the context-length-extended models are token-matched to the 100B models of the previous sections. GDN-2 serves as a reference model in this experiment since it also decouples erase and write. Further details on training are described in Appendix A7.1. Table 4 shows the commonsense reasoning, LAMBADA, and recall results of the extended models. Both models benefit from length extension on the reasoning and recall tasks, and perplexity improves by about 4 perplexity points. KronLSTM keeps its lead: it has the higher average accuracy and the lower perplexity, and it is better on five of the six recall tasks.

Results for context extension at the RULER tasks are given in Figure 4 and Table A4. As expected, KronLSTM shows its advantage by extending the training context length. While both architectures perform strongly on single-needle retrieval at shorter contexts, KronLSTM increasingly outperforms GDN-2 on the more challenging NIAH tasks, ranging from 8k to 32k. At 16k, this advantage is particularly pronounced on S-3 and MV, with KronLSTM leading on most tasks except S1, where GDN-2 remains stronger. At 32k, KronLSTM maintains its lead across all five tasks, although both architectures experience a substantial drop in retrieval accuracy compared to 16k. The gap between the two models widens with haystack size, as predicted by the interference analysis in Section 2.1: longer contexts accumulate more interference, and KronLSTM’s update rule suffers less of it.

3.4  State Tracking Capabilities

KronLSTM can perform state tracking by setting βt=2​σ​(𝒘β⊤​𝒙t+bβ)∈(0,2)\beta_{t}=2\sigma(\bm{w}_{\beta}^{\top}\bm{x}_{t}+b_{\beta})\in(0,2), as described in Grazzi et al. (2025) for DeltaNet. We evaluate KronLSTM’s state tracking capabilities on parity, S3S_{3} permutation, and modulo arithmetic. We train up to sequence length 128 and evaluate up to 1024. Figure 5 shows that KronLSTM has similar state tracking capabilities as Gated DeltaNet on the parity and S3S_{3} tasks, both ahead of Mamba-3, which wins on modulo arithmetic.

3.5  Training Efficiency

Figure 3.5 reports end-to-end training throughput of the purely linear 1.5B models on a single NVIDIA H100 (80 GB), following Hatamizadeh et al. (2026): each step processes 16,384 tokens, split from 2K×\times8 to 16K×\times1 (sequence length ×\times batch size), and all models share the same training stack. KronLSTM reaches 36.8–44.5K tokens/s, 11–18% more than GDN-2 at every shape and within 4–8% of KDA up to 8K×\times2. GDN, whose scalar decay admits the cheapest kernels, remains the fastest. Throughput is nearly flat while a step holds at least two sequences; at 16K×\times1 all models slow down, since the inter-chunk recurrence parallelizes only over sequences and heads.

4  Conclusion

We have introduced the Kronecker Delta Rule, an update rule for associative matrix memories that corrects a scalar association along a single direction, and KronLSTM, which embeds this rule in a gated linear attention mixer. We proved that the memory dynamics converge to a unique steady state and that the expected memory norm is bounded at every step. KronLSTM has the best average accuracy on commonsense reasoning and real-world recall, both as a linear model and as a hybrid. Averaged over the context lengths, it is the best or second-best linear model on every natural-text RULER task, and on S1 it is the only one that retrieves needles beyond the sliding attention window in hybrid models. After extending the context to 32k, KronLSTM outperforms GDN-2 on all natural-text retrieval tasks from 16k onward. Future work includes scaling up KronLSTM and training hybrid models containing full softmax attention layers.

AI use statement

The Kronecker Delta Rule and the KronLSTM architecture originated with the authors without AI assistance. LLMs were used to assist in developing the theoretical results and in implementing the method. Claude Fable 5 and Claude Fable 5.1 assisted in deriving the properties of the Kronecker Delta Rule and the convergence and memory norm bounds of Section 2.1 and Appendix A3; every statement and proof was checked independently by the authors, who take full responsibility for their correctness. Claude Fable 5 was further used to examine candidate formulations of the Kronecker Delta Rule, in particular the coupled, decoupled, and unit-target write variants, for their viability; the choice of the form in (10) based on was made by the authors on the basis of ablation studies such as in Appendix A6. Fable 5.1 was used to assist in deriving the chunkwise-parallel formulation of KronLSTM. The formulation was subsequently checked thoroughly by our team. Claude Fable 5 and Claude Fable 5.1 were used to optimize the chunkwise-parallel and recurrent kernels of KronLSTM; the resulting kernels were numerically verified against naive reference implementations written by the authors. We did not use generative AI tools to interpret results or to design experiments. We have not used generative AI tools to generate synthetic data or to propose hypotheses, and translation, dataset cleaning and reformatting, and qualitative or thematic data analysis do not apply to this work. Additionally, we used Claude Fable 5 and Claude Opus 5 to draft parts of the manuscript and to edit it for readability. All AI-drafted text was revised by the authors. We have reviewed all AI-assisted work and take responsibility for the final content of this work, including text, claims, and artifacts produced with the aid of generative AI.

Appendix A2 Related Work

To the best of our knowledge, no existing work uses exactly this update that is a scalar bilinear read-out 𝒗⊤​𝑺​𝒌\bm{v}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{k} regressed onto the constant target 11. The established delta-rule linear attention family uses the vector read-out 𝑺​𝒌→𝒗\bm{S}\bm{k}\to\bm{v}. The rule studied here is therefore the bilinear-readout, scalar-target member of the delta-rule. The constraints are ⟨𝒗​𝒌⊤,𝑺⟩F=1{{\left\langle\bm{v}\bm{k}^{\top},\bm{S}\right\rangle}}_{\mathrm{F}}=1 rather than 𝑺​𝒌=𝒗\bm{S}\bm{k}=\bm{v}.

A2.1  Long Short-Term Memory

KronLSTM belongs to the xLSTM (Beck et al., 2024) family that revisits LSTM (Hochreiter, 1991; Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997) for the era of large language models (LLMs) with two modifications: exponential gating and a redesigned memory. mLSTM replaces the scalar cell state by a matrix memory and drops memory mixing, making the recurrence fully parallelizable over the sequence. mLSTM enables recurrent LLMs with fast, constant-memory inference at scale (Beck et al., 2025a), and Beck et al. (2026) establish scaling behavior competitive with Transformers at linear time complexity. xLSTM has also been applied to language modeling (Beck et al., 2025b), vision (Alkin et al., 2025), biological and chemical sequences (Schmidinger et al., 2025), and robotics (Schmied et al., 2025).

The matrix memory of mLSTM can be viewed as a classical correlation-based associative memory (Kohonen, 1972; Anderson, 1972) embedded within LSTM-style gating. In addition to providing an efficient mechanism for storing and retrieving associations, the exponential gates allow mLSTM to revise storage decisions. This distinguishes mLSTM from purely accumulative linear attention mechanisms. KronLSTM follows this line of research by retaining the matrix memory and the ability to revise storage decisions, while introducing a different memory-update rule.

A central challenge of recurrent architectures with growing memory is maintaining stable memory dynamics over long sequences. The original LSTM uses a bounded squashing function for the exposed cell state, while xLSTM introduces a normalizer state and a stabilizer state to control the scale of its matrix memory and retrievals. However, normalization based on ratios of large quantities can lead to numerical and optimization difficulties, particularly in large networks (Beck et al., 2025b). MC-LSTM (Hoedt et al., 2021) instead redistributes its cell state with column-stochastic matrices, which conserve mass and never amplify the state. These considerations motivate alternative matrix-memory update rules that retain memory revision while providing stable memory dynamics. The Kronecker Delta Rule addresses this issue and provides convergence to a steady-state distribution with a norm-bounded memory in expectation. Furthermore, KronLSTM yields advantageous gradient flow over time compared with mLSTM (Hochreiter et al., 2000).

A2.2  The delta-rule linear attention family

The direct ancestor is the fast weight programmer perspective of Schlag et al. (2021), who introduced the delta-rule write 𝑺t+1=𝑺t−β⁡(𝑺t​𝒌t−𝒗t)​𝒌t⊤\bm{S}_{t+1}=\bm{S}_{t}-\beta\,(\bm{S}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}-\bm{v}_{t})\,\bm{k}_{t}^{\top} into linear attention (Katharopoulos et al., 2020), building on the fast-weight programmers of the early 1990s (Schmidhuber, 1992). Yang et al. (2024) (DeltaNet) made this rule hardware-efficient by exploiting the WY representation of the resulting products of generalized Householder matrices. This is exactly the product structure the bilinear rule inherits, with the Kronecker product 𝒌t⊗𝒗t\bm{k}_{t}\otimes\bm{v}_{t} taking the role of 𝒌t\bm{k}_{t}. Subsequent extensions include Gated DeltaNet (Yang et al., 2025), which adds a scalar forget gate αt​𝑺t\alpha_{t}\bm{S}_{t}; RWKV-7 (Peng et al., 2025), which employs a generalized delta rule with a decoupled in-context learning rate; and DeltaProduct (Siems et al., 2025), which applies multiple Householder factors per token to improve state tracking. This is directly relevant to the negative-eigenvalue regime β​‖𝒂t‖2∈(1,2)\beta\left\lVert\bm{a}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}\in(1,2) of the transition factors 𝑰−β​𝒂t​𝒂t⊤\bm{I}-\beta\bm{a}_{t}\bm{a}_{t}^{\top}, which allows state-tracking.

A2.3  The online-learning perspective

Longhorn (Liu et al., 2025) derives state-space recurrences explicitly as closed-form solutions of per-token online learning objectives; the bilinear rule fits this template with the objective 12​(𝒗⊤​𝑺​𝒌−1)2\tfrac{1}{2}\,(\bm{v}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{k}-1)^{2}. Test-time training (TTT) layers (Sun et al., 2024) and Titans (Behrouz et al., 2025) treat the memory as a model trained by gradient descent at inference time. Most relevant as a unifying framework is the Miras taxonomy of Behrouz et al. (2026), which classifies memory architectures by their attentional-bias objective, retention mechanism, and optimizer. The new bilinear rule occupies a new place of that taxonomy: it is a bilinear attentional bias with a constant scalar target. A recent related observation is that test-time training with key–value binding is secretly linear attention (Liu et al., 2026). The mesa-optimization line (von Oswald et al., 2023) provides the complementary least-squares-solver perspective on such layers.

A2.4  Classical update and learning rules

When vectorized, the rule is the Widrow–Hoff LMS / delta rule (Widrow and Hoff, 1960) applied to the Kronecker product input 𝒂t=𝒌t⊗𝒗t\bm{a}_{t}=\bm{k}_{t}\otimes\bm{v}_{t} with target 11. The stability range β​‖𝒂t‖2∈(0,2)\beta\left\lVert\bm{a}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}\in(0,2) is the classical LMS step-size condition. The projection interpretation is Kaczmarz’s method (Kaczmarz, 1937): with the Newton step β⋆=1/(‖𝒌‖2​‖𝒗‖2)\beta^{\star}=1/(\left\lVert\bm{k}\right\rVert^{2}\,\left\lVert\bm{v}\right\rVert^{2}), the update is the orthogonal projection onto the hyperplane {𝑺:⟨𝒗​𝒌⊤,𝑺⟩F=1}\{\bm{S}:{{\left\langle\bm{v}\bm{k}^{\top},\bm{S}\right\rangle}}_{\mathrm{F}}=1\}, and general β\beta gives relaxed projections. The modern convergence theory, including the linear rate under random sampling of constraints, is due to Strohmer and Vershynin (2009). The connections between Kaczmarz iterations, stochastic gradient descent, and learning are surveyed by Chen (2018). Fejér monotonicity and relaxed projection methods are standard in the projection-methods literature (Cegielski, 2012).

A2.5  Relation to cognitive and neuroscience

Because 𝑺\bm{S} scores key–value pairs rather than retrieving values, the closest relative in the cognitive and neuroscience literature is familiarity (recognition) memory: the anti-Hebbian model of familiarity discrimination in perirhinal cortex of Bogacz and Brown (2003) shows that scoring memories attain a far higher capacity than retrieval memories, which is the same d2d^{2}-versus-dd capacity separation derived for the bilinear rule. The classical retrieval-side background is given by correlation matrix memories (Kohonen, 1972; Anderson, 1972) for the Hebbian write, and by delta-rule / pseudoinverse associative memories for capacity under Widrow–Hoff learning (Prados and Kak, 1989).

Appendix A3 Kronecker Delta Rule: Setting, Name, Properties

A3.1  Setup and notation.

We use the notation of the main paper (Section 2.1), specialized to dk=dv=:dd_{k}=d_{v}=:d as in our experiments (where dq​k=dvd_{qk}=d_{v}); the general dv×dkd_{v}\times d_{k} case is identical with d2d^{2} replaced by dk​dvd_{k}d_{v}. Let 𝑺t∈ℝd×d\bm{S}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} be the memory matrix, 𝒌t∈ℝd\bm{k}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} the key and 𝒗t∈ℝd\bm{v}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} the value at step tt, ct∈ℝc_{t}\in\mathbb{R} a scalar target, and βt\beta_{t} a step size. The scalar 𝒗t⊤​𝑺t​𝒌t\bm{v}_{t}^{\top}\bm{S}_{t}\bm{k}_{t} measures how strongly the memory associates 𝒌t\bm{k}_{t} with 𝒗t\bm{v}_{t}; the Kronecker Delta Rule corrects it towards the target ctc_{t} along the outer product 𝒗t​𝒌t⊤\bm{v}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top},

𝑺t+1=𝑺t−βt​(𝒗t⊤​𝑺t​𝒌t−ct)​𝒗t​𝒌t⊤,\boxed{\;\bm{S}_{t+1}\;=\;\bm{S}_{t}\;-\;\beta_{t}\big(\bm{v}_{t}^{\top}\bm{S}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}\,-\,c_{t}\big)\,\bm{v}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top}\,,\;} (A1)

which is Eq. (3) of the main paper. For the analysis, we abbreviate the scalar read-out and its residual,

yt\displaystyle y_{t}\; :=𝒗t⊤​𝑺t​𝒌t\displaystyle:=\;\bm{v}_{t}^{\top}\bm{S}_{t}\bm{k}_{t} (scalar read-out),\displaystyle\text{(scalar read-out)}, (A2)
ψt\displaystyle\psi_{t}\; :=yt−ct\displaystyle:=\;y_{t}-c_{t} (residual),\displaystyle\text{(residual)}, (A3)

so that the update reads compactly 𝑺t+1=𝑺t−βt​rt​𝒗t​𝒌t⊤\bm{S}_{t+1}=\bm{S}_{t}-\beta_{t}\,r_{t}\,\bm{v}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top}. The target sequence ctc_{t} subsumes different variants: ct≡1c_{t}\equiv 1 is the basic Kronecker Delta Rule with target 11, ct≡c>0c_{t}\equiv c>0 the Constant-Target Kronecker Delta Rule, ct=‖𝒗t‖2c_{t}=\left\lVert\bm{v}_{t}\right\rVert^{2} the Norm-Target Kronecker Delta Rule, and ct=‖𝒌t‖​‖𝒗t‖c_{t}=\left\lVert\bm{k}_{t}\right\rVert\left\lVert\bm{v}_{t}\right\rVert the Double-Norm-Target Kronecker Delta Rule. The target ctc_{t} may also be produced by a gate or a network, so that what is written becomes itself input-dependent. Throughout we use 𝒗⊤​𝑺​𝒌=Tr⁡(𝑺​𝒌​𝒗⊤)=⟨𝒗​𝒌⊤,𝑺⟩F\bm{v}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{k}=\mathbf{\mathrm{Tr}}\!\big(\bm{S}\,\bm{k}\bm{v}^{\top}\big)={{\left\langle\bm{v}\bm{k}^{\top},\bm{S}\right\rangle}}_{\mathrm{F}}.

A3.2  Name Kronecker Delta Rule

We use the Kronecker product

𝒂t=𝒌t⊗𝒗t\bm{a}_{t}\;=\;\bm{k}_{t}\otimes\bm{v}_{t} (A4)

in a vectorized update rule. 𝒂t\bm{a}_{t} is a vector of length d2d^{2}, where the vector 𝒗t\bm{v}_{t} is multiplied by each component of 𝒌t\bm{k}_{t} and then stacked to one vector. However, we have 𝒗t​𝒌t⊤=𝒗t⊗𝒌t⊤\bm{v}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top}=\bm{v}_{t}\otimes\bm{k}_{t}^{\top}. Let 𝒔=vec⁡(𝑺)∈ℝd2\bm{s}=\vecop(\bm{S})\in\mathbb{R}^{d^{2}} and 𝒂t=𝒌t⊗𝒗t∈ℝd2\bm{a}_{t}=\bm{k}_{t}\otimes\bm{v}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d^{2}}, so that 𝒗t⊤​𝑺​𝒌t=𝒂t⊤​𝒔\bm{v}_{t}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{k}_{t}=\bm{a}_{t}^{\top}\bm{s}. The rule becomes

𝒔t+1=(𝑰−β​𝒂t​𝒂t⊤)​𝒔t+β​ct​𝒂t,\bm{s}_{t+1}\;=\;\big(\bm{I}-\beta\,\bm{a}_{t}\bm{a}_{t}^{\top}\big)\,\bm{s}_{t}+\beta\,c_{t}\,\bm{a}_{t}, (A5)

which is exactly Delta Rule with Kronecker product input 𝒂t\bm{a}_{t} and target ctc_{t}.

A3.3  Properties

Property A1 (Memory Space is Hilbert Space and Kronecker Update Rule is a Projection onto a Hyperplane).

The memory space ℝd×d\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} is a Hilbert space endowed with the Frobenius inner product

⟨𝑿,𝒀⟩F=Tr⁡(𝑿⊤​𝒀),{{\left\langle\bm{X},\bm{Y}\right\rangle}}_{\mathrm{F}}\,=\,\mathbf{\mathrm{Tr}}\left(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{Y}\right)\,,

where 𝐗,𝐘∈ℝd×d\bm{X},\bm{Y}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}. Hence the target condition

𝒗t⊤​𝑺​𝒌t=ct\bm{v}_{t}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{k}_{t}\,=\,c_{t}

is a hyperplane in this Hilbert space. The update

𝑺t+1=𝑺t−β⁡(𝒗t⊤​𝑺t​𝒌t−ct)​𝒗t​𝒌t⊤\bm{S}_{t+1}\,=\,\bm{S}_{t}-\beta\left(\bm{v}_{t}^{\top}\bm{S}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}-c_{t}\right)\bm{v}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top}

is a orthogonal projection onto it, if

β=1‖𝒌t‖22​‖𝒗t‖22.\beta\,=\,\frac{1}{\left\lVert\bm{k}_{t}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\left\lVert\bm{v}_{t}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}\,.

The update

𝑺t+1=𝑺t−β⁡(𝒗t⊤​𝑺t​𝒌t−ct)​𝒗t​𝒌t⊤\bm{S}_{t+1}\,=\,\bm{S}_{t}-\beta\left(\bm{v}_{t}^{\top}\bm{S}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}-c_{t}\right)\bm{v}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top}

is a relaxed orthogonal projection onto it, with relaxation parameter

ωt=β​‖𝒌t‖22​‖𝒗t‖22.\omega_{t}\,=\,\beta\left\lVert\bm{k}_{t}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\left\lVert\bm{v}_{t}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\,.
Property A2 (Exact online gradient descent: a bilinear delta rule with target ctc_{t}).

The rule (A1) is stochastic gradient descent with step size β\beta on the instantaneous loss

Lt​(𝑺)=12​(𝒗t⊤​𝑺​𝒌t−ct)2,∇SLt​(𝑺)=(𝒗t⊤​𝑺​𝒌t−ct)​𝒗t​𝒌t⊤.\mathrm{L}_{t}(\bm{S})=\tfrac{1}{2}\,\big(\bm{v}_{t}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{k}_{t}-c_{t}\big)^{2},\qquad\nabla_{S}\,\mathrm{L}_{t}(\bm{S})=\big(\bm{v}_{t}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{k}_{t}-c_{t}\big)\,\bm{v}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top}. (A6)

It differs from DeltaNet, which performs SGD on 12​‖𝐒​𝐤t−𝐯t‖2\tfrac{1}{2}\left\lVert\bm{S}\bm{k}_{t}-\bm{v}_{t}\right\rVert^{2} with update 𝐒t+1=𝐒t−β⁡(𝐒t​𝐤t−𝐯t)​𝐤t⊤\bm{S}_{t+1}=\bm{S}_{t}-\beta(\bm{S}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}-\bm{v}_{t})\bm{k}_{t}^{\top}: there the target is the vector 𝐯t\bm{v}_{t} (imposing dd constraints per pair), whereas here the target is the scalar ctc_{t} and the pair (𝐤t,𝐯t)(\bm{k}_{t},\bm{v}_{t}) jointly forms the input, imposing a single bilinear constraint 𝐯t⊤​𝐒​𝐤t=ct\bm{v}_{t}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{k}_{t}=c_{t} per pair.

Property A3 (Superposition: the memory is linear in the target sequence).

For a fixed pair sequence (𝐤t,𝐯t)t=1T(\bm{k}_{t},\bm{v}_{t})_{t=1}^{T} and step size β\beta, the map from the target sequence 𝐜=(c1,…,cT)\bm{c}=(c_{1},\dots,c_{T}) to the final memory 𝐒T​(𝐜)\bm{S}_{T}(\bm{c}) with 𝐒0=𝟎\bm{S}_{0}=\bm{0} is linear:

𝑺T​(𝒄+𝒄′)=𝑺T​(𝒄)+𝑺T​(𝒄′),𝑺T​(α​𝒄)=α​𝑺T​(𝒄),\bm{S}_{T}(\bm{c}+\bm{c}^{\prime})\;=\;\bm{S}_{T}(\bm{c})\,+\,\bm{S}_{T}(\bm{c}^{\prime}),\qquad\bm{S}_{T}(\alpha\,\bm{c})\;=\;\alpha\ \bm{S}_{T}(\bm{c})\,, (A7)

explicitly, with 𝐚t=𝐤t⊗𝐯t\bm{a}_{t}=\bm{k}_{t}\otimes\bm{v}_{t},

vec⁡(𝑺T​(𝒄))=β​∑t=1Tct​[∏τ=t+1T(𝑰−β​𝒂τ​𝒂τ⊤)]​𝒂t.\vecop\big(\bm{S}_{T}(\bm{c})\big)\;=\;\beta\sum_{t=1}^{T}c_{t}\Bigg[\prod_{\tau=t+1}^{T}\big(\bm{I}-\beta\bm{a}_{\tau}\bm{a}_{\tau}^{\top}\big)\Bigg]\bm{a}_{t}\,. (A8)

Memories written with different target sequences over the same pairs superpose exactly. The pure-gain homogeneity of the constant-target rule (𝐒t(c)=c​𝐒t(1)\bm{S}_{t}^{(c)}=c\,\bm{S}_{t}^{(1)}) is the special case 𝐜=c​ 1\bm{c}=c\,\bm{1}. The pair sequence determines where the memory can write (the reachable subspace span⁡{𝐚1,…,𝐚T}\spanop\{\bm{a}_{1},\dots,\bm{a}_{T}\} and the interference pattern); the target sequence linearly selects what is written into it.

Property A4 (Per-step reparameterization to the unit target).

For every step with ct≠0c_{t}\neq 0, rule (A1) with pair (𝐤t,𝐯t)(\bm{k}_{t},\bm{v}_{t}) and step β\beta coincides exactly with the unit-target rule applied to the rescaled value 𝐯~t=𝐯t/ct\tilde{\bm{v}}_{t}=\bm{v}_{t}/c_{t} with the time-varying effective step β~t=β​ct2\tilde{\beta}_{t}=\beta\,c_{t}^{2}:

𝑺−β⁡(𝒗⊤​𝑺​𝒌−ct)​𝒗​𝒌⊤=𝑺−β~t​(𝒗~⊤​𝑺​𝒌−1)​𝒗~​𝒌⊤.\bm{S}-\beta\big(\bm{v}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{k}-c_{t}\big)\bm{v}\bm{k}^{\top}\;=\;\bm{S}-\tilde{\beta}_{t}\,\big(\tilde{\bm{v}}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{k}-1\big)\,\tilde{\bm{v}}\bm{k}^{\top}. (A9)

In contrast to the constant-target case, the effective step size now varies over time, so the time-varying rule is not globally a reparameterized unit-target rule; steps with ct=0c_{t}=0 have no unit-target counterpart at all (see Property A5 (iii)).

Property A5 (Distinguished targets).

Three choices of ctc_{t} are structurally special.

  1. 1.

    (i) Norm target, ct=‖𝒗t‖2c_{t}=\left\lVert\bm{v}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}. The residual becomes the value-projected retrieval error rt=𝒗t⊤​(𝑺t​𝒌t−𝒗t)r_{t}=\bm{v}_{t}^{\top}(\bm{S}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}-\bm{v}_{t}); every exact retrieval memory (𝑺​𝒌i=𝒗i\bm{S}\bm{k}_{i}=\bm{v}_{i}) satisfies all constraints, and in the autoassociative case 𝒌t=𝒗t\bm{k}_{t}=\bm{v}_{t} the identity 𝑺=𝑰\bm{S}=\bm{I} is a universal fixed point.

  2. (ii) Correlation target, ct=𝒗t⊤​𝒌tc_{t}=\bm{v}_{t}^{\top}\bm{k}_{t}. The identity 𝑺=𝑰\bm{S}=\bm{I} is a universal fixed point even heteroassociatively: 𝒗⊤​𝑰​𝒌=𝒗⊤​𝒌\bm{v}^{\top}\bm{I}\bm{k}=\bm{v}^{\top}\bm{k} for all pairs. The rule then learns deviations of the bilinear map from the standard inner product, i.e. 𝑺\bm{S} is naturally parameterized around the identity, and the read-out 𝒗⊤​𝑺​𝒌−𝒗⊤​𝒌\bm{v}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{k}-\bm{v}^{\top}\bm{k} measures the learned (in-context) part of the similarity.

  3. (iii) Erasure target, ct=0c_{t}=0. The update drives 𝒗t⊤​𝑺​𝒌t→0\bm{v}_{t}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{k}_{t}\to 0: with the Newton step β⋆=1/(‖𝒌t‖2​‖𝒗t‖2)\beta^{\star}=1/(\left\lVert\bm{k}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}\left\lVert\bm{v}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}) the association is deleted in one shot, while every read-out with 𝒌′⟂𝒌t\bm{k}^{\prime}\perp\bm{k}_{t} or 𝒗′⟂𝒗t\bm{v}^{\prime}\perp\bm{v}_{t} is exactly unchanged. Hence, ct=0c_{t}=0 is a targeted unlearning of a single key–value binding. Alternating write targets (ct≠0c_{t}\neq 0) and erasure targets (ct=0c_{t}=0) turns the memory into an editable scalar store (see also Property A10 on overwriting).

Property A6 (One-step error contraction and stability range for β\beta).

The target never enters the homogeneous part of the dynamics. Re-reading with the same pair and the same target after one update,

𝒗t⊤​𝑺t+1​𝒌t=yt−β​rt​‖𝒌t‖2​‖𝒗t‖2\displaystyle\qquad\;\bm{v}_{t}^{\top}\bm{S}_{t+1}\bm{k}_{t}\;=\;y_{t}-\beta\,r_{t}\,\left\lVert\bm{k}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}\,\left\lVert\bm{v}_{t}\right\rVert^{2} (A10)
⟺𝒗t⊤​𝑺t+1​𝒌t−ct=yt−ct−β​rt​‖𝒌t‖2​‖𝒗t‖2\displaystyle\Longleftrightarrow\bm{v}_{t}^{\top}\bm{S}_{t+1}\bm{k}_{t}-c_{t}\;=\;y_{t}-c_{t}-\beta\,r_{t}\,\left\lVert\bm{k}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}\,\left\lVert\bm{v}_{t}\right\rVert^{2} (A11)
⟺rt+1=rt−β​rt​‖𝒌t‖2​‖𝒗t‖2\displaystyle\Longleftrightarrow r_{t+1}\;=\;r_{t}-\beta\,r_{t}\,\left\lVert\bm{k}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}\,\left\lVert\bm{v}_{t}\right\rVert^{2} (A12)
⟺rt+1=(1−β​‖𝒌t‖2​‖𝒗t‖2)​rt,\displaystyle\Longleftrightarrow r_{t+1}\;=\;\big(1-\beta\,\left\lVert\bm{k}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}\left\lVert\bm{v}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}\big)\,r_{t}\;, (A13)

where rt+1r_{t+1} is computed for the same (𝐤t,𝐯t,ct)(\bm{k}_{t},\bm{v}_{t},c_{t}). The residual contracts if and only if

0<β<2‖𝒌t‖2​‖𝒗t‖2,0\;<\;\beta\;<\;\frac{2}{\left\lVert\bm{k}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}\,\left\lVert\bm{v}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}}, (A14)

and the loss shrinks by the factor (1−β​‖𝐤t‖2​‖𝐯t‖2)2\big(1-\beta\left\lVert\bm{k}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}\,\left\lVert\bm{v}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}\big)^{2}. Since Lt\mathrm{L}_{t} is quadratic along the ray 𝐒−η​rt​𝐯t​𝐤t⊤\bm{S}-\eta\,r_{t}\,\bm{v}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top},, the choice

β⋆=1‖𝒌t‖2​‖𝒗t‖2\beta^{\star}\;=\;\frac{1}{\left\lVert\bm{k}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}\,\left\lVert\bm{v}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}} (A15)

is a Newton step: the constraint 𝐯t⊤​𝐒​𝐤t=ct\bm{v}_{t}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{k}_{t}=c_{t} is interpolated exactly in one update, for every value of ctc_{t}.

Property A7 (Delta Rule / Widrow–Hoff LMS in vectorized form).

Let 𝐬=vec⁡(𝐒)∈ℝd2\bm{s}=\vecop(\bm{S})\in\mathbb{R}^{d^{2}} and 𝐚t=𝐤t⊗𝐯t∈ℝd2\bm{a}_{t}=\bm{k}_{t}\otimes\bm{v}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d^{2}} the Kronecker product, so that 𝐯t⊤​𝐒​𝐤t=𝐚t⊤​𝐬\bm{v}_{t}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{k}_{t}=\bm{a}_{t}^{\top}\bm{s} and ‖𝐚t‖2=‖𝐤t‖2​‖𝐯t‖2\left\lVert\bm{a}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}=\left\lVert\bm{k}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}\,\left\lVert\bm{v}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}. The rule becomes

𝒔t+1=(𝑰−β​𝒂t​𝒂t⊤)​𝒔t+β​ct​𝒂t,\bm{s}_{t+1}\;=\;\big(\bm{I}-\beta\,\bm{a}_{t}\bm{a}_{t}^{\top}\big)\,\bm{s}_{t}\;+\;\beta\,c_{t}\,\bm{a}_{t}\,, (A16)

which is exactly the Widrow–Hoff LMS/delta rule with input 𝐚t\bm{a}_{t} and target ctc_{t}. This is the classical setting of LMS, which regresses a time-varying desired signal onto the input. The transition matrix 𝐈−β​𝐚t​𝐚t⊤\bm{I}-\beta\bm{a}_{t}\bm{a}_{t}^{\top} does not depend on ctc_{t}: it has eigenvalue 1−β​‖𝐚t‖21-\beta\left\lVert\bm{a}_{t}\right\rVert^{2} on span⁡(𝐚t)\spanop(\bm{a}_{t}) and eigenvalue 11 on the orthogonal complement (dimension d2−1d^{2}-1). Unrolling the recurrence,

𝒔T=∏t=1T(𝑰−β​𝒂t​𝒂t⊤)​𝒔0+β​∑t=1Tct​[∏τ=t+1T(𝑰−β​𝒂τ​𝒂τ⊤)]​𝒂t,\bm{s}_{T}\;=\;\prod_{t=1}^{T}\big(\bm{I}-\beta\bm{a}_{t}\bm{a}_{t}^{\top}\big)\,\bm{s}_{0}\;+\;\beta\sum_{t=1}^{T}c_{t}\Bigg[\prod_{\tau=t+1}^{T}\big(\bm{I}-\beta\bm{a}_{\tau}\bm{a}_{\tau}^{\top}\big)\Bigg]\bm{a}_{t}\;, (A17)

gives the same product-of-generalized-Householder structure as DeltaNet. Hence, the WY-representation / chunkwise-parallel training techniques apply verbatim with 𝐚t=𝐤t⊗𝐯t\bm{a}_{t}=\bm{k}_{t}\otimes\bm{v}_{t} in place of 𝐤t\bm{k}_{t}, and the targets ctc_{t} enter only the driving (inhomogeneous) term. Expressivity consequence: for β​‖𝐚t‖2∈(1,2)\beta\left\lVert\bm{a}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}\in(1,2) the factor has a negative eigenvalue (reaching −1-1 at β​‖𝐚t‖2=2\beta\left\lVert\bm{a}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}=2), the same mechanism that gives DeltaNet-style models state-tracking power beyond linear RNNs restricted to nonnegative eigenvalues. This is independent of the target sequence.

Property A8 (Homogeneous part of the update in non-expansive).

For β​‖𝐚t‖2∈[0,2]\beta\left\lVert\bm{a}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}\in[0,2] every factor 𝐈−β​𝐚t​𝐚t⊤\bm{I}-\beta\bm{a}_{t}\bm{a}_{t}^{\top} has spectral norm at most 11, so the homogeneous part of the recurrence never amplifies and ‖𝐒t‖\left\lVert\bm{S}_{t}\right\rVert cannot blow up. In contrast the Hebbian write 𝐒t+1=𝐒t+𝐯t​𝐤t⊤\bm{S}_{t+1}=\bm{S}_{t}+\bm{v}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top} of vanilla linear attention leads to states that grow without bound. Moreover, the update is surgical: it modifies 𝐒\bm{S} only along the rank-one direction 𝐯t​𝐤t⊤\bm{v}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top}. For any test pair with 𝐤′⟂𝐤t\bm{k}^{\prime}\perp\bm{k}_{t} or 𝐯′⟂𝐯t\bm{v}^{\prime}\perp\bm{v}_{t} the read-out 𝐯′⁣⊤​𝐒​𝐤′\bm{v}^{\prime\top}\bm{S}\bm{k}^{\prime} is exactly unchanged.

Property A9 (Doubly gated interference).

For a previously stored pair (𝐤i,𝐯i)(\bm{k}_{i},\bm{v}_{i}), an update with (𝐤t,𝐯t,ct)(\bm{k}_{t},\bm{v}_{t},c_{t}) perturbs the stored read-out by

Δ⁡(𝒗i⊤​𝑺​𝒌i)=−β​rt​(𝒗i⊤​𝒗t)​(𝒌t⊤​𝒌i),\Delta\big(\bm{v}_{i}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{k}_{i}\big)\;=\;-\,\beta\,r_{t}\,\big(\bm{v}_{i}^{\top}\bm{v}_{t}\big)\big(\bm{k}_{t}^{\top}\bm{k}_{i}\big)\,, (A18)

i.e. interference is proportional to the product of the key overlap and the value overlap. Orthogonality in either factor suffices to protect a memory, which is a milder interference profile than the Hebbian rule (crosstalk from key overlap alone) and than DeltaNet (gated by key overlap only). The formula is target-independent, since the target enters only through the residual rtr_{t}. Consequently, writes whose read-out is already correct (rt≈0r_{t}\approx 0) cause no interference at all, regardless of ctc_{t}.

Property A10 (Relaxed Kaczmarz iteration, Fejér monotonicity, convergence, and overwriting).

The constraint 𝐯t⊤​𝐒​𝐤t=ct\bm{v}_{t}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{k}_{t}=c_{t} defines the hyperplane ℋt={𝐒:⟨𝐯t​𝐤t⊤,𝐒⟩F=ct}\mathcal{H}_{t}=\{\bm{S}:{{\left\langle\bm{v}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top},\bm{S}\right\rangle}}_{\mathrm{F}}=c_{t}\} in ℝd×d\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} with Frobenius geometry. With β=β⋆\beta=\beta^{\star} the update (A1) is the orthogonal projection onto ℋt\mathcal{H}_{t}; general β\beta gives a relaxed projection. In contrast to a constant target, consistency of the system {𝐯i⊤𝐒𝐤i=ci}i\{\bm{v}_{i}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{k}_{i}=c_{i}\}_{i} is now a genuine condition: it holds if and only if the target vector (ci)i(c_{i})_{i} lies in the range of the matrix stacking the rows 𝐚i⊤\bm{a}_{i}^{\top}. In particular, this always holds, whenever the {𝐚i}\{\bm{a}_{i}\} are linearly independent (at most d2d^{2} of them). If the system is consistent, then for every solution 𝐒⋆\bm{S}^{\star} and any βt∈[0, 2/‖𝐚t‖2]\beta_{t}\in\big[0,\,2/\left\lVert\bm{a}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}\big],

‖𝑺t+1−𝑺⋆‖F≤‖𝑺t−𝑺⋆‖F(Fejér monotonicity),\left\lVert\bm{S}_{t+1}-\bm{S}^{\star}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}\;\leq\;\left\lVert\bm{S}_{t}-\bm{S}^{\star}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}\qquad\text{(Fej\'{e}r monotonicity)}, (A19)

and cycling or randomly sampling over the pairs converges linearly to a solution, at a rate governed by the smallest singular value of the stacked 𝐚i⊤\bm{a}_{i}^{\top}. From 𝐒0=𝟎\bm{S}_{0}=\bm{0} the limit is the minimum-Frobenius-norm solution. The canonical inconsistent case is a repeated pair with a changed target, (𝐤,𝐯,c)(\bm{k},\bm{v},c) followed later by (𝐤,𝐯,c′)(\bm{k},\bm{v},c^{\prime}) with c′≠cc^{\prime}\neq c: the two hyperplanes are parallel, and the iteration resolves the conflict by overwriting. The contraction of Property A6 drives the read-out to the most recent target, in one shot for β=β⋆\beta=\beta^{\star}. In expectation over a stationary distribution of triples (𝐤,𝐯,c)(\bm{k},\bm{v},c), the fixed-point condition is

E⁡[(𝒂⊤​𝒔−c)​𝒂]=𝟎,\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[\big(\bm{a}^{\top}\bm{s}-c\big)\bm{a}\big]=\bm{0}\,, (A20)

the normal equation of the least-squares regression of the target cc on the feature 𝐚=𝐤⊗𝐯\bm{a}=\bm{k}\otimes\bm{v}: the memory is an online linear regressor that learns, in context, to predict the scalar signal ctc_{t} from the key–value pair.

Property A11 (Capacity: memory can store d2d^{2} associations).

Each triple (𝐤i,𝐯i,ci)(\bm{k}_{i},\bm{v}_{i},c_{i}) contributes one linear constraint on the d2d^{2} parameters of 𝐒\bm{S}, so up to d2d^{2} arbitrary scalars cic_{i} can be stored exactly for pairs with linearly independent {𝐤i⊗𝐯i}\{\bm{k}_{i}\otimes\bm{v}_{i}\} (d2d^{2} scalar components). Compare to DeltaNet with goal 𝐒​𝐤i=𝐯i\bm{S}\bm{k}_{i}=\bm{v}_{i} that represent dd value vectors. In an orthonormal design ({𝐤i}\{\bm{k}_{i}\} orthonormal and {𝐯i}\{\bm{v}_{i}\} orthonormal), the minimum-norm solution has the closed form

𝑺⋆=∑ici​𝒗i​𝒌i⊤,𝒗j⊤​𝑺⋆​𝒌i=ci​δi​j,\bm{S}^{\star}\;=\;\sum_{i}c_{i}\,\bm{v}_{i}\bm{k}_{i}^{\top}\,,\qquad\bm{v}_{j}^{\top}\bm{S}^{\star}\bm{k}_{i}\;=\;c_{i}\ \delta_{ij}\,, (A21)

a target-weighted Hebbian superposition realizing the learned Kronecker delta with per-pair gains. The memory is thus best understood as a pair-addressed scalar table. It stores a number cic_{i} at the address (𝐤i,𝐯i)(\bm{k}_{i},\bm{v}_{i}), writes by rank-one updates, reads by the bilinear probe 𝐯⊤​𝐒​𝐤\bm{v}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{k}, rewrites by presenting the same pair with a new target, and deletes via c=0c=0 (Property A5 (iii)).

Next, we exemplify the fact that KronLSTM can store d2d^{2} numbers. Assume dd orthonormal keys {𝒌1,…,𝒌d}\{\bm{k}_{1},\ldots,\bm{k}_{d}\} and dd orthonormal values {𝒗1,…,𝒗d}\{\bm{v}_{1},\ldots,\bm{v}_{d}\}. Then we can build d2d^{2} key-value pairs (𝒌i,𝒗j)(\bm{k}_{i},\bm{v}_{j}) with their associated d2d^{2} numbers ci​jc_{ij}. We set β=1\beta=1 and start with 𝑺0=𝟎\bm{S}_{0}=\bm{0}, then we iteratively update 𝑺t\bm{S}_{t} with randomly chosen ii and jj:

𝑺t+1=𝑺t−β⁡(𝒗j⊤​𝑺t​𝒌i−ci​j)​𝒗j​𝒌i⊤.\bm{S}_{t+1}\;=\;\bm{S}_{t}-\beta\,\big(\bm{v}_{j}^{\top}\,\bm{S}_{t}\,\bm{k}_{i}\,-\,c_{ij}\big)\>\bm{v}_{j}\,\bm{k}_{i}^{\top}\,. (A22)

If all pairs (𝒌i,𝒗j)(\bm{k}_{i},\bm{v}_{j}) or numbers ci​jc_{ij} are seen at least once, the update converged. If pair (𝒌i,𝒗j)(\bm{k}_{i},\bm{v}_{j}) has already been used in the update rule, then 𝒗j⊤​𝑺t​𝒌i=ci​j\bm{v}_{j}^{\top}\bm{S}_{t}\bm{k}_{i}=c_{ij} and 𝑺t+1=𝑺t\bm{S}_{t+1}=\bm{S}_{t}. Therefore, if all pairs are seen, 𝑺t\bm{S}_{t} does not change any more and the update converged. If pair (𝒌i,𝒗j)(\bm{k}_{i},\bm{v}_{j}) has NOT been stored, then 𝒗j⊤​𝑺t​𝒌i=0\bm{v}_{j}^{\top}\bm{S}_{t}\bm{k}_{i}=0 and 𝑺t+1=𝑺t+ci​j​𝒗j​𝒌i⊤\bm{S}_{t+1}=\bm{S}_{t}+c_{ij}\bm{v}_{j}\bm{k}_{i}^{\top}. Therefore, if all pairs (𝒌i,𝒗j)(\bm{k}_{i},\bm{v}_{j}) or numbers ci​jc_{ij} are seen at least once, the memory matrix 𝑺t\bm{S}_{t} is

𝑺t\displaystyle\bm{S}_{t}\; =∑i=1,j=1d,dci​j​𝒗j​𝒌i⊤=𝑽​𝑪⊤​𝑲⊤,\displaystyle=\;\sum_{i=1,j=1}^{d,d}c_{ij}\,\bm{v}_{j}\,\bm{k}_{i}^{\top}\;=\;\bm{V}\,\bm{C}^{\top}\,\bm{K}^{\top}\,, (A23)

with

𝑲\displaystyle\bm{K}\, =[𝒌1,…,𝒌d]∈ℝd×d,𝑽=[𝒗1,…,𝒗d]∈ℝd×d,𝑪=(ci​j)i,j=1d∈ℝd×d.\displaystyle=\,\left[\bm{k}_{1},\,\dots,\,\bm{k}_{d}\right]\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\,,\quad\bm{V}\,=\,\left[\bm{v}_{1},\,\dots,\,\bm{v}_{d}\right]\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\,,\quad\bm{C}\,=\,\left(c_{ij}\right)_{i,j=1}^{d}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\,. (A24)

Since 𝒗j⊤​𝑺t​𝒌i=ci​j\bm{v}_{j}^{\top}\bm{S}_{t}\bm{k}_{i}=c_{ij}, we can now retrieve d2d^{2} stored numbers.

We have

𝑪⊤\displaystyle\bm{C}^{\top}\; =𝑽⊤​𝑺t​𝑲,\displaystyle=\;\bm{V}^{\top}\,\bm{S}_{t}\,\bm{K}\,, (A25)

since 𝑲\bm{K} and 𝑽\bm{V} are orthogonal. The transpose appears because the first index of 𝑪\bm{C} is the key index while the first index of 𝑺t\bm{S}_{t} is the value index.

Property A12 (Norm and energy dynamics).

Using ⟨𝐯t​𝐤t⊤,𝐒t⟩F=yt=rt+ct{{\left\langle\bm{v}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top},\bm{S}_{t}\right\rangle}}_{\mathrm{F}}=y_{t}=r_{t}+c_{t},

‖𝑺t+1‖F2−‖𝑺t‖F2=− 2​β​rt​(rt+ct)+β2​rt2​‖𝒌t‖2​‖𝒗t‖2,\left\lVert\bm{S}_{t+1}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}-\left\lVert\bm{S}_{t}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}\;=\;-\,2\beta\,r_{t}(r_{t}+c_{t})\;+\;\beta^{2}r_{t}^{2}\,\left\lVert\bm{k}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}\,\left\lVert\bm{v}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}, (A26)

so within the stable range, the state norm stays bounded whenever the constraint system is consistent. This is a consequence of Fejér monotonicity: the distance to any fixed solution is non-increasing.

Summary.

The time-varying-target rule (A1) is the most general member of the Kronecker Delta Rule family: SGD on the scalar quadratic loss 12​(𝒗t⊤​𝑺​𝒌t−ct)2\tfrac{1}{2}(\bm{v}_{t}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{k}_{t}-c_{t})^{2}, equivalently Widrow–Hoff LMS on the feature 𝒂t=𝒌t⊗𝒗t\bm{a}_{t}=\bm{k}_{t}\otimes\bm{v}_{t} with desired signal ctc_{t}, equivalently relaxed Kaczmarz on the hyperplanes ⟨𝒗t​𝒌t⊤,𝑺⟩F=ct{{\left\langle\bm{v}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top},\bm{S}\right\rangle}}_{\mathrm{F}}=c_{t}. The entire analytic framework is target-independent. That comprises stability range and Newton step β⋆\beta^{\star}, generalized-Householder transition factors with their parallelization and negative-eigenvalue state-tracking regime, doubly gated interference, Fejér-monotone linear convergence, d2d^{2} capacity. The targets enter only the driving term, linearly: memories superpose in (ct)(c_{t}), and in an orthonormal design the memory converges to the target-weighted Hebbian superposition ∑ici​𝒗i​𝒌i⊤\sum_{i}c_{i}\bm{v}_{i}\bm{k}_{i}^{\top} realizing 𝒗j⊤​𝑺​𝒌i=ci​δi​j\bm{v}_{j}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{k}_{i}=c_{i}\,\delta_{ij}. Distinguished targets recover ct≡1c_{t}\equiv 1, ct≡cc_{t}\equiv c, ct=‖𝒗t‖2c_{t}=\left\lVert\bm{v}_{t}\right\rVert^{2} and add two new members: the correlation target ct=𝒗t⊤​𝒌tc_{t}=\bm{v}_{t}^{\top}\bm{k}_{t}, for which the identity is a universal fixed point and 𝑺\bm{S} parameterizes learned deviations from the standard inner product, and the erasure target ct=0c_{t}=0, which deletes a single binding in one Newton step. Functionally, 𝑺\bm{S} is a pair-addressed scalar table with write, read, rewrite, and delete operations, therefore it is an editable d2d^{2}-slot scalar memory. In the stochastic view, it is an online in-context regressor of the signal ctc_{t} on the bilinear feature.

A3.4  Minimally Invasive Memory Revision

The Kronecker Delta Rule is not merely a correction of the addressed association: at the Newton step it is the smallest possible one, in every sense in which smallness can reasonably be asked for. This section elaborates on this topic. Throughout, 𝑺t∈ℝd×d\bm{S}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}, the read-out of the pair (𝒌t,𝒗t)(\bm{k}_{t},\bm{v}_{t}) is 𝒗t⊤​𝑺t​𝒌t\bm{v}_{t}^{\top}\bm{S}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}, the target is ctc_{t}, and

rt:=𝒗t⊤​𝑺t​𝒌t−ctr_{t}\;:=\;\bm{v}_{t}^{\top}\bm{S}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}\,-\,c_{t} (A27)

is the residual that should be pushed to zero.

A3.4.1  The admissible set

A correction is a matrix 𝑬∈ℝd×d\bm{E}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} added to the memory. It corrects the addressed association if 𝒗t⊤​(𝑺t+𝑬)​𝒌t=ct\bm{v}_{t}^{\top}(\bm{S}_{t}+\bm{E})\bm{k}_{t}=c_{t}. Using 𝒗t⊤​𝑬​𝒌t=⟨𝒗t​𝒌t⊤,𝑬⟩F\bm{v}_{t}^{\top}\bm{E}\bm{k}_{t}={{\left\langle\bm{v}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top},\bm{E}\right\rangle}}_{\mathrm{F}}, the set of such corrections is

ℰt:={𝑬∈ℝd×d:⟨𝒗t​𝒌t⊤,𝑬⟩F=−rt},\mathcal{E}_{t}\;:=\;\Big\{\bm{E}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\;:\;{{\left\langle\bm{v}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top},\,\bm{E}\right\rangle}}_{\mathrm{F}}\;=\;-\,r_{t}\Big\}\,, (A28)

an affine hyperplane in the Hilbert space (ℝd×d,⟨⋅,⋅⟩F)(\mathbb{R}^{d\times d},{{\left\langle\cdot,\cdot\right\rangle}}_{\mathrm{F}}): it is nonempty, and it is a proper affine subspace because 𝒗t​𝒌t⊤≠𝟎\bm{v}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top}\neq\bm{0} whenever the pair is nondegenerate. Every statement below compares members of ℰt\mathcal{E}_{t}. We hold the requirement fixed (the addressed association must come out right) and ask which correction achieves it with the least collateral change. Write

𝑬⋆:=−rt‖𝒌t‖2​‖𝒗t‖2​𝒗t​𝒌t⊤=ct−𝒗t⊤​𝑺t​𝒌t‖𝒌t‖2​‖𝒗t‖2​𝒗t​𝒌t⊤,\bm{E}^{\star}\;:=\;-\,\frac{r_{t}}{\left\lVert\bm{k}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}\left\lVert\bm{v}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}}\;\bm{v}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top}\;=\;\frac{c_{t}-\bm{v}_{t}^{\top}\bm{S}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}}{\left\lVert\bm{k}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}\left\lVert\bm{v}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}}\;\bm{v}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top}\,, (A29)

which is exactly the Kronecker Delta Rule update at the Newton step β=β⋆=1/(‖𝒌t‖2​‖𝒗t‖2)\beta=\beta^{\star}=1/(\left\lVert\bm{k}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}\left\lVert\bm{v}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}).

A3.4.2  Minimality in norm

Theorem A1 (The Newton step is the smallest correction).

𝑬⋆∈ℰt\bm{E}^{\star}\in\mathcal{E}_{t}, and for every 𝐄∈ℰt\bm{E}\in\mathcal{E}_{t}

‖𝑬‖F≥|rt|‖𝒌t‖​‖𝒗t‖=‖𝑬⋆‖F,\left\lVert\bm{E}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}\;\;\geq\;\;\frac{{{\left|r_{t}\right|}}}{\left\lVert\bm{k}_{t}\right\rVert\,\left\lVert\bm{v}_{t}\right\rVert}\;\;=\;\;\left\lVert\bm{E}^{\star}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}\,, (A30)

with equality if and only if 𝐄=𝐄⋆\bm{E}=\bm{E}^{\star}.

Proof.

Admissibility is a computation: ⟨𝒗t𝒌t⊤,𝑬⋆⟩F=−rt‖𝒗t𝒌t⊤‖F2/(‖𝒌t‖2‖𝒗t‖2)=−rt{{\left\langle\bm{v}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top},\bm{E}^{\star}\right\rangle}}_{\mathrm{F}}=-r_{t}\left\lVert\bm{v}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}/(\left\lVert\bm{k}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}\left\lVert\bm{v}_{t}\right\rVert^{2})=-r_{t}, using ‖𝒗t​𝒌t⊤‖F=‖𝒌t‖​‖𝒗t‖\left\lVert\bm{v}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}=\left\lVert\bm{k}_{t}\right\rVert\left\lVert\bm{v}_{t}\right\rVert. For the bound, apply Cauchy–Schwarz to the constraint in (A28):

|rt|=|⟨𝒗t​𝒌t⊤,𝑬⟩F|≤‖𝒗t​𝒌t⊤‖F​‖𝑬‖F=‖𝒌t‖​‖𝒗t‖​‖𝑬‖F,{{\left|r_{t}\right|}}\;=\;{{\left|{{\left\langle\bm{v}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top},\bm{E}\right\rangle}}_{\mathrm{F}}\right|}}\;\leq\;\left\lVert\bm{v}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}\,\left\lVert\bm{E}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}\;=\;\left\lVert\bm{k}_{t}\right\rVert\,\left\lVert\bm{v}_{t}\right\rVert\,\left\lVert\bm{E}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}\,, (A31)

which is (A30). Cauchy–Schwarz holds with equality exactly when 𝑬\bm{E} is a scalar multiple of 𝒗t​𝒌t⊤\bm{v}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top}, and the constraint then pins that scalar to −rt/(‖𝒌t‖2‖𝒗t‖2)-r_{t}/(\left\lVert\bm{k}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}\left\lVert\bm{v}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}), i.e. 𝑬=𝑬⋆\bm{E}=\bm{E}^{\star}. ∎

Equivalently the geometric view: 𝑺t+𝑬⋆\bm{S}_{t}+\bm{E}^{\star} is the orthogonal projection of 𝑺t\bm{S}_{t} onto the constraint hyperplane ℋt={𝑺:𝒗t⊤​𝑺​𝒌t=ct}\mathcal{H}_{t}=\{\bm{S}:\bm{v}_{t}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{k}_{t}=c_{t}\}, so the Newton step moves the memory along the shortest path from where it is to where the constraint is satisfied.

Theorem A2 (Minimality in every unitarily invariant norm).

Let |||⋅|||{\left|\kern-1.07639pt\left|\kern-1.07639pt\left|\cdot\right|\kern-1.07639pt\right|\kern-1.07639pt\right|} be any unitarily invariant norm on ℝd×d\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}. Then

min𝑬∈ℰt⁡‖|𝑬|‖=‖|𝑬⋆|‖,\min_{\bm{E}\in\mathcal{E}_{t}}{\left|\kern-1.07639pt\left|\kern-1.07639pt\left|\bm{E}\right|\kern-1.07639pt\right|\kern-1.07639pt\right|}\;=\;{\left|\kern-1.07639pt\left|\kern-1.07639pt\left|\bm{E}^{\star}\right|\kern-1.07639pt\right|\kern-1.07639pt\right|}\,, (A32)

i.e. the same 𝐄⋆\bm{E}^{\star} is optimal simultaneously for all of them. In particular, for every Schatten-pp norm, 1≤p≤∞1\leq p\leq\infty,

min𝑬∈ℰt⁡‖𝑬‖Sp=‖𝑬⋆‖Sp=|rt|‖𝒌t‖​‖𝒗t‖,\min_{\bm{E}\in\mathcal{E}_{t}}\left\lVert\bm{E}\right\rVert_{S_{p}}\;=\;\left\lVert\bm{E}^{\star}\right\rVert_{S_{p}}\;=\;\frac{{{\left|r_{t}\right|}}}{\left\lVert\bm{k}_{t}\right\rVert\,\left\lVert\bm{v}_{t}\right\rVert}\,, (A33)

the same number for all pp. Therefore, the nuclear, Frobenius and spectral norms of the optimal correction coincide. The minimizer is unique for strictly convex norms (Schatten 1<p<∞1<p<\infty). For the spectral and nuclear norms 𝐄⋆\bm{E}^{\star} is a minimizer but need not be the only one.

Proof.

Let |||⋅|||′{\left|\kern-1.07639pt\left|\kern-1.07639pt\left|\cdot\right|\kern-1.07639pt\right|\kern-1.07639pt\right|}^{\prime} be the dual norm, so that |⟨𝑨,𝑬⟩F|≤‖|𝑨|‖′​‖|𝑬|‖{{\left|{{\left\langle\bm{A},\bm{E}\right\rangle}}_{\mathrm{F}}\right|}}\leq{\left|\kern-1.07639pt\left|\kern-1.07639pt\left|\bm{A}\right|\kern-1.07639pt\right|\kern-1.07639pt\right|}^{\prime}{\left|\kern-1.07639pt\left|\kern-1.07639pt\left|\bm{E}\right|\kern-1.07639pt\right|\kern-1.07639pt\right|} for all 𝑨,𝑬\bm{A},\bm{E}. Applying this to the constraint gives, for every 𝑬∈ℰt\bm{E}\in\mathcal{E}_{t},

‖|𝑬|‖≥|rt|‖|𝒗t​𝒌t⊤|‖′.{\left|\kern-1.07639pt\left|\kern-1.07639pt\left|\bm{E}\right|\kern-1.07639pt\right|\kern-1.07639pt\right|}\;\;\geq\;\;\frac{{{\left|r_{t}\right|}}}{{\left|\kern-1.07639pt\left|\kern-1.07639pt\left|\bm{v}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top}\right|\kern-1.07639pt\right|\kern-1.07639pt\right|}^{\prime}}\,. (A34)

By von Neumann’s theorem a unitarily invariant norm is a symmetric gauge function Φ\Phi of the singular values, and the dual norm is the gauge Φ′\Phi^{\prime} of the singular values. ‖|𝒗t​𝒌t⊤|‖=‖𝒌t‖​‖𝒗t‖​Φ​(𝒆1),‖|𝒗t​𝒌t⊤|‖′=‖𝒌t‖​‖𝒗t‖​Φ′​(𝒆1).{\left|\kern-1.07639pt\left|\kern-1.07639pt\left|\bm{v}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top}\right|\kern-1.07639pt\right|\kern-1.07639pt\right|}=\left\lVert\bm{k}_{t}\right\rVert\left\lVert\bm{v}_{t}\right\rVert\,\Phi(\bm{e}_{1})\,,\qquad{\left|\kern-1.07639pt\left|\kern-1.07639pt\left|\bm{v}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top}\right|\kern-1.07639pt\right|\kern-1.07639pt\right|}^{\prime}=\left\lVert\bm{k}_{t}\right\rVert\left\lVert\bm{v}_{t}\right\rVert\,\Phi^{\prime}(\bm{e}_{1})\,. (A35)

Now Φ⁡(𝒆1)​Φ′​(𝒆1)=1\Phi(\bm{e}_{1})\Phi^{\prime}(\bm{e}_{1})=1: indeed Φ′​(𝒆1)=sup{x1:Φ⁡(𝒙)≤1}\Phi^{\prime}(\bm{e}_{1})=\sup\{x_{1}:\Phi(\bm{x})\leq 1\}, and since a symmetric gauge is nondecreasing in each |xi|{{\left|x_{i}\right|}}, replacing 𝒙\bm{x} by (x1,0,…,0)(x_{1},0,\dots,0) does not increase Φ\Phi, so the supremum is attained on the first axis and equals 1/Φ⁡(𝒆1)1/\Phi(\bm{e}_{1}). ‖|𝑬⋆|‖=|rt|‖𝒌t‖​‖𝒗t‖​Φ​(𝒆1)=|rt|‖|𝒗t​𝒌t⊤|‖′,{\left|\kern-1.07639pt\left|\kern-1.07639pt\left|\bm{E}^{\star}\right|\kern-1.07639pt\right|\kern-1.07639pt\right|}\;=\;\frac{{{\left|r_{t}\right|}}}{\left\lVert\bm{k}_{t}\right\rVert\left\lVert\bm{v}_{t}\right\rVert}\,\Phi(\bm{e}_{1})\;=\;\frac{{{\left|r_{t}\right|}}}{{\left|\kern-1.07639pt\left|\kern-1.07639pt\left|\bm{v}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top}\right|\kern-1.07639pt\right|\kern-1.07639pt\right|}^{\prime}}\,, (A36)

which is exactly the lower bound (A34): 𝑬⋆\bm{E}^{\star} attains it.
