A3.4.3  Minimality of support: the correction is surgical

Norm-optimality says the correction is small. The next theorem has a stronger statement even: it is the only correction that stays inside the addressed directions at all. No optimization is involved.

Theorem A3 (Unique correction with addressed support).

𝑬⋆\bm{E}^{\star} is the unique 𝐄∈ℰt\bm{E}\in\mathcal{E}_{t} whose column space is contained in span⁡{𝐯t}\spanop\{\bm{v}_{t}\} and whose row space is contained in span⁡{𝐤t}\spanop\{\bm{k}_{t}\}.

Proof.

A matrix has column space in span⁡{𝒗t}\spanop\{\bm{v}_{t}\} and row space in span⁡{𝒌t}\spanop\{\bm{k}_{t}\} if and only if it is of the form 𝑬=γ​𝒗t​𝒌t⊤\bm{E}=\gamma\,\bm{v}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top} for some γ∈ℝ\gamma\in\mathbb{R}. Admissibility forces γ​‖𝒌t‖2​‖𝒗t‖2=−rt\gamma\left\lVert\bm{k}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}\left\lVert\bm{v}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}=-r_{t}, hence γ=−rt/(‖𝒌t‖2‖𝒗t‖2)\gamma=-r_{t}/(\left\lVert\bm{k}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}\left\lVert\bm{v}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}) and 𝑬=𝑬⋆\bm{E}=\bm{E}^{\star}. ∎

Every other admissible correction like every DeltaNet-style correction necessarily writes into at least one key direction other than 𝒌t\bm{k}_{t} or one value direction other than 𝒗t\bm{v}_{t}, i.e. into directions the task never asked about.

A3.4.4  Minimality of interference

Smallness in norm translates into smallness of the damage done to other associations.

Theorem A4 (Interference caused by the correction).

Let (𝐤′,𝐯′)(\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{v}^{\prime}) be any probe pair and let Δ⁡(𝐤′,𝐯′):=𝐯′⁣⊤​𝐄​𝐤′\Delta(\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{v}^{\prime}):=\bm{v}^{\prime\top}\bm{E}\bm{k}^{\prime} be the change its read-out suffers.

  1. (i) Exact form and protection. For 𝑬=𝑬⋆\bm{E}=\bm{E}^{\star},

    Δ⁡(𝒌′,𝒗′)=−rt‖𝒌t‖2​‖𝒗t‖2​(𝒗′⁣⊤​𝒗t)​(𝒌t⊤​𝒌′),\Delta(\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{v}^{\prime})\;=\;-\,\frac{r_{t}}{\left\lVert\bm{k}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}\left\lVert\bm{v}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}}\,\big(\bm{v}^{\prime\top}\bm{v}_{t}\big)\big(\bm{k}_{t}^{\top}\bm{k}^{\prime}\big)\,, (A37)

    which vanishes whenever 𝒗′⟂𝒗t\bm{v}^{\prime}\perp\bm{v}_{t} or 𝒌′⟂𝒌t\bm{k}^{\prime}\perp\bm{k}_{t}, and obeys |Δ⁡(𝒌′,𝒗′)|≤|rt|​‖𝒌′‖​‖𝒗′‖/(‖𝒌t‖​‖𝒗t‖){{\left|\Delta(\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{v}^{\prime})\right|}}\leq{{\left|r_{t}\right|}}\,\left\lVert\bm{k}^{\prime}\right\rVert\left\lVert\bm{v}^{\prime}\right\rVert/(\left\lVert\bm{k}_{t}\right\rVert\left\lVert\bm{v}_{t}\right\rVert). The condition is a property of the inputs alone: it can be checked in advance and does not depend on what 𝑺t\bm{S}_{t} currently holds.

  2. (ii) Minimum expected interference. Suppose probe pairs are drawn with 𝒌′\bm{k}^{\prime} and 𝒗′\bm{v}^{\prime} independent and isotropic, E⁡[𝒌′​𝒌′⁣⊤]=σk2​𝑰\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\bm{k}^{\prime}\bm{k}^{\prime\top}]=\sigma_{k}^{2}\bm{I} and E⁡[𝒗′​𝒗′⁣⊤]=σv2​𝑰\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\bm{v}^{\prime}\bm{v}^{\prime\top}]=\sigma_{v}^{2}\bm{I}. Then for every 𝑬∈ℝd×d\bm{E}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}

    E⁡[(𝒗′⁣⊤​𝑬​𝒌′)2]=σk2​σv2​‖𝑬‖F2.\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\Big[\big(\bm{v}^{\prime\top}\bm{E}\bm{k}^{\prime}\big)^{2}\Big]\;=\;\sigma_{k}^{2}\,\sigma_{v}^{2}\;\left\lVert\bm{E}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}\,. (A38)

    Consequently

    𝑬⋆=argmin𝑬∈ℰtE⁡[(𝒗′⁣⊤​𝑬​𝒌′)2],min𝑬∈ℰt⁡E⁡[Δ2]=σk2​σv2​rt2‖𝒌t‖2​‖𝒗t‖2,\bm{E}^{\star}\;=\;\mathop{\mathrm{argmin}\,}_{\bm{E}\in\mathcal{E}_{t}}\;\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\Big[\big(\bm{v}^{\prime\top}\bm{E}\bm{k}^{\prime}\big)^{2}\Big]\,,\qquad\min_{\bm{E}\in\mathcal{E}_{t}}\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[\Delta^{2}\big]\;=\;\frac{\sigma_{k}^{2}\sigma_{v}^{2}\,r_{t}^{2}}{\left\lVert\bm{k}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}\left\lVert\bm{v}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}}\,, (A39)

    and the minimizer is unique.

Proof.

(i) Substitute (A29) and use 𝒗′⁣⊤​(𝒗t​𝒌t⊤)​𝒌′=(𝒗′⁣⊤​𝒗t)​(𝒌t⊤​𝒌′)\bm{v}^{\prime\top}(\bm{v}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top})\bm{k}^{\prime}=(\bm{v}^{\prime\top}\bm{v}_{t})(\bm{k}_{t}^{\top}\bm{k}^{\prime}); the inequality is Cauchy–Schwarz on each factor. (ii) Vectorize: with 𝒆=vec⁡(𝑬)\bm{e}=\vecop(\bm{E}) and 𝒂′=𝒌′⊗𝒗′\bm{a}^{\prime}=\bm{k}^{\prime}\otimes\bm{v}^{\prime} we have 𝒗′⁣⊤​𝑬​𝒌′=𝒂′⁣⊤​𝒆\bm{v}^{\prime\top}\bm{E}\bm{k}^{\prime}=\bm{a}^{\prime\top}\bm{e}, hence

E⁡[(𝒂′⁣⊤​𝒆)2]=𝒆⊤​E​[𝒂′​𝒂′⁣⊤]​𝒆=𝒆⊤​(E⁡[𝒌′​𝒌′⁣⊤]⊗E⁡[𝒗′​𝒗′⁣⊤])​𝒆=σk2​σv2​‖𝒆‖2,\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[(\bm{a}^{\prime\top}\bm{e})^{2}\big]\;=\;\bm{e}^{\top}\,\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[\bm{a}^{\prime}\bm{a}^{\prime\top}\big]\,\bm{e}\;=\;\bm{e}^{\top}\Big(\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\bm{k}^{\prime}\bm{k}^{\prime\top}]\otimes\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\bm{v}^{\prime}\bm{v}^{\prime\top}]\Big)\bm{e}\;=\;\sigma_{k}^{2}\sigma_{v}^{2}\left\lVert\bm{e}\right\rVert^{2}, (A40)

using independence and ‖𝒆‖=‖𝑬‖F\left\lVert\bm{e}\right\rVert=\left\lVert\bm{E}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}. The objective is therefore a positive multiple of ‖𝑬‖F2\left\lVert\bm{E}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}, so minimizing it over ℰt\mathcal{E}_{t} is the problem already solved by Theorem A1, with the same unique solution. ∎

Part (ii) is what justifies the name: for isotropic probe statistics, minimum norm and minimum expected interference are literally the same objective, so the Newton step is minimally invasive in the operational sense and not merely in the geometric one. It causes the least expected damage to the rest of the memory.

A3.4.5  Relaxed steps: the correction never moves away from a correct memory

In practice, β\beta is a learned gate rather than β⋆\beta^{\star}. Write β=λ​β⋆\beta=\lambda\beta^{\star}, so that the actual update is 𝑺t+1=𝑺t+λ​𝑬⋆\bm{S}_{t+1}=\bm{S}_{t}+\lambda\bm{E}^{\star} with relaxation ω=β​‖𝒌t‖2​‖𝒗t‖2\omega=\beta\left\lVert\bm{k}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}\left\lVert\bm{v}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}.

Theorem A5 (Exact Fejér identity).

Let 𝐒∘\bm{S}^{\circ} be any memory that already satisfies the addressed association, 𝐯t⊤​𝐒∘​𝐤t=ct\bm{v}_{t}^{\top}\bm{S}^{\circ}\bm{k}_{t}=c_{t}. Then

‖𝑺t+1−𝑺∘‖F2=‖𝑺t−𝑺∘‖F2−λ⁡(2−λ)​rt2‖𝒌t‖2​‖𝒗t‖2.\left\lVert\bm{S}_{t+1}-\bm{S}^{\circ}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}\;=\;\left\lVert\bm{S}_{t}-\bm{S}^{\circ}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}\;-\;\lambda\,(2-\lambda)\;\frac{r_{t}^{2}}{\left\lVert\bm{k}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}\left\lVert\bm{v}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}}\,. (A41)

Hence for every λ∈(0,2)\lambda\in(0,2) the update strictly decreases the distance to every correct memory, the decrease is largest at the Newton step λ=1\lambda=1, and at λ∈{0,2}\lambda\in\{0,2\} the distance is unchanged.

Proof.

Expand, using ⟨𝑬⋆,𝑺t−𝑺∘⟩F=−rt‖𝒌t‖2​‖𝒗t‖2(𝒗t⊤𝑺t𝒌t−𝒗t⊤𝑺∘𝒌t)=−rt2/(‖𝒌t‖2‖𝒗t‖2)=−‖𝑬⋆‖F2{{\left\langle\bm{E}^{\star},\bm{S}_{t}-\bm{S}^{\circ}\right\rangle}}_{\mathrm{F}}=-\,\tfrac{r_{t}}{\left\lVert\bm{k}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}\left\lVert\bm{v}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}}\,\big(\bm{v}_{t}^{\top}\bm{S}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}-\bm{v}_{t}^{\top}\bm{S}^{\circ}\bm{k}_{t}\big)=-\,r_{t}^{2}/(\left\lVert\bm{k}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}\left\lVert\bm{v}_{t}\right\rVert^{2})=-\left\lVert\bm{E}^{\star}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}:

‖𝑺t−𝑺∘+λ​𝑬⋆‖F2=‖𝑺t−𝑺∘‖F2+2​λ​⟨𝑬⋆,𝑺t−𝑺∘⟩F+λ2​‖𝑬⋆‖F2,\left\lVert\bm{S}_{t}-\bm{S}^{\circ}+\lambda\bm{E}^{\star}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}=\left\lVert\bm{S}_{t}-\bm{S}^{\circ}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}+2\lambda{{\left\langle\bm{E}^{\star},\bm{S}_{t}-\bm{S}^{\circ}\right\rangle}}_{\mathrm{F}}+\lambda^{2}\left\lVert\bm{E}^{\star}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}, (A42)

which is (A41) after inserting ‖𝑬⋆‖F2=rt2/(‖𝒌t‖2​‖𝒗t‖2)\left\lVert\bm{E}^{\star}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}=r_{t}^{2}/(\left\lVert\bm{k}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}\left\lVert\bm{v}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}). ∎

This is the strongest sense in which a single write is harmless: it does not merely perturb other associations little, it moves the memory closer to every memory that is consistent with the association being written and that simultaneously, for all of them.

A3.4.6  Greedy minimality is global minimality

Per-step optimality does not by itself imply that a sequence of such steps is optimal. We show that our does.

Proposition 1 (The limit is the minimum-norm memory).

Let {(𝐤i,𝐯i,ci)}i=1n\{(\bm{k}_{i},\bm{v}_{i},c_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n} be a consistent system of associations. Apply the rule from 𝐒0=𝟎\bm{S}_{0}=\bm{0} with relaxation ω∈(0,2)\omega\in(0,2), visiting each pair infinitely often either cyclically or by random sampling. Then 𝐒t\bm{S}_{t} converges to

𝑺♯=argmin{‖𝑺‖F:𝒗i⊤​𝑺​𝒌i=ci​for all ​i},\bm{S}^{\sharp}\;=\;\mathop{\mathrm{argmin}\,}\Big\{\left\lVert\bm{S}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}\;:\;\bm{v}_{i}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{k}_{i}=c_{i}\;\;\text{for all }i\Big\}\,, (A43)

the minimum Frobenius-norm memory satisfying all the associations.

Proof.

This is the classical convergence theorem for relaxed Kaczmarz iterations (Kaczmarz, 1937; Cegielski, 2012), applied to the vectorized system 𝒂i⊤​𝒔=ci\bm{a}_{i}^{\top}\bm{s}=c_{i} with 𝒂i=𝒌i⊗𝒗i\bm{a}_{i}=\bm{k}_{i}\otimes\bm{v}_{i}. Each iterate stays in 𝒔0+span⁡{𝒂1,…,𝒂n}\bm{s}_{0}+\spanop\{\bm{a}_{1},\dots,\bm{a}_{n}\}, which for 𝒔0=𝟎\bm{s}_{0}=\bm{0} is the row space of the system; the iterates converge to a solution, and the unique solution in the row space is the minimum-norm one. ∎

So the memory built by a stream of minimally invasive revisions is itself the least-norm memory compatible with everything it was asked to store: locally and globally, the rule writes as little as the task permits.

A3.4.7  Less invasive than DeltaNet

Theorems A1–A4 hold given the requirement encoded in ℰt\mathcal{E}_{t}: make the scalar read-out of the addressed pair equal to ctc_{t}, and do nothing else. DeltaNet’s step has to solve the dd constraints 𝑺​𝒌t=𝒗t\bm{S}\bm{k}_{t}=\bm{v}_{t}, therefore its correction is necessarily larger. The claim here is therefore not that DeltaNet is suboptimal for its own task, but that the two tasks differ: a recognition memory needs one scalar corrected, and the Kronecker Delta Rule corrects it with provably minimal disturbance, whereas a retrieval memory must rewrite an entire value vector and pays for it in footprint.

A3.5  Convergence of the KronLSTM memory

We analyze the expected solution and steady state of the randomized Kronecker Delta Rule with more than d2d^{2} associations. Running memories i.e. online updates are covered via the steady state considerations.

A3.5.1  Overview

We analyze the Kronecker Delta Rule 𝑺t+1=𝑺t−β⁡(𝒗it⊤​𝑺t​𝒌it−cit)​𝒗it​𝒌it⊤\bm{S}_{t+1}=\bm{S}_{t}-\beta\,(\bm{v}_{i_{t}}^{\top}\bm{S}_{t}\bm{k}_{i_{t}}-c_{i_{t}})\,\bm{v}_{i_{t}}\bm{k}_{i_{t}}^{\top} with randomly drawn indices when the number of associations exceeds the capacity: n>d2n>d^{2}. The system is then generically inconsistent, and the iterates no longer converge to a point. Instead we have: (i) The expected iterate converges linearly to the sampling-weighted least-squares solution 𝑺LS=argmin𝑺∑ipi​(𝒗i⊤​𝑺​𝒌i−ci)2\bm{S}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}=\mathop{\mathrm{argmin}\,}_{\bm{S}}\sum_{i}p_{i}(\bm{v}_{i}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{k}_{i}-c_{i})^{2}. This is for uniform sampling exactly the minimizer of the loss L\mathrm{L}. (ii) The iterates converge in distribution to a unique stationary distribution whose mean is exactly 𝑺LS\bm{S}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}} (no bias at any order in β\beta) and whose covariance is O⁡(β)O(\beta), given by a Lyapunov-type equation driven by the residuals at 𝑺LS\bm{S}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}. (iii) The steady-state loss exceeds the minimum by the classical LMS misadjustment, E⁡[L]−Lmin=β2​E​[ρi2​‖𝒌i‖2​‖𝒗i‖2]+O⁡(β2)\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\mathrm{L}]-\mathrm{L}_{\min}=\tfrac{\beta}{2}\,\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[\rho_{i}^{2}\left\lVert\bm{k}_{i}\right\rVert^{2}\left\lVert\bm{v}_{i}\right\rVert^{2}\big]+O(\beta^{2}), where ρi\rho_{i} are the optimal residuals.

This appendix contains complete proofs of both theorems: the mean dynamics are solved exactly; existence, uniqueness, and geometric convergence of the stationary distribution are established by a synchronous-coupling contraction in the Wasserstein-2 metric; the stationary mean and the exact covariance equation are derived with all cross terms accounted for; the misadjustment follows from an exact trace identity with two-sided bounds; and the transient is controlled by an explicit geometric-plus-horizon estimate. Exact convergence can be recovered by diminishing step sizes or by iterate averaging, and it survives n>d2n>d^{2} unharmed whenever the targets remain consistent. Notably, exact convergence is always obtain for the correlation target ci=𝒗i⊤​𝒌ic_{i}=\bm{v}_{i}^{\top}\bm{k}_{i} and the norm target ci=‖𝒗i‖2c_{i}=\left\lVert\bm{v}_{i}\right\rVert^{2} whenever an exact retrieval memory exists.

A3.5.2  Setting and notation

Let n>d2n>d^{2} associations (𝒌i,𝒗i,ci)(\bm{k}_{i},\bm{v}_{i},c_{i}), 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n, be given. Vectorized, with 𝒔=vec⁡(𝑺)∈ℝd2\bm{s}=\vecop(\bm{S})\in\mathbb{R}^{d^{2}} and 𝒂i=𝒌i⊗𝒗i\bm{a}_{i}=\bm{k}_{i}\otimes\bm{v}_{i}, therefore ‖𝒂i‖=‖𝒌i‖​‖𝒗i‖\left\lVert\bm{a}_{i}\right\rVert=\left\lVert\bm{k}_{i}\right\rVert\left\lVert\bm{v}_{i}\right\rVert. The associations form the linear system 𝑨​𝒔=𝒄\bm{A}\bm{s}=\bm{c} with 𝑨∈ℝn×d2\bm{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d^{2}} stacking the rows 𝒂i⊤\bm{a}_{i}^{\top}. We assume 𝑨\bm{A} has full column rank d2d^{2} i.e. the features span ℝd2\mathbb{R}^{d^{2}}. Since n>d2n>d^{2}, the system is generically inconsistent: no 𝑺\bm{S} satisfies all associations, and

L⁡(𝑺)=1n​∑i=1n(𝒗i⊤​𝑺​𝒌i−ci)2\mathrm{L}(\bm{S})\;=\;\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\big(\bm{v}_{i}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{k}_{i}-c_{i}\big)^{2} (A44)

has a positive minimum Lmin>0\mathrm{L}_{\min}>0. At each step an index iti_{t} is drawn with probabilities pi>0p_{i}>0, independently of the past, and the rule is applied with fixed step size β\beta satisfying

0<β​‖𝒂i‖2< 2for all ​i.0\;<\;\beta\,\left\lVert\bm{a}_{i}\right\rVert^{2}\;<\;2\qquad\text{for all }i\,. (A45)

We define

𝑨¯\displaystyle\bar{\bm{A}}\; :=E⁡[𝒂​𝒂⊤]=∑i=1npi​𝒂i​𝒂i⊤≻ 0,\displaystyle:=\;\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[\bm{a}\bm{a}^{\top}\big]\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}\,\bm{a}_{i}\bm{a}_{i}^{\top}\;\succ\;\bm{0}\,, 𝒃¯\displaystyle\bar{\bm{b}}\; :=E⁡[c​𝒂]=∑i=1npi​ci​𝒂i,\displaystyle:=\;\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[c\,\bm{a}\big]\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}\,c_{i}\,\bm{a}_{i}\,, (A46)
𝒔LS\displaystyle\bm{s}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}\; :=𝑨¯−1​𝒃¯=argmin𝒔∑i=1npi​(𝒂i⊤​𝒔−ci)2,\displaystyle:=\;\bar{\bm{A}}^{-1}\bar{\bm{b}}\;=\;\mathop{\mathrm{argmin}\,}_{\bm{s}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}\big(\bm{a}_{i}^{\top}\bm{s}-c_{i}\big)^{2}\,, ρi\displaystyle\rho_{i}\; :=ci−𝒂i⊤𝒔LS(optimal residuals),\displaystyle:=\;c_{i}-\bm{a}_{i}^{\top}\bm{s}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}\quad\text{(optimal residuals)}\,, (A47)

so that the normal equations read

E[ρ𝒂]=∑i=1npiρi𝒂i= 0⟺𝒃¯=𝑨¯𝒔LS.\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[\rho\,\bm{a}\big]\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}\,\rho_{i}\,\bm{a}_{i}\;=\;\bm{0}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad\bar{\bm{b}}\;=\;\bar{\bm{A}}\,\bm{s}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}\,. (A48)

For uniform sampling, 𝑨¯=1n​𝑨⊤​𝑨\bar{\bm{A}}=\tfrac{1}{n}\bm{A}^{\top}\bm{A} and 𝒔LS=(𝑨⊤​𝑨)−1​𝑨⊤​𝒄\bm{s}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}=(\bm{A}^{\top}\bm{A})^{-1}\bm{A}^{\top}\bm{c} is the ordinary least-squares solution, i.e. the unique minimizer of L\mathrm{L}. Throughout, expectations without subscript are over i∼pi\sim p, and Eπ\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}_{\pi} denotes expectation of a random state distributed according to a law π\pi. Vectorized, the rule and its error form are

𝒔t+1=𝑴it​𝒔t+β​cit​𝒂it,𝒆t+1=𝑴it​𝒆t+β​ρit​𝒂it,𝑴i:=𝑰−β​𝒂i​𝒂i⊤,\bm{s}_{t+1}\;=\;\bm{M}_{i_{t}}\bm{s}_{t}+\beta\,c_{i_{t}}\bm{a}_{i_{t}}\,,\qquad\bm{e}_{t+1}\;=\;\bm{M}_{i_{t}}\,\bm{e}_{t}\;+\;\beta\,\rho_{i_{t}}\,\bm{a}_{i_{t}}\,,\qquad\bm{M}_{i}\;:=\;\bm{I}-\beta\,\bm{a}_{i}\bm{a}_{i}^{\top}\,, (A49)

with 𝒆t:=𝒔t−𝒔LS\bm{e}_{t}:=\bm{s}_{t}-\bm{s}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}; the error form follows by inserting ci=𝒂i⊤​𝒔LS+ρic_{i}=\bm{a}_{i}^{\top}\bm{s}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}+\rho_{i}. The constants

γβ:=mini⁡β⁡(2−β​‖𝒂i‖2)> 0,ρ¯:=γβ​λmin​(𝑨¯)∈(0,1],σ2:=E⁡[ρ2​‖𝒂‖2]\gamma_{\beta}\;:=\;\min_{i}\,\beta\,\big(2-\beta\left\lVert\bm{a}_{i}\right\rVert^{2}\big)\;>\;0\,,\qquad\bar{\rho}\;:=\;\gamma_{\beta}\,\lambda_{\min}(\bar{\bm{A}})\;\in\;(0,1]\,,\qquad\sigma^{2}\;:=\;\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[\rho^{2}\left\lVert\bm{a}\right\rVert^{2}\big] (A50)

appear throughout (0<ρ¯≤10<\bar{\rho}\leq 1 is shown in Lemma A1).

A3.5.3  Theorems on expected and steady state solution

Theorem A6 (Expected solution: exact, unbiased least squares).

Under (A45), the expected iterate obeys the exact deterministic recursion

E[𝒔t+1]=(𝑰−β𝑨¯)E[𝒔t]+β𝒃¯⟺E[𝒆t+1]=(𝑰−β𝑨¯)E[𝒆t],\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[\bm{s}_{t+1}\big]\;=\;\big(\bm{I}-\beta\bar{\bm{A}}\big)\,\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[\bm{s}_{t}\big]\;+\;\beta\,\bar{\bm{b}}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[\bm{e}_{t+1}\big]\;=\;\big(\bm{I}-\beta\bar{\bm{A}}\big)\,\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[\bm{e}_{t}\big]\,, (A51)

whose unique fixed point is 𝐬LS\bm{s}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}, and

‖E⁡[𝑺t]−𝑺LS‖F≤rt​‖𝑺0−𝑺LS‖F,r:=maxk⁡|1−β​λk​(𝑨¯)|< 1,\left\lVert\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\bm{S}_{t}]-\bm{S}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}\;\leq\;r^{t}\,\left\lVert\bm{S}_{0}-\bm{S}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}\,,\qquad r\;:=\;\max_{k}\,{{\left|1-\beta\lambda_{k}(\bar{\bm{A}})\right|}}\;<\;1\,, (A52)

so E⁡[𝐒t]→𝐒LS\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\bm{S}_{t}]\to\bm{S}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}} linearly. The convergence of the mean is exactly unbiased: the fixed point of (A51) is 𝐬LS\bm{s}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}} itself, with no O⁡(β)O(\beta) correction.

Theorem A7 (Steady state: stationary distribution around 𝑺LS\bm{S}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}).

Under (A45), the iterates form a Markov chain on ℝd2\mathbb{R}^{d^{2}} that has a unique stationary distribution πβ\pi_{\beta} with finite second moment, and the law of 𝐬t\bm{s}_{t} converges to πβ\pi_{\beta} geometrically in the Wasserstein-2 metric:

𝒲2​(law​(𝒔t),πβ)≤(1−ρ¯)t/2​𝒲2​(law​(𝒔0),πβ).\mathcal{W}_{2}\big(\text{law}(\bm{s}_{t}),\,\pi_{\beta}\big)\;\leq\;\big(1-\bar{\rho}\big)^{t/2}\;\mathcal{W}_{2}\big(\text{law}(\bm{s}_{0}),\,\pi_{\beta}\big)\,. (A53)

Under πβ\pi_{\beta}, with 𝐞:=𝐬−𝐬LS\bm{e}:=\bm{s}-\bm{s}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}:

  1. (i) Mean: Eπβ​[𝑺]=𝑺LS\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}_{\pi_{\beta}}[\bm{S}]=\bm{S}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}} exactly.

  2. (ii) Covariance: 𝑽β:=Eπβ​[𝒆​𝒆⊤]\bm{V}_{\beta}:=\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}_{\pi_{\beta}}[\bm{e}\bm{e}^{\top}] satisfies the exact stationarity equation

    𝑨¯​𝑽β+𝑽β​𝑨¯−β​E​[(𝒂⊤​𝑽β​𝒂)​𝒂​𝒂⊤]=β​E​[ρ2​𝒂​𝒂⊤],\bar{\bm{A}}\bm{V}_{\beta}+\bm{V}_{\beta}\bar{\bm{A}}\;-\;\beta\,\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[\big(\bm{a}^{\top}\bm{V}_{\beta}\,\bm{a}\big)\,\bm{a}\bm{a}^{\top}\big]\;=\;\beta\,\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[\rho^{2}\,\bm{a}\bm{a}^{\top}\big]\,, (A54)

    and obeys the two-sided trace bounds

    β​σ22≤tr⁡(𝑨¯​𝑽β)≤β​σ22−β​maxi​‖𝒂i‖2,\displaystyle\frac{\beta\,\sigma^{2}}{2}\;\leq\;\tr\big(\bar{\bm{A}}\bm{V}_{\beta}\big)\;\leq\;\frac{\beta\,\sigma^{2}}{2-\beta\max_{i}\left\lVert\bm{a}_{i}\right\rVert^{2}}\,, (A55)
    Eπβ​[‖𝑺−𝑺LS‖F2]≤β​σ2(2−β​maxi​‖𝒂i‖2)​λmin​(𝑨¯);\displaystyle\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}_{\pi_{\beta}}\!\left[\left\lVert\bm{S}-\bm{S}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}\right]\;\leq\;\frac{\beta\,\sigma^{2}}{\big(2-\beta\max_{i}\left\lVert\bm{a}_{i}\right\rVert^{2}\big)\,\lambda_{\min}(\bar{\bm{A}})}\,;

    in particular 𝑽β=O⁡(β)\bm{V}_{\beta}=O(\beta), and to leading order (A54) is the Lyapunov equation 𝑨¯​𝑽+𝑽​𝑨¯=β​E​[ρ2​𝒂​𝒂⊤]\bar{\bm{A}}\bm{V}+\bm{V}\bar{\bm{A}}=\beta\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\rho^{2}\bm{a}\bm{a}^{\top}].

  3. (iii) Steady-state loss (misadjustment): for uniform sampling,

    Eπβ​[L⁡(𝑺)]−Lmin=tr⁡(𝑨¯​𝑽β)=β2​(σ2+E⁡[(𝒂⊤​𝑽β​𝒂)​‖𝒂‖2]),\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}_{\pi_{\beta}}\big[\mathrm{L}(\bm{S})\big]\;-\;\mathrm{L}_{\min}\;=\;\tr\big(\bar{\bm{A}}\bm{V}_{\beta}\big)\;=\;\frac{\beta}{2}\Big(\sigma^{2}+\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[\big(\bm{a}^{\top}\bm{V}_{\beta}\bm{a}\big)\left\lVert\bm{a}\right\rVert^{2}\big]\Big)\,, (A56)

    an exact identity, whence

    β2​σ2≤Eπβ​[L⁡(𝑺)]−Lmin≤β2​σ2⋅22−β​maxi​‖𝒂i‖2,σ2=E⁡[ρi2​‖𝒌i‖2​‖𝒗i‖2],\frac{\beta}{2}\,\sigma^{2}\;\leq\;\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}_{\pi_{\beta}}\big[\mathrm{L}(\bm{S})\big]-\mathrm{L}_{\min}\;\leq\;\frac{\beta}{2}\,\sigma^{2}\cdot\frac{2}{2-\beta\max_{i}\left\lVert\bm{a}_{i}\right\rVert^{2}}\,,\qquad\sigma^{2}=\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[\rho_{i}^{2}\left\lVert\bm{k}_{i}\right\rVert^{2}\left\lVert\bm{v}_{i}\right\rVert^{2}\big]\,, (A57)

    i.e. Eπβ​[L]=Lmin+β2​σ2+O⁡(β2)\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}_{\pi_{\beta}}[\mathrm{L}]=\mathrm{L}_{\min}+\tfrac{\beta}{2}\sigma^{2}+O(\beta^{2}). This is the classical Widrow–Hoff LMS misadjustment for the bilinear feature 𝒂=𝒌⊗𝒗\bm{a}=\bm{k}\otimes\bm{v}.

  4. (iv) Transient: with 𝒘:=E⁡[ρ​‖𝒂‖2​𝒂]\bm{w}:=\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[\rho\left\lVert\bm{a}\right\rVert^{2}\bm{a}\big],

    E​‖𝒆t‖2≤(1−ρ¯2)t​‖𝒆0‖2+2​β2​σ2ρ¯+4​β4​‖𝒘‖2ρ¯2,\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\left\lVert\bm{e}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}\;\leq\;\Big(1-\tfrac{\bar{\rho}}{2}\Big)^{t}\left\lVert\bm{e}_{0}\right\rVert^{2}\;+\;\frac{2\beta^{2}\sigma^{2}}{\bar{\rho}}\;+\;\frac{4\beta^{4}\left\lVert\bm{w}\right\rVert^{2}}{\bar{\rho}^{2}}\,, (A58)

    a geometric approach to an O⁡(β)O(\beta) horizon (note ρ¯=Θ⁡(β)\bar{\rho}=\Theta(\beta)): overload does not slow the transient, it only replaces the limit point by a limit distribution.

A3.5.4  Proofs of the theorems

Throughout, ℱt:=σ⁡(𝒔0,i0,…,it−1)\mathcal{F}_{t}:=\sigma(\bm{s}_{0},i_{0},\dots,i_{t-1}) denotes the filtration of the past; iti_{t} is independent of ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t} by assumption. We repeatedly use that (A49) is linear in the state with coefficients independent of the state.

Two lemmas crucial for the proofs of the theorems.
Lemma A1 (One-step mean-square contraction of the homogeneous part).

For every fixed 𝐱∈ℝd2\bm{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d^{2}},

E⁡[‖𝑴i​𝒙‖2]=‖𝒙‖2−∑i=1npi​β​(2−β​‖𝒂i‖2)​(𝒂i⊤​𝒙)2≤(1−ρ¯)​‖𝒙‖2,\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[\left\lVert\bm{M}_{i}\,\bm{x}\right\rVert^{2}\big]\;=\;\left\lVert\bm{x}\right\rVert^{2}\;-\;\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}\,\beta\big(2-\beta\left\lVert\bm{a}_{i}\right\rVert^{2}\big)\big(\bm{a}_{i}^{\top}\bm{x}\big)^{2}\;\leq\;\big(1-\bar{\rho}\big)\,\left\lVert\bm{x}\right\rVert^{2}\,, (A59)

and ρ¯∈(0,1]\bar{\rho}\in(0,1].

Proof.

Since 𝑴i\bm{M}_{i} is symmetric,

‖𝑴i​𝒙‖2=𝒙⊤​(𝑰−β​𝒂i​𝒂i⊤)2​𝒙=‖𝒙‖2−2​β​(𝒂i⊤​𝒙)2+β2​‖𝒂i‖2​(𝒂i⊤​𝒙)2,\left\lVert\bm{M}_{i}\bm{x}\right\rVert^{2}\;=\;\bm{x}^{\top}\big(\bm{I}-\beta\bm{a}_{i}\bm{a}_{i}^{\top}\big)^{2}\bm{x}\;=\;\left\lVert\bm{x}\right\rVert^{2}-2\beta\big(\bm{a}_{i}^{\top}\bm{x}\big)^{2}+\beta^{2}\left\lVert\bm{a}_{i}\right\rVert^{2}\big(\bm{a}_{i}^{\top}\bm{x}\big)^{2}\,, (A60)

which is the equality in (A59) after averaging over i∼pi\sim p. By (A45), β⁡(2−β​‖𝒂i‖2)≥γβ>0\beta(2-\beta\left\lVert\bm{a}_{i}\right\rVert^{2})\geq\gamma_{\beta}>0 for every ii, and ∑ipi​(𝒂i⊤​𝒙)2=𝒙⊤​𝑨¯​𝒙≥λmin​(𝑨¯)​‖𝒙‖2\sum_{i}p_{i}(\bm{a}_{i}^{\top}\bm{x})^{2}=\bm{x}^{\top}\bar{\bm{A}}\bm{x}\geq\lambda_{\min}(\bar{\bm{A}})\left\lVert\bm{x}\right\rVert^{2}, hence the inequality with ρ¯=γβ​λmin​(𝑨¯)\bar{\rho}=\gamma_{\beta}\lambda_{\min}(\bar{\bm{A}}). Finally ρ¯≤1\bar{\rho}\leq 1 because the left-hand side of (A59) is nonnegative for every 𝒙\bm{x}. We assumed that 𝑨¯\bar{\bm{A}} has full rank, therefore 0<λmin​(𝑨¯)0<\lambda_{\min}(\bar{\bm{A}}) and with 0<γβ0<\gamma_{\beta} we have 0<ρ¯0<\bar{\rho}. ∎

Lemma A2 (The chain lives in 𝒫2\mathcal{P}_{2} and its kernel is a 𝒲2\mathcal{W}_{2}-contraction).

Let PP denote the transition kernel of (A49) and let 𝒫2\mathcal{P}_{2} be the space of probability laws on ℝd2\mathbb{R}^{d^{2}} with finite second moment, equipped with the Wasserstein-2 metric 𝒲2\mathcal{W}_{2}. Then PP maps 𝒫2\mathcal{P}_{2} into 𝒫2\mathcal{P}_{2}, and for all μ,ν∈𝒫2\mu,\nu\in\mathcal{P}_{2},

𝒲2​(μ​P,ν​P)≤1−ρ¯​𝒲2​(μ,ν).\mathcal{W}_{2}\big(\mu P,\,\nu P\big)\;\leq\;\sqrt{1-\bar{\rho}}\;\,\mathcal{W}_{2}(\mu,\nu)\,. (A61)

Consequently PP has a unique invariant law πβ∈𝒫2\pi_{\beta}\in\mathcal{P}_{2} and (A53) holds.

Proof.

PP preserves 𝒫2\mathcal{P}_{2}: for 𝒆∼μ∈𝒫2\bm{e}\sim\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{2} and an independent index ii, E​‖𝑴i​𝒆+β​ρi​𝒂i‖2≤2​E​‖𝑴i​𝒆‖2+2​β2​E​[ρ2​‖𝒂‖2]≤2​E​‖𝒆‖2+2​β2​σ2<∞\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\left\lVert\bm{M}_{i}\bm{e}+\beta\rho_{i}\bm{a}_{i}\right\rVert^{2}\leq 2\,\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\left\lVert\bm{M}_{i}\bm{e}\right\rVert^{2}+2\beta^{2}\,\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\rho^{2}\left\lVert\bm{a}\right\rVert^{2}]\leq 2\,\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\left\lVert\bm{e}\right\rVert^{2}+2\beta^{2}\sigma^{2}<\infty, using Lemma A1.

Contraction: let (𝒙,𝒚)(\bm{x},\bm{y}) be an optimal 𝒲2\mathcal{W}_{2}-coupling of (μ,ν)(\mu,\nu) and couple the two chains synchronously: draw one index ii (independent of (𝒙,𝒚)(\bm{x},\bm{y})) and set 𝒙′=𝑴i​𝒙+β​ρi​𝒂i\bm{x}^{\prime}=\bm{M}_{i}\bm{x}+\beta\rho_{i}\bm{a}_{i}, 𝒚′=𝑴i​𝒚+β​ρi​𝒂i\bm{y}^{\prime}=\bm{M}_{i}\bm{y}+\beta\rho_{i}\bm{a}_{i}. The additive terms cancel in the difference,

𝒙′−𝒚′=𝑴i​(𝒙−𝒚),\bm{x}^{\prime}-\bm{y}^{\prime}\;=\;\bm{M}_{i}\,(\bm{x}-\bm{y})\,, (A62)

so by Lemma A1, first conditionally on (𝒙,𝒚)(\bm{x},\bm{y}) and then in expectation,

E​‖𝒙′−𝒚′‖2≤(1−ρ¯)​E​‖𝒙−𝒚‖2=(1−ρ¯)​𝒲2​(μ,ν)2.\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\left\lVert\bm{x}^{\prime}-\bm{y}^{\prime}\right\rVert^{2}\;\leq\;(1-\bar{\rho})\,\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\left\lVert\bm{x}-\bm{y}\right\rVert^{2}\;=\;(1-\bar{\rho})\,\mathcal{W}_{2}(\mu,\nu)^{2}\,. (A63)

Since (𝒙′,𝒚′)(\bm{x}^{\prime},\bm{y}^{\prime}) is some coupling of (μ​P,ν​P)(\mu P,\nu P), 𝒲2​(μ​P,ν​P)2≤E​‖𝒙′−𝒚′‖2\mathcal{W}_{2}(\mu P,\nu P)^{2}\leq\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\left\lVert\bm{x}^{\prime}-\bm{y}^{\prime}\right\rVert^{2}, which is (A61).

Conclusion: (𝒫2,𝒲2)(\mathcal{P}_{2},\mathcal{W}_{2}) is a complete metric space (see, e.g., (Villani, 2009, Theorem 6.18)), so Banach’s fixed-point theorem yields a unique πβ∈𝒫2\pi_{\beta}\in\mathcal{P}_{2} with πβ​P=πβ\pi_{\beta}P=\pi_{\beta} and 𝒲2​(μ​Pt,πβ)≤(1−ρ¯)t/2​𝒲2​(μ,πβ)\mathcal{W}_{2}(\mu P^{t},\pi_{\beta})\leq(1-\bar{\rho})^{t/2}\mathcal{W}_{2}(\mu,\pi_{\beta}) for every μ∈𝒫2\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{2}, which is (A53). Convergence in 𝒲2\mathcal{W}_{2} implies convergence in distribution together with convergence of first and second moments. ∎

Comments to the proof of Lemma A2 in 9 bullet points.
∙\bullet 1) Overview. How a mixture of non-contractive matrices produces a contraction: the kernel PP and the coupling argument. The matrices 𝑴i\bm{M}_{i} are not themselves contractions - by Lemma A1, ‖𝑴i‖2=1\left\lVert\bm{M}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}=1 for every single ii, since 𝑴i\bm{M}_{i} has eigenvalue 11 on 𝒂i⟂\bm{a}_{i}^{\perp}. Contractivity in Lemma A2 is a property of the mixture PP, not of any individual 𝑴i\bm{M}_{i}, and PP is not a matrix at all: it is a Markov kernel acting on laws in 𝒫2\mathcal{P}_{2}, and the relevant notion of size for it is the Wasserstein metric 𝒲2\mathcal{W}_{2} on 𝒫2\mathcal{P}_{2} itself - not any norm on ℝd2\mathbb{R}^{d^{2}} from which PP’s contraction could be read off the 𝑴i\bm{M}_{i}’s directly. This note spells out how PP is built from the 𝑴i\bm{M}_{i}’s, in what sense PP does and does not have an “operator norm,” and why the coupling argument nonetheless produces the contraction (A61).

∙\bullet 2) Constructing PP from the 𝐌i\bm{M}_{i}. For a fixed state 𝒙∈ℝd2\bm{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d^{2}}, define the nn deterministic affine maps

Φi(𝒙):=𝑴i𝒙+βρi𝒂i,i=1,…,n.\Phi_{i}(\bm{x})\;:=\;\bm{M}_{i}\bm{x}+\beta\rho_{i}\bm{a}_{i}\,,\qquad i=1,\dots,n\,. (A64)

One step of the chain from 𝒙\bm{x} lands at Φi​(𝒙)\Phi_{i}(\bm{x}) with probability pip_{i}, so the transition kernel is the mixture of point masses

P⁡(𝒙,⋅):=∑i=1npi​δΦi​(𝒙)​(⋅),P(\bm{x},\cdot)\;:=\;\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}\,\delta_{\Phi_{i}(\bm{x})}(\cdot)\,, (A65)

and, for a law μ\mu, μ​P\mu P is defined by (μ​P)​(B)=∫P⁡(𝒙,B)​μ​(𝑑𝒙)(\mu P)(B)=\int P(\bm{x},B)\,\mu(d\bm{x}) - equivalently, μ​P\mu P is the law of ΦI​(𝑿)\Phi_{I}(\bm{X}) for 𝑿∼μ\bm{X}\sim\mu and I∼pI\sim p drawn independently of 𝑿\bm{X}.

BB is a Borel (measurable) subset of ℝd2\mathbb{R}^{d^{2}} - an arbitrary test set, held fixed, to which the kernel assigns a probability. Concretely,

P(𝒙,B):=Pr(ΦI(𝒙)∈B)=∑i=1npi 1[Φi(𝒙)∈B]=∑i=1npiδΦi​(𝒙)(B),P(\bm{x},B)\;:=\;\mathbf{\mathrm{Pr}}\big(\Phi_{I}(\bm{x})\in B\big)\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}\;\mathbbm{1}\big[\Phi_{i}(\bm{x})\in B\big]\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}\;\delta_{\Phi_{i}(\bm{x})}(B)\,, (A66)

where Φi​(𝒙)=𝑴i​𝒙+β​ρi​𝒂i\Phi_{i}(\bm{x})=\bm{M}_{i}\bm{x}+\beta\rho_{i}\bm{a}_{i} is the (fixed, deterministic) image of 𝒙\bm{x} under transition ii, and I∼pI\sim p is the random index selecting which transition fires. In words: P⁡(𝒙,B)P(\bm{x},B) is the probability that one step of the chain, started at 𝒙\bm{x}, lands in BB - obtained by summing the weights pip_{i} of every index ii whose image Φi​(𝒙)\Phi_{i}(\bm{x}) happens to fall inside BB.

PP as a function of each argument separately. The kernel P:ℝd2×ℬ⁡(ℝd2)→[0,1]P:\mathbb{R}^{d^{2}}\times\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^{d^{2}})\to[0,1] plays a different role in each of its two slots:

  • •

    Fixed 𝒙\bm{x}, varying BB: P⁡(𝒙,⋅)P(\bm{x},\cdot) is itself a probability measure on ℝd2\mathbb{R}^{d^{2}} - concretely, the discrete measure

    P⁡(𝒙,⋅)=∑i=1npi​δΦi​(𝒙)​(⋅)P(\bm{x},\cdot)\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}\,\delta_{\Phi_{i}(\bm{x})}(\cdot) (A67)

    putting mass pip_{i} on the point Φi​(𝒙)\Phi_{i}(\bm{x}) for each ii (masses are summed if several Φi​(𝒙)\Phi_{i}(\bm{x}) coincide). This is the law of the chain’s next state, given that it is currently at 𝒙\bm{x}.

  • •

    Fixed BB, varying 𝒙\bm{x}: P⁡(⋅,B)P(\cdot,B) is a bounded measurable function of 𝒙\bm{x}, since each indicator 𝟙[Φi(𝒙)∈B]\mathbbm{1}[\Phi_{i}(\bm{x})\in B] is measurable in 𝒙\bm{x} and the sum is finite.

This is the standard convention for a Markov transition kernel: measurable in the first argument, a probability measure in the second.

∙\bullet 3) the pushforward measure μ​P\mu P is well defined. For a law μ\mu of the current state, the one-step-ahead law μ​P\mu P is defined by integrating the second argument BB (held fixed) against μ\mu acting on the first argument 𝒙\bm{x}:

(μ​P)​(B):=∫ℝd2P⁡(𝒙,B)​μ​(𝑑𝒙).(\mu P)(B)\;:=\;\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d^{2}}}P(\bm{x},B)\;\mu(d\bm{x})\,. (A68)

Equivalently, μ​P\mu P is the law of ΦI​(𝑿)\Phi_{I}(\bm{X}) for 𝑿∼μ\bm{X}\sim\mu and I∼pI\sim p drawn independently of 𝑿\bm{X}: draw a random current state 𝑿\bm{X}, draw an independent random index II, and output ΦI​(𝑿)\Phi_{I}(\bm{X}). The two roles of BB above are exactly what make this integral meaningful: for each fixed 𝒙\bm{x} in the integral, P⁡(𝒙,B)P(\bm{x},B) is a number in [0,1][0,1] (the probability mass the one-step law from 𝒙\bm{x} places on BB); integrating that number against μ⁡(d​𝒙)\mu(d\bm{x}) averages it over the randomness in the current state, and the result, as a function of BB, is again a probability measure. It is the law μ​P\mu P appearing throughout the steady-state analysis of the rule.

∙\bullet 4) PP has no operator norm on ℝd2\mathbb{R}^{d^{2}}. Thus PP is linear as an operator on (signed) measures ((α​μ+(1−α)​ν)​P=α​μ​P+(1−α)​ν​P(\alpha\mu+(1-\alpha)\nu)P=\alpha\mu P+(1-\alpha)\nu P), but this linearity lives on the infinite-dimensional space of measures, not on ℝd2\mathbb{R}^{d^{2}}: there is no d2×d2d^{2}\times d^{2} matrix representing PP, so PP has no operator norm on (ℝd2,‖⋅‖)(\mathbb{R}^{d^{2}},\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert) the way each 𝑴i\bm{M}_{i} does. What PP does have is an operator norm in the sense appropriate to its actual domain: a Lipschitz modulus on the metric space (𝒫2,𝒲2)(\mathcal{P}_{2},\mathcal{W}_{2}), namely the smallest LL such that 𝒲2​(μ​P,ν​P)≤L​𝒲2​(μ,ν)\mathcal{W}_{2}(\mu P,\nu P)\leq L\,\mathcal{W}_{2}(\mu,\nu) for all μ,ν∈𝒫2\mu,\nu\in\mathcal{P}_{2}. That modulus is exactly what (A61) bounds by 1−ρ¯<1\sqrt{1-\bar{\rho}}<1. It cannot be read off a per-map bound such as maxi⁡‖𝑴i‖2\max_{i}\left\lVert\bm{M}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}, which equals 11 by Lemma A1 and would certify no contraction whatsoever; obtaining a modulus strictly below 11 requires the coupling argument below, precisely because it is a statement about PP acting on laws, not about any 𝑴i\bm{M}_{i} acting on ℝd2\mathbb{R}^{d^{2}}.

∙\bullet 5) The Wasserstein metric is essential to prove the contraction. The definition

𝒲2​(μ,ν)2=infγ∈Γ⁡(μ,ν)Eγ​[‖𝑿−𝒀‖2]\mathcal{W}_{2}(\mu,\nu)^{2}\;=\;\inf_{\gamma\in\Gamma(\mu,\nu)}\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}_{\gamma}\big[\left\lVert\bm{X}-\bm{Y}\right\rVert^{2}\big] (A69)

is an infimum over all couplings γ\gamma of (μ,ν)(\mu,\nu) (joint laws with the prescribed marginals). This has an immediate but crucial consequence: to upper-bound 𝒲2​(μ​P,ν​P)\mathcal{W}_{2}(\mu P,\nu P) it suffices to exhibit any single coupling of (μ​P,ν​P)(\mu P,\nu P) and compute its second moment. Note that we never need the optimal coupling of the outputs, let alone an explicit formula for PP as an operator.

∙\bullet 6) The synchronous coupling. We are free to choose how the randomness that drives one step of each chain is generated, and we exploit that freedom by reusing the same random index for both chains. Concretely: let (𝒙,𝒚)(\bm{x},\bm{y}) be an optimal coupling of (μ,ν)(\mu,\nu), i.e. a joint law with 𝒙∼μ\bm{x}\sim\mu, 𝒚∼ν\bm{y}\sim\nu, and E​‖𝒙−𝒚‖2=𝒲2​(μ,ν)2\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\left\lVert\bm{x}-\bm{y}\right\rVert^{2}=\mathcal{W}_{2}(\mu,\nu)^{2} (such a coupling exists because ℝd2\mathbb{R}^{d^{2}} is Polish; see (Villani, 2009, Theorem 4.1)). Draw a single index i∼pi\sim p, independent of (𝒙,𝒚)(\bm{x},\bm{y}), and set

𝒙′:=Φi​(𝒙)=𝑴i​𝒙+β​ρi​𝒂i,𝒚′:=Φi​(𝒚)=𝑴i​𝒚+β​ρi​𝒂i.\bm{x}^{\prime}\;:=\;\Phi_{i}(\bm{x})\;=\;\bm{M}_{i}\bm{x}+\beta\rho_{i}\bm{a}_{i}\,,\qquad\bm{y}^{\prime}\;:=\;\Phi_{i}(\bm{y})\;=\;\bm{M}_{i}\bm{y}+\beta\rho_{i}\bm{a}_{i}\,. (A70)

Marginally, 𝒙′∼μ​P\bm{x}^{\prime}\sim\mu P and 𝒚′∼ν​P\bm{y}^{\prime}\sim\nu P by the very definition (A65) of μ​P\mu P, applied separately to each starting law; hence (𝒙′,𝒚′)(\bm{x}^{\prime},\bm{y}^{\prime}) is a valid coupling of (μ​P,ν​P)(\mu P,\nu P). This coupling is not necessarily the optimal one, but that is all the argument requires.

∙\bullet 7) The additive target terms cancel. Because 𝒙′\bm{x}^{\prime} and 𝒚′\bm{y}^{\prime} are built from the same draw ii, the inhomogeneous term β​ρi​𝒂i\beta\rho_{i}\bm{a}_{i}is identical in both and cancels exactly in the difference:

𝒙′−𝒚′=(𝑴i​𝒙+β​ρi​𝒂i)−(𝑴i​𝒚+β​ρi​𝒂i)=𝑴i​(𝒙−𝒚).\bm{x}^{\prime}-\bm{y}^{\prime}\;=\;\big(\bm{M}_{i}\bm{x}+\beta\rho_{i}\bm{a}_{i}\big)-\big(\bm{M}_{i}\bm{y}+\beta\rho_{i}\bm{a}_{i}\big)\;=\;\bm{M}_{i}\,(\bm{x}-\bm{y})\,. (A71)

The part of the update that cancels out is exactly the part carrying the targets cic_{i}. This is the crux of the construction: it converts a statement about two inhomogeneous, randomly driven affine updates into a statement about a single homogeneous linear map, 𝑴i\bm{M}_{i}, applied to the fixed vector 𝒙−𝒚\bm{x}-\bm{y}. This is exactly the object Lemma A1 controls. Had we instead coupled the two chains using independent indices for 𝒙′\bm{x}^{\prime} and 𝒚′\bm{y}^{\prime}, the noise terms would not cancel and the argument would not go through; the whole content of the synchronous-coupling trick is this cancellation.

∙\bullet 8) Deriving the contraction. Since ii is independent of (𝒙,𝒚)(\bm{x},\bm{y}), condition on (𝒙,𝒚)(\bm{x},\bm{y}) first and average over ii:

E[‖𝒙′−𝒚′‖2|𝒙,𝒚]=∑i=1npi‖𝑴i(𝒙−𝒚)‖2≤(1−ρ¯)‖𝒙−𝒚‖2\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[\left\lVert\bm{x}^{\prime}-\bm{y}^{\prime}\right\rVert^{2}\,\big|\,\bm{x},\bm{y}\big]\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}\,\left\lVert\bm{M}_{i}(\bm{x}-\bm{y})\right\rVert^{2}\;\leq\;\big(1-\bar{\rho}\big)\,\left\lVert\bm{x}-\bm{y}\right\rVert^{2} (A72)

by Lemma A1, applied pointwise to the vector 𝒙−𝒚\bm{x}-\bm{y} (fixed once we condition). Taking the outer expectation over (𝒙,𝒚)(\bm{x},\bm{y}) and using that this coupling was chosen optimal,

E​‖𝒙′−𝒚′‖2≤(1−ρ¯)​E​‖𝒙−𝒚‖2=(1−ρ¯)​𝒲2​(μ,ν)2.\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\left\lVert\bm{x}^{\prime}-\bm{y}^{\prime}\right\rVert^{2}\;\leq\;\big(1-\bar{\rho}\big)\,\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\left\lVert\bm{x}-\bm{y}\right\rVert^{2}\;=\;\big(1-\bar{\rho}\big)\,\mathcal{W}_{2}(\mu,\nu)^{2}\,. (A73)

Finally, since (𝒙′,𝒚′)(\bm{x}^{\prime},\bm{y}^{\prime}) is a coupling of (μ​P,ν​P)(\mu P,\nu P), the infimum defining 𝒲2​(μ​P,ν​P)2\mathcal{W}_{2}(\mu P,\nu P)^{2} is at most the cost of this particular coupling:

𝒲2​(μ​P,ν​P)2≤E​‖𝒙′−𝒚′‖2≤(1−ρ¯)​𝒲2​(μ,ν)2,\mathcal{W}_{2}(\mu P,\nu P)^{2}\;\leq\;\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\left\lVert\bm{x}^{\prime}-\bm{y}^{\prime}\right\rVert^{2}\;\leq\;\big(1-\bar{\rho}\big)\,\mathcal{W}_{2}(\mu,\nu)^{2}\,, (A74)

and taking square roots recovers (A61) exactly.

∙\bullet 9) Summary of the approach. Three ingredients combine, none of which is a bound on PP as an operator on ℝd2\mathbb{R}^{d^{2}}: (1) 𝒲2\mathcal{W}_{2} is an infimum over couplings, so any one coupling of the images gives a valid upper bound; (2) the synchronous coupling is reusing the same random index for both copies and is a legitimate choice precisely because PP is defined by mixing over that same randomness, and it makes the target-dependent noise cancel identically; (3) what remains is a bound on Ei​‖𝑴i​𝒛‖2\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}_{i}\left\lVert\bm{M}_{i}\bm{z}\right\rVert^{2} for the fixed vector 𝒛=𝒙−𝒚\bm{z}=\bm{x}-\bm{y}, which is exactly the pointwise mean-square contraction already established in Lemma A1. This lemma is a statement purely about the 𝑴i\bm{M}_{i}’s and 𝑨¯=∑ipi​𝒂i​𝒂i⊤\bar{\bm{A}}=\sum_{i}p_{i}\bm{a}_{i}\bm{a}_{i}^{\top}, requiring no coupling of its own. The contraction of PP in 𝒲2\mathcal{W}_{2} is thus assembled entirely from the per-index contraction of Lemma A1, transported to the space of distributions by the coupling device. It is not, and could not be, a statement recoverable from maxi⁡‖𝑴i‖2\max_{i}\left\lVert\bm{M}_{i}\right\rVert_{2} alone.

Proof of Theorem A6.
Proof.

Exact mean recursion. The update (A49) is linear in 𝒔t\bm{s}_{t}, and iti_{t} is independent of ℱt⊇σ⁡(𝒔t)\mathcal{F}_{t}\supseteq\sigma(\bm{s}_{t}). Hence, conditioning on ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t},

E⁡[𝒔t+1|ℱt]=E⁡[𝑴it]​𝒔t+β​E​[cit​𝒂it]=(𝑰−β​𝑨¯)​𝒔t+β​𝒃¯,\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[\bm{s}_{t+1}\,\big|\,\mathcal{F}_{t}\big]\;=\;\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[\bm{M}_{i_{t}}\big]\,\bm{s}_{t}+\beta\,\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[c_{i_{t}}\bm{a}_{i_{t}}\big]\;=\;\big(\bm{I}-\beta\bar{\bm{A}}\big)\,\bm{s}_{t}+\beta\,\bar{\bm{b}}\,, (A75)

and the tower property gives (A51). This equation holds with equality and is not an approximation: no linearization was needed because the update itself is linear. Subtracting the fixed-point relation 𝒔LS=(𝑰−β​𝑨¯)​𝒔LS+β​𝒃¯\bm{s}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}=(\bm{I}-\beta\bar{\bm{A}})\bm{s}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}+\beta\bar{\bm{b}}, which holds by the normal equations (A48) (𝒃¯=𝑨¯​𝒔LS\bar{\bm{b}}=\bar{\bm{A}}\bm{s}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}), yields the error form and, by induction,

E⁡[𝒆t]=(𝑰−β​𝑨¯)t​E​[𝒆0].\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[\bm{e}_{t}\big]\;=\;\big(\bm{I}-\beta\bar{\bm{A}}\big)^{t}\,\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[\bm{e}_{0}\big]\,. (A76)

Spectral radius. 𝑨¯\bar{\bm{A}} is symmetric positive definite; let 0<λmin=λ1≤⋯≤λd2=λmax0<\lambda_{\min}=\lambda_{1}\leq\dots\leq\lambda_{d^{2}}=\lambda_{\max} be its eigenvalues. For any unit vector 𝒙\bm{x}, 𝒙⊤​𝑨¯​𝒙=∑ipi​(𝒂i⊤​𝒙)2≤maxi⁡‖𝒂i‖2\bm{x}^{\top}\bar{\bm{A}}\bm{x}=\sum_{i}p_{i}(\bm{a}_{i}^{\top}\bm{x})^{2}\leq\max_{i}\left\lVert\bm{a}_{i}\right\rVert^{2}, so

β​λmax≤β​maxi​‖𝒂i‖2< 2\beta\,\lambda_{\max}\;\leq\;\beta\,\max_{i}\left\lVert\bm{a}_{i}\right\rVert^{2}\;<\;2 (A77)

by (A45). Hence, every eigenvalue 1−β​λk1-\beta\lambda_{k} of 𝑰−β​𝑨¯\bm{I}-\beta\bar{\bm{A}} lies in (−1,1)(-1,1): 1−β​λk<11-\beta\lambda_{k}<1 since β​λk>0\beta\lambda_{k}>0, and 1−β​λk>−11-\beta\lambda_{k}>-1 since β​λk<2\beta\lambda_{k}<2. The matrix is symmetric, so its spectral norm equals r=maxk⁡|1−β​λk|<1r=\max_{k}|1-\beta\lambda_{k}|<1 and ‖E⁡[𝒆t]‖≤rt​‖𝒆0‖\left\lVert\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\bm{e}_{t}]\right\rVert\leq r^{t}\left\lVert\bm{e}_{0}\right\rVert, i.e. linear convergence of E⁡[𝑺t]\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\bm{S}_{t}] to 𝑺LS\bm{S}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}} in Frobenius norm (‖𝒔‖2=‖𝑺‖F\left\lVert\bm{s}\right\rVert_{2}=\left\lVert\bm{S}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}).

Exact unbiasedness. The fixed point of the affine map 𝒛↦(𝑰−β​𝑨¯)​𝒛+β​𝒃¯\bm{z}\mapsto(\bm{I}-\beta\bar{\bm{A}})\bm{z}+\beta\bar{\bm{b}} is unique (β​𝑨¯\beta\bar{\bm{A}} invertible) and equals 𝑨¯−1​𝒃¯=𝒔LS\bar{\bm{A}}^{-1}\bar{\bm{b}}=\bm{s}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}} for every β\beta in the admissible range: the limit of the mean does not depend on β\beta and carries no O⁡(β)O(\beta) correction. ∎

Proof of Theorem A7.
Proof.

Existence, uniqueness, membership in 𝒫2\mathcal{P}_{2}, and the geometric 𝒲2\mathcal{W}_{2}-convergence (A53) are Lemma A2. We have to prove (i)–(iv). In stationarity we write 𝒆∼πβ\bm{e}\sim\pi_{\beta} (centered at 𝒔LS\bm{s}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}), draw a fresh index ii independent of 𝒆\bm{e}, and use that

𝒆′:=𝑴i​𝒆+β​ρi​𝒂i​=𝑑​𝒆,\bm{e}^{\prime}\;:=\;\bm{M}_{i}\,\bm{e}+\beta\,\rho_{i}\,\bm{a}_{i}\;\overset{d}{=}\;\bm{e}\,, (A78)

with all first and second moments finite (πβ∈𝒫2\pi_{\beta}\in\mathcal{P}_{2}). Here =𝑑\overset{d}{=} means equality in distribution.

(i) Stationary mean. Taking expectations in (A78) and using the independence of ii and 𝒆\bm{e} together with the normal equations E⁡[ρ​𝒂]=𝟎\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\rho\bm{a}]=\bm{0}:

E⁡[𝒆]=E⁡[𝒆′]=E⁡[𝑴i]​E​[𝒆]+β​E​[ρi​𝒂i]=(𝑰−β​𝑨¯)​E​[𝒆],\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\bm{e}]\;=\;\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\bm{e}^{\prime}]\;=\;\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[\bm{M}_{i}\big]\,\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\bm{e}]+\beta\,\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[\rho_{i}\bm{a}_{i}\big]\;=\;\big(\bm{I}-\beta\bar{\bm{A}}\big)\,\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\bm{e}]\,, (A79)

hence β​𝑨¯​E​[𝒆]=𝟎\beta\bar{\bm{A}}\,\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\bm{e}]=\bm{0}, and since 𝑨¯\bar{\bm{A}} is invertible, E⁡[𝒆]=𝟎\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\bm{e}]=\bm{0}, i.e. Eπβ​[𝑺]=𝑺LS\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}_{\pi_{\beta}}[\bm{S}]=\bm{S}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}, which holds exactly.

(ii) Exact covariance equation. Expand 𝒆′​𝒆′⁣⊤\bm{e}^{\prime}\bm{e}^{\prime\top} from (A78):

𝒆′​𝒆′⁣⊤=𝑴i​𝒆​𝒆⊤​𝑴i+β​ρi​𝑴i​𝒆​𝒂i⊤+β​ρi​𝒂i​𝒆⊤​𝑴i+β2​ρi2​𝒂i​𝒂i⊤.\bm{e}^{\prime}\bm{e}^{\prime\top}\;=\;\bm{M}_{i}\bm{e}\bm{e}^{\top}\bm{M}_{i}\;+\;\beta\,\rho_{i}\,\bm{M}_{i}\bm{e}\,\bm{a}_{i}^{\top}\;+\;\beta\,\rho_{i}\,\bm{a}_{i}\bm{e}^{\top}\bm{M}_{i}\;+\;\beta^{2}\rho_{i}^{2}\,\bm{a}_{i}\bm{a}_{i}^{\top}\,. (A80)

Take expectations term by term, using the independence of ii and 𝒆\bm{e} and writing 𝑽β=E⁡[𝒆​𝒆⊤]\bm{V}_{\beta}=\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\bm{e}\bm{e}^{\top}].

Homogeneous term. Since 𝑴i​𝑽​𝑴i=𝑽−β⁡(𝒂i​𝒂i⊤​𝑽+𝑽​𝒂i​𝒂i⊤)+β2​(𝒂i⊤​𝑽​𝒂i)​𝒂i​𝒂i⊤\bm{M}_{i}\bm{V}\bm{M}_{i}=\bm{V}-\beta\big(\bm{a}_{i}\bm{a}_{i}^{\top}\bm{V}+\bm{V}\bm{a}_{i}\bm{a}_{i}^{\top}\big)+\beta^{2}\big(\bm{a}_{i}^{\top}\bm{V}\bm{a}_{i}\big)\bm{a}_{i}\bm{a}_{i}^{\top} (using 𝒂i​𝒂i⊤​𝑽​𝒂i​𝒂i⊤=(𝒂i⊤​𝑽​𝒂i)​𝒂i​𝒂i⊤\bm{a}_{i}\bm{a}_{i}^{\top}\bm{V}\bm{a}_{i}\bm{a}_{i}^{\top}=(\bm{a}_{i}^{\top}\bm{V}\bm{a}_{i})\,\bm{a}_{i}\bm{a}_{i}^{\top}),

E⁡[𝑴i​𝒆​𝒆⊤​𝑴i]=𝑽β−β⁡(𝑨¯​𝑽β+𝑽β​𝑨¯)+β2​E​[(𝒂⊤​𝑽β​𝒂)​𝒂​𝒂⊤].\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[\bm{M}_{i}\bm{e}\bm{e}^{\top}\bm{M}_{i}\big]\;=\;\bm{V}_{\beta}-\beta\big(\bar{\bm{A}}\bm{V}_{\beta}+\bm{V}_{\beta}\bar{\bm{A}}\big)+\beta^{2}\,\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[\big(\bm{a}^{\top}\bm{V}_{\beta}\bm{a}\big)\bm{a}\bm{a}^{\top}\big]\,. E⁡[ρi​𝑴i​𝒆​𝒂i⊤]=Ei​[ρi​𝑴i​E​[𝒆]​𝒂i⊤]= 0,\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[\rho_{i}\,\bm{M}_{i}\bm{e}\,\bm{a}_{i}^{\top}\big]\;=\;\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}_{i}\big[\rho_{i}\,\bm{M}_{i}\,\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\bm{e}]\,\bm{a}_{i}^{\top}\big]\;=\;\bm{0}\,, (A82)

Stationarity. Setting E⁡[𝒆′​𝒆′⁣⊤]=𝑽β\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\bm{e}^{\prime}\bm{e}^{\prime\top}]=\bm{V}_{\beta} and collecting,

Since 𝑽β⪰𝟎\bm{V}_{\beta}\succeq\bm{0}, we have 𝒂⊤​𝑽β​𝒂≥0\bm{a}^{\top}\bm{V}_{\beta}\bm{a}\geq 0, which gives the lower bound in (A55); and E⁡[(𝒂⊤​𝑽β​𝒂)​‖𝒂‖2]≤maxi⁡‖𝒂i‖2​E​[𝒂⊤​𝑽β​𝒂]=maxi⁡‖𝒂i‖2​tr⁡(𝑨¯​𝑽β)\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[(\bm{a}^{\top}\bm{V}_{\beta}\bm{a})\left\lVert\bm{a}\right\rVert^{2}]\leq\max_{i}\left\lVert\bm{a}_{i}\right\rVert^{2}\,\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\bm{a}^{\top}\bm{V}_{\beta}\bm{a}]=\max_{i}\left\lVert\bm{a}_{i}\right\rVert^{2}\,\tr(\bar{\bm{A}}\bm{V}_{\beta}), so

(2−β​maxi​‖𝒂i‖2)​tr⁡(𝑨¯​𝑽β)≤β​σ2,\big(2-\beta\max_{i}\left\lVert\bm{a}_{i}\right\rVert^{2}\big)\,\tr\big(\bar{\bm{A}}\bm{V}_{\beta}\big)\;\leq\;\beta\,\sigma^{2}\,, (A85)

the upper bound (the prefactor is positive by (A45)). Finally tr⁡𝑽β≤tr⁡(𝑨¯​𝑽β)/λmin​(𝑨¯)\tr\bm{V}_{\beta}\leq\tr(\bar{\bm{A}}\bm{V}_{\beta})/\lambda_{\min}(\bar{\bm{A}}) gives the Frobenius bound in (A55), and tr⁡𝑽β=O⁡(β)\tr\bm{V}_{\beta}=O(\beta) makes the quartic term in (A54) O⁡(β2)O(\beta^{2}), leaving the Lyapunov equation at leading order.

(iii) Misadjustment. For uniform sampling, 𝑨¯=1n​𝑨⊤​𝑨\bar{\bm{A}}=\tfrac{1}{n}\bm{A}^{\top}\bm{A} and L⁡(𝒔)=1n​‖𝑨​𝒔−𝒄‖2\mathrm{L}(\bm{s})=\tfrac{1}{n}\left\lVert\bm{A}\bm{s}-\bm{c}\right\rVert^{2}. Decompose with 𝑨​𝒔−𝒄=𝑨​𝒆−𝝆\bm{A}\bm{s}-\bm{c}=\bm{A}\bm{e}-\bm{\rho}, where 𝝆=(ρ1,…,ρn)⊤\bm{\rho}=(\rho_{1},\dots,\rho_{n})^{\top}: since 𝑨⊤​𝝆=n​E​[ρ​𝒂]=𝟎\bm{A}^{\top}\bm{\rho}=n\,\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\rho\bm{a}]=\bm{0},

L⁡(𝒔)=1n​‖𝑨​𝒆‖2−2n​𝒆⊤​𝑨⊤​𝝆+1n​‖𝝆‖2=1n​‖𝑨​𝒆‖2+Lmin,\mathrm{L}(\bm{s})\;=\;\tfrac{1}{n}\left\lVert\bm{A}\bm{e}\right\rVert^{2}-\tfrac{2}{n}\,\bm{e}^{\top}\bm{A}^{\top}\bm{\rho}+\tfrac{1}{n}\left\lVert\bm{\rho}\right\rVert^{2}\;=\;\tfrac{1}{n}\left\lVert\bm{A}\bm{e}\right\rVert^{2}+\mathrm{L}_{\min}\,, (A86)

Eπβ​[L]−Lmin=1n​E​[𝒆⊤​𝑨⊤​𝑨​𝒆]=tr⁡(𝑨¯​𝑽β),\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}_{\pi_{\beta}}[\mathrm{L}]-\mathrm{L}_{\min}\;=\;\tfrac{1}{n}\,\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[\bm{e}^{\top}\bm{A}^{\top}\bm{A}\,\bm{e}\big]\;=\;\tr\big(\bar{\bm{A}}\,\bm{V}_{\beta}\big)\,, (A87)

and inserting the exact trace identity (A84) gives (A56). The two-sided bound (A57) follows from the trace bounds (A55). Since the upper and lower bounds differ by a factor 2/(2−β​maxi​‖𝒂i‖2)=1+O⁡(β)2/(2-\beta\max_{i}\left\lVert\bm{a}_{i}\right\rVert^{2})=1+O(\beta), the excess loss equals β2​σ2​(1+O⁡(β))\tfrac{\beta}{2}\sigma^{2}(1+O(\beta)).

(iv) Transient. Condition on ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t} and expand (A49):

E⁡[‖𝒆t+1‖2|ℱt]=E⁡[‖𝑴i​𝒆t‖2|ℱt]+ 2​β​E​[ρi​𝒂i⊤​𝑴i]​𝒆t+β2​σ2.\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[\left\lVert\bm{e}_{t+1}\right\rVert^{2}\,\big|\,\mathcal{F}_{t}\big]\;=\;\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[\left\lVert\bm{M}_{i}\bm{e}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}\,\big|\,\mathcal{F}_{t}\big]\;+\;2\beta\,\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[\rho_{i}\,\bm{a}_{i}^{\top}\bm{M}_{i}\big]\,\bm{e}_{t}\;+\;\beta^{2}\sigma^{2}\,. (A88)

For the middle term, 𝒂i⊤​𝑴i=(1−β​‖𝒂i‖2)​𝒂i⊤\bm{a}_{i}^{\top}\bm{M}_{i}=(1-\beta\left\lVert\bm{a}_{i}\right\rVert^{2})\,\bm{a}_{i}^{\top}, so by the normal equations

with 𝒘=E⁡[ρ​‖𝒂‖2​𝒂]\bm{w}=\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\rho\left\lVert\bm{a}\right\rVert^{2}\bm{a}] as in the statement. Outside stationarity this cross term does not vanish, and it is O⁡(β2)O(\beta^{2}) in total. Lemma A1 and Young’s inequality −2​β2​𝒘⊤​𝒆≤ρ¯2​‖𝒆‖2+2​β4ρ¯​‖𝒘‖2-2\beta^{2}\bm{w}^{\top}\bm{e}\leq\tfrac{\bar{\rho}}{2}\left\lVert\bm{e}\right\rVert^{2}+\tfrac{2\beta^{4}}{\bar{\rho}}\left\lVert\bm{w}\right\rVert^{2} give

E⁡[‖𝒆t+1‖2|ℱt]≤(1−ρ¯2)​‖𝒆t‖2+β2​σ2+2​β4ρ¯​‖𝒘‖2.\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[\left\lVert\bm{e}_{t+1}\right\rVert^{2}\,\big|\,\mathcal{F}_{t}\big]\;\leq\;\Big(1-\tfrac{\bar{\rho}}{2}\Big)\left\lVert\bm{e}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}\;+\;\beta^{2}\sigma^{2}\;+\;\tfrac{2\beta^{4}}{\bar{\rho}}\left\lVert\bm{w}\right\rVert^{2}\,. (A90)

Taking full expectations and iterating the affine recursion (its geometric series is bounded by 2/ρ¯2/\bar{\rho}) yields (A58). Since ρ¯=γβ​λmin=Θ⁡(β)\bar{\rho}=\gamma_{\beta}\lambda_{\min}=\Theta(\beta), the horizon 2​β2​σ2/ρ¯+4​β4​‖𝒘‖2/ρ¯22\beta^{2}\sigma^{2}/\bar{\rho}+4\beta^{4}\left\lVert\bm{w}\right\rVert^{2}/\bar{\rho}^{2} is O⁡(β)O(\beta), consistent with (A55). ∎

Corollary A1 (Recovering exact convergence to 𝑺LS\bm{S}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}).

Three standard mechanisms remove the O⁡(β)O(\sqrt{\beta}) fluctuation:

  1. (i) Diminishing step sizes (Robbins–Monro): βt↓0\beta_{t}\downarrow 0, ∑tβt=∞\sum_{t}\beta_{t}=\infty (e.g. βt∝1/t\beta_{t}\propto 1/t) gives 𝑺t→𝑺LS\bm{S}_{t}\to\bm{S}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}} almost surely.

  2. (ii) Iterate averaging (Polyak–Ruppert / ergodic average): with constant β\beta, the time average 𝑺¯T=1T​∑t≤T𝑺t→Eπβ​[𝑺]=𝑺LS\bar{\bm{S}}_{T}=\tfrac{1}{T}\sum_{t\leq T}\bm{S}_{t}\to\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}_{\pi_{\beta}}[\bm{S}]=\bm{S}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}} almost surely - and by Theorem A7 (i) the average is exactly unbiased.

  3. (iii) Small-β\beta limit: by (A55), πβ\pi_{\beta} concentrates on 𝑺LS\bm{S}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}} as β→0\beta\to 0, with the explicit bias–variance trade-off: larger β\beta tracks nonstationary targets faster, smaller β\beta reduces the steady-state loss excess (A57), which is the standard LMS trade-off, inherited verbatim.

Corollary A2 (Consistent targets).

The inconsistency, not the count n>d2n>d^{2}, is what forbids exact convergence. Let us assume that the targets happen to be realizable, that is ci=𝐯i⊤​𝐒∘​𝐤ic_{i}=\bm{v}_{i}^{\top}\bm{S}^{\circ}\bm{k}_{i} for some 𝐒∘\bm{S}^{\circ}. In this case Lmin=0\mathrm{L}_{\min}=0, all residuals ρi\rho_{i} vanish, the driving noise in (A49) disappears, and the Fejér-monotone argument of the consistent case applies unchanged: 𝐒t→𝐒∘\bm{S}_{t}\to\bm{S}^{\circ} (unique by full column rank) almost surely, linearly, for arbitrarily many associations. Two distinguished targets realize this structurally:

  1. (i) the correlation target ci=𝒗i⊤​𝒌ic_{i}=\bm{v}_{i}^{\top}\bm{k}_{i}, solved by 𝑺=𝑰\bm{S}=\bm{I} for every nn;

  2. (ii) the norm target ci=‖𝒗i‖2c_{i}=\left\lVert\bm{v}_{i}\right\rVert^{2}, solved by any exact retrieval memory 𝑺​𝒌i=𝒗i\bm{S}\bm{k}_{i}=\bm{v}_{i} (in particular autoassociatively by 𝑺=𝑰\bm{S}=\bm{I}).

For these targets the recognition memory has effectively unbounded association count as long as realizability holds.

A3.5.5  Remarks

Memory for the overloaded setting.

Beyond capacity, 𝑺\bm{S} is no longer a table but an online linear regressor: the read-out 𝒗⊤​𝑺LS​𝒌\bm{v}^{\top}\bm{S}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}\bm{k} is the best linear prediction (in the pp-weighted least-squares sense) of the scalar signal cc from the bilinear feature 𝒌⊗𝒗\bm{k}\otimes\bm{v}. Degradation is graceful since overload produces averaging plus an O⁡(β)O(\sqrt{\beta}) jitter, never blow-up, since the homogeneous factors keep spectral norm ≤1\leq 1.

Assumptions for the proofs.

Independence of iti_{t} from the past makes the mean recursion exact and factorizes the covariance cross terms; the normal equations kill the driving term in the mean and the cross terms in stationarity (via E⁡[𝒆]=𝟎\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\bm{e}]=\bm{0}); the step condition (A45) enters three times: (1) γβ>0\gamma_{\beta}>0 (contraction), (2) β​λmax​(𝑨¯)<2\beta\lambda_{\max}(\bar{\bm{A}})<2 (mean stability), and (3) 2−β​maxi​‖𝒂i‖2>02-\beta\max_{i}\left\lVert\bm{a}_{i}\right\rVert^{2}>0 (trace upper bound). Full column rank gives λmin​(𝑨¯)>0\lambda_{\min}(\bar{\bm{A}})>0, used for uniqueness of 𝒔LS\bm{s}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}, for ρ¯>0\bar{\rho}>0, and to convert tr⁡(𝑨¯​𝑽β)\tr(\bar{\bm{A}}\bm{V}_{\beta}) into a bound on tr⁡𝑽β\tr\bm{V}_{\beta}. Linearity of the update in the state is what makes every step of the argument exact rather than a Taylor expansion which we obtain from the quadratic loss.

Conflicting targets on the same pair: averaging vs. overwriting.

The canonical inconsistency is one pair (𝒌,𝒗)(\bm{k},\bm{v}) presented with different targets. Under random sampling with probabilities pjp_{j} over targets cjc_{j}, the stationary mean read-out is the weighted average, 𝒗⊤​Eπβ​[𝑺]​𝒌=∑jpj​cj/∑jpj\bm{v}^{\top}\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}_{\pi_{\beta}}[\bm{S}]\,\bm{k}=\sum_{j}p_{j}c_{j}/\sum_{j}p_{j} (the LS solution for identical rows). Under sequential presentation the same rule overwrites: the contraction drives the read-out to the most recent target. Random replay averages; ordered replay recencies, therefore the sampling protocol, not the rule, decides about overwrite behavior.

Forget gate: recency-weighted least squares.

With the scalar gated variant 𝑺t+1=ft​𝑺t−β⁡(𝒗t⊤​ft​𝑺t​𝒌t−ct)​𝒗t​𝒌t⊤\bm{S}_{t+1}=\mathrm{f}_{t}\bm{S}_{t}-\beta(\bm{v}_{t}^{\top}\mathrm{f}_{t}\bm{S}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}-c_{t})\bm{v}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top}, ft∈(0,1)\mathrm{f}_{t}\in(0,1), the steady state is the corresponding exponentially weighted least-squares solution: old associations are geometrically down-weighted, so the effective association count is finite (∼1/(1−f)\sim 1/(1-\mathrm{f})) and the memory tracks a drifting target distribution. Therefore, the overloaded regime is exactly where the forget gate is most relevant.

Summary.

For n>d2n>d^{2} associations the randomized Kronecker Delta Rule with constant β\beta does not converge to a point but to a stationary distribution: its mean is exactly the sampling-weighted least-squares memory 𝑺LS=argmin∑ipi​(𝒗i⊤​𝑺​𝒌i−ci)2\bm{S}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}=\mathop{\mathrm{argmin}\,}\sum_{i}p_{i}(\bm{v}_{i}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{k}_{i}-c_{i})^{2} (the minimizer of L\mathrm{L} for uniform sampling), its covariance is O⁡(β)O(\beta) and solves the exact stationarity equation (A54) driven by the optimal residuals, and its loss sits at Lmin+β2​E​[ρi2​‖𝒌i‖2​‖𝒗i‖2]\mathrm{L}_{\min}+\tfrac{\beta}{2}\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\rho_{i}^{2}\left\lVert\bm{k}_{i}\right\rVert^{2}\left\lVert\bm{v}_{i}\right\rVert^{2}] up to an explicit 1+O⁡(β)1+O(\beta) factor. All of this is proven from first principles: an exact linear mean recursion with spectral radius <1<1; a synchronous-coupling 𝒲2\mathcal{W}_{2}-contraction plus Banach fixed point for existence, uniqueness, and geometric convergence of πβ\pi_{\beta}; exact moment identities in stationarity for mean and covariance; an exact trace identity for the misadjustment; and a Young-inequality recursion for the transient. Averaging or annealing β\beta recovers 𝑺LS\bm{S}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}} exactly; consistent target structures (correlation target, norm target with a retrieval solution) escape the capacity limit altogether; and a forget gate turns the steady state into recency-weighted least squares.

A3.6  Norm Bounds for the KronLSTM with Steady-State Solution

We derive a two-sided norm bound for the steady state of the randomized Kronecker Delta Rule with more than d2d^{2} associations. Running memories or data stream i.e. online updates are covered via the steady state, therefore we obtain an expected bound on the online updated memory.

A3.6.1  Overview

For the overloaded KronLSTM (nn associations, features 𝒂i=𝒌i⊗𝒗i\bm{a}_{i}=\bm{k}_{i}\otimes\bm{v}_{i}, sampling weights pip_{i}) the randomized Kronecker Delta Rule converges around the weighted least-squares memory 𝑺LS\bm{S}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}. We derive a two-sided bound on its Frobenius norm from an exact energy (Pythagoras) identity:

E⁡[c2]−E⁡[ρ2]λmax​(𝑨¯)≤‖𝑺LS‖F2≤E⁡[c2]−E⁡[ρ2]λmin​(𝑨¯),\frac{\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[c^{2}]-\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\rho^{2}]}{\lambda_{\max}(\bar{\bm{A}})}\;\leq\;\left\lVert\bm{S}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}\;\leq\;\frac{\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[c^{2}]-\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\rho^{2}]}{\lambda_{\min}(\bar{\bm{A}})}\,,

where ρi\rho_{i} are the optimal residuals and 𝑨¯=E⁡[𝒂​𝒂⊤]\bar{\bm{A}}=\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\bm{a}\bm{a}^{\top}] is the feature second moment. The numerator is the explained target energy; the bound is attained (both sides coincide) for isotropic designs, and in the orthonormal design it reproduces ‖𝑺⋆‖F2=∑ici2\left\lVert\bm{S}^{\star}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}=\sum_{i}c_{i}^{2} of the target-weighted Hebbian superposition exactly. Combined with the steady-state analysis, it yields an a-priori bound on the expected memory norm of the running iterates.

A3.6.2  Setting and nomenclature

As before, we assume nn associations (𝒌i,𝒗i,ci)(\bm{k}_{i},\bm{v}_{i},c_{i}) with features 𝒂i=𝒌i⊗𝒗i∈ℝd2\bm{a}_{i}=\bm{k}_{i}\otimes\bm{v}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d^{2}}, ‖𝒂i‖=‖𝒌i‖​‖𝒗i‖\left\lVert\bm{a}_{i}\right\rVert=\left\lVert\bm{k}_{i}\right\rVert\left\lVert\bm{v}_{i}\right\rVert, sampling probabilities pi>0p_{i}>0, and

𝑨¯\displaystyle\bar{\bm{A}}\; =E⁡[𝒂​𝒂⊤]=∑i=1npi​𝒂i​𝒂i⊤,𝒔LS=argmin𝒔E⁡[(𝒂⊤​𝒔−c)2]=𝑨¯−1​E​[c​𝒂],\displaystyle=\;\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[\bm{a}\bm{a}^{\top}\big]\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}\,\bm{a}_{i}\bm{a}_{i}^{\top}\,,\qquad\bm{s}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}\;=\;\mathop{\mathrm{argmin}\,}_{\bm{s}}\;\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[(\bm{a}^{\top}\bm{s}-c)^{2}\big]\;=\;\bar{\bm{A}}^{-1}\,\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[c\,\bm{a}\big]\,, (A91)
ρi\displaystyle\rho_{i}\; =ci−𝒂i⊤𝒔LS,E[ρ𝒂]= 0(normal equations),\displaystyle=\;c_{i}-\bm{a}_{i}^{\top}\bm{s}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}\,,\qquad\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[\rho\,\bm{a}\big]\;=\;\bm{0}\quad\text{(normal equations)}\,, (A92)

assuming 𝑨¯≻𝟎\bar{\bm{A}}\succ\bm{0} (features span ℝd2\mathbb{R}^{d^{2}}; the rank-deficient case is treated in the remarks). All expectations are over i∼pi\sim p. Recall ‖𝒔‖2=‖𝑺‖F\left\lVert\bm{s}\right\rVert_{2}=\left\lVert\bm{S}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}} for 𝒔=vec⁡(𝑺)\bm{s}=\vecop(\bm{S}), and that for uniform sampling E⁡[ρ2]=Lmin\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\rho^{2}]=\mathrm{L}_{\min}, the minimum of the loss L\mathrm{L}.

A3.6.3  An exact energy identity

Lemma A3 (Energy identity).

Let yi:=𝐚i⊤​𝐬LS=𝐯i⊤​𝐒LS​𝐤iy_{i}:=\bm{a}_{i}^{\top}\bm{s}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}=\bm{v}_{i}^{\top}\bm{S}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}\bm{k}_{i} be the optimal read-outs. Then E⁡[ρ​y]=0\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\rho\,y]=0 and

E⁡[c2]=E⁡[y2]+E⁡[ρ2],(𝒔LS)⊤​𝑨¯​𝒔LS=E⁡[y2]=E⁡[c2]−E⁡[ρ2].\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[c^{2}\big]\;=\;\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[y^{2}\big]\;+\;\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[\rho^{2}\big]\,,\qquad\big(\bm{s}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}\big)^{\!\top}\bar{\bm{A}}\;\bm{s}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}\;=\;\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[y^{2}\big]\;=\;\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[c^{2}\big]-\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[\rho^{2}\big]\,. (A93)
Proof.

E⁡[ρ​y]=E​[ρ​𝒂]⊤​𝒔LS=0\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\rho\,y]=\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\rho\,\bm{a}]^{\top}\bm{s}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}=0 by the normal equations; with c=y+ρc=y+\rho this gives the first identity. The second follows from E⁡[y2]=(𝒔LS)⊤​E​[𝒂​𝒂⊤]​𝒔LS\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[y^{2}]=(\bm{s}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}})^{\top}\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\bm{a}\bm{a}^{\top}]\,\bm{s}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}. ∎

The stored read-out energy of the least-squares memory equals the target energy minus the unexplained (residual) energy. Therefore, the memory can only be as large as the part of the target signal that the bilinear features can explain.

A3.6.4  The Norm Bound

Theorem A8 (Two-sided Frobenius-norm bound).

With λmin,λmax\lambda_{\min},\lambda_{\max} the extreme eigenvalues of 𝐀¯\bar{\bm{A}},

E⁡[c2]−E⁡[ρ2]λmax​(𝑨¯)≤‖𝑺LS‖F2≤E⁡[c2]−E⁡[ρ2]λmin​(𝑨¯).\boxed{\;\frac{\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[c^{2}\big]-\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[\rho^{2}\big]}{\lambda_{\max}(\bar{\bm{A}})}\;\leq\;\left\lVert\bm{S}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}\;\leq\;\frac{\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[c^{2}\big]-\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[\rho^{2}\big]}{\lambda_{\min}(\bar{\bm{A}})}\,.\;} (A94)

In particular, since σmax​(𝐒LS)≤‖𝐒LS‖F\sigma_{\max}(\bm{S}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}})\leq\left\lVert\bm{S}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}},

σmax​(𝑺LS)≤E⁡[c2]−E⁡[ρ2]λmin​(𝑨¯)≤E⁡[c2]λmin​(𝑨¯).\sigma_{\max}\big(\bm{S}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}\big)\;\leq\;\sqrt{\frac{\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[c^{2}\big]-\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[\rho^{2}\big]}{\lambda_{\min}(\bar{\bm{A}})}}\;\leq\;\sqrt{\frac{\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[c^{2}\big]}{\lambda_{\min}(\bar{\bm{A}})}}\,. (A95)
Proof.

Sandwich the quadratic form: λmin​‖𝒔LS‖2≤(𝒔LS)⊤​𝑨¯​𝒔LS≤λmax​‖𝒔LS‖2\lambda_{\min}\left\lVert\bm{s}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}\right\rVert^{2}\leq(\bm{s}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}})^{\top}\bar{\bm{A}}\,\bm{s}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}\leq\lambda_{\max}\left\lVert\bm{s}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}\right\rVert^{2}, and insert (A93). ∎

Corollary A3 (First-moment variant).

From λmin​‖𝐬‖2≤𝐬⊤​𝐀¯​𝐬=𝐬⊤​E​[c​𝐚]≤‖𝐬‖​E​[|c|​‖𝐚‖]\lambda_{\min}\left\lVert\bm{s}\right\rVert^{2}\leq\bm{s}^{\top}\bar{\bm{A}}\bm{s}=\bm{s}^{\top}\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[c\bm{a}]\leq\left\lVert\bm{s}\right\rVert\,\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[|c|\,\left\lVert\bm{a}\right\rVert],

‖𝑺LS‖F≤E⁡[|ci|​‖𝒌i‖​‖𝒗i‖]λmin​(𝑨¯).\left\lVert\bm{S}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}\;\leq\;\frac{\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[\,|c_{i}|\,\left\lVert\bm{k}_{i}\right\rVert\left\lVert\bm{v}_{i}\right\rVert\big]}{\lambda_{\min}(\bar{\bm{A}})}\,. (A96)

The accumulated write mass β​ct​‖𝐤t‖​‖𝐯t‖\beta\,c_{t}\left\lVert\bm{k}_{t}\right\rVert\left\lVert\bm{v}_{t}\right\rVert is exactly the quantity whose first moment appears here. The second moment bound (A94) is usually much sharper (it divides by λmin\lambda_{\min} only once, under the square root).

A3.6.5  Tightness and special cases

Isotropic design gives equality.

If 𝑨¯=E⁡[‖𝒂‖2]d2​𝑰\bar{\bm{A}}=\tfrac{\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\left\lVert\bm{a}\right\rVert^{2}]}{d^{2}}\,\bm{I} (features spread evenly over ℝd2\mathbb{R}^{d^{2}}), then λmin=λmax\lambda_{\min}=\lambda_{\max} and (A94) collapses to the identity

‖𝑺LS‖F2=d2​(E⁡[c2]−E⁡[ρ2])E⁡[‖𝒂‖2].\left\lVert\bm{S}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}\;=\;\frac{d^{2}\,\big(\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[c^{2}]-\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\rho^{2}]\big)}{\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\left\lVert\bm{a}\right\rVert^{2}]}\,. (A97)
Orthonormal design recovers the Hebbian superposition norm.

For n=d2n=d^{2} with orthonormal {𝒌i}\{\bm{k}_{i}\}, orthonormal {𝒗i}\{\bm{v}_{i}\}, and uniform sampling, the features are orthonormal, 𝑨¯=𝑰/d2\bar{\bm{A}}=\bm{I}/d^{2}, the system is consistent (ρ≡0\rho\equiv 0), and (A94) holds with equality:

‖𝑺⋆‖F2=d2​E​[c2]=∑i=1d2ci2,\left\lVert\bm{S}^{\star}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}\;=\;d^{2}\;\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[c^{2}]\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^{d^{2}}c_{i}^{2}\,, (A98)

exactly the Frobenius norm of the target-weighted Hebbian superposition 𝑺⋆=∑ici​𝒗i​𝒌i⊤\bm{S}^{\star}=\sum_{i}c_{i}\bm{v}_{i}\bm{k}_{i}^{\top}. The bound is therefore attained, not merely an estimate.

Unit-norm keys and values give a d2d^{2} conditioning factor.

If ‖𝒌i‖=‖𝒗i‖=1\left\lVert\bm{k}_{i}\right\rVert=\left\lVert\bm{v}_{i}\right\rVert=1 then tr⁡𝑨¯=E⁡[‖𝒂‖2]=1\tr\bar{\bm{A}}=\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\left\lVert\bm{a}\right\rVert^{2}]=1, so λmin≤1/d2≤λmax\lambda_{\min}\leq 1/d^{2}\leq\lambda_{\max}: the lower bound in (A94) is at most E⁡[c2]−E⁡[ρ2]\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[c^{2}]-\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\rho^{2}], the upper bound at least d2​(E⁡[c2]−E⁡[ρ2])d^{2}(\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[c^{2}]-\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\rho^{2}]), with both collapsing to the latter in the isotropic case. Ill-spread designs pay in λmin\lambda_{\min}: the worst case is a target profile aligned with the least-covered feature direction, and the 1/λmin1/\lambda_{\min} dependence is unavoidable in general.

Consistent case where association errors are zero.

If the system is consistent (ρ≡0\rho\equiv 0; e.g. n≤d2n\leq d^{2} with independent features, or the correlation/norm targets), then 𝑺LS=𝑺⋆\bm{S}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}=\bm{S}^{\star} is the exact solution and

‖𝑺⋆‖F2≤E⁡[c2]λmin​(𝑨¯).\left\lVert\bm{S}^{\star}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}\;\leq\;\frac{\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[c^{2}]}{\lambda_{\min}(\bar{\bm{A}})}\,. (A99)

Residual energy can only shrink the memory: overload (inconsistency) makes the least-squares memory smaller than a consistent memory with the same target energy, never larger.

Rank-deficient features.

If the features do not span ℝd2\mathbb{R}^{d^{2}} (n<d2n<d^{2} or dependent 𝒂i\bm{a}_{i}), replace 𝑺LS\bm{S}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}} by the minimum-Frobenius-norm least-squares solution and λmin\lambda_{\min} by the smallest nonzero eigenvalue of 𝑨¯\bar{\bm{A}}: since 𝒔LS∈span⁡{𝒂i}\bm{s}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}\in\spanop\{\bm{a}_{i}\} (as do the iterates from 𝑺0=𝟎\bm{S}_{0}=\bm{0}), the sandwich argument applies on that subspace and (A94) holds verbatim with λmin+\lambda_{\min}^{+}.

A3.6.6  Bound on the memory norm for steady-state and all updates

Bound on the memory norm for steady-state distribution.

First, we consider a bound on the memory norm under the steady-state distribution.

Corollary A4 (Bound on the steady-state memory norm).

Under the randomized rule with step size 0<β<2/maxi⁡‖𝐚i‖20<\beta<2/\max_{i}\left\lVert\bm{a}_{i}\right\rVert^{2}, the stationary distribution πβ\pi_{\beta} has mean exactly 𝐒LS\bm{S}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}, so the second moment decomposes orthogonally, Eπβ​‖𝐒‖F2=‖𝐒LS‖F2+tr⁡𝐕β\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}_{\pi_{\beta}}\left\lVert\bm{S}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}=\left\lVert\bm{S}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}+\tr\bm{V}_{\beta}, and with the covariance trace bound of the steady-state note,

Eπβ​[‖𝑺‖F2]≤E⁡[c2]−E⁡[ρ2]λmin​(𝑨¯)+β​E​[ρ2​‖𝒌‖2​‖𝒗‖2](2−β​maxi​‖𝒂i‖2)​λmin​(𝑨¯).\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}_{\pi_{\beta}}\!\left[\left\lVert\bm{S}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}\right]\;\leq\;\frac{\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[c^{2}]-\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\rho^{2}]}{\lambda_{\min}(\bar{\bm{A}})}\;+\;\frac{\beta\;\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[\rho^{2}\left\lVert\bm{k}\right\rVert^{2}\left\lVert\bm{v}\right\rVert^{2}\big]}{\big(2-\beta\max_{i}\left\lVert\bm{a}_{i}\right\rVert^{2}\big)\,\lambda_{\min}(\bar{\bm{A}})}\,. (A100)

The first term is the size of the memory content, the second the O⁡(β)O(\beta) fluctuation; for β→0\beta\to 0 or in the consistent case the bound reduces to Theorem A8.

Theorem A9 (Two-sided memory norm bound for the steady state).

Let πβ\pi_{\beta} be the steady-state law of (A16), 𝐕β=Eπβ​[𝐞​𝐞⊤]\bm{V}_{\beta}=\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}_{\pi_{\beta}}[\bm{e}\bm{e}^{\top}] its covariance as in Theorem A7 (ii) (the two coincide because the stationary mean is exactly 𝐬LS\bm{s}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}), σ2=E⁡[ρ2​‖𝐚‖2]\sigma^{2}=\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\rho^{2}\left\lVert\bm{a}\right\rVert^{2}], and write

Amax2:=maxi⁡‖𝒂i‖2=maxi⁡‖𝒌i‖2​‖𝒗i‖2,κ:=β​Amax2∈(0,2),A_{\max}^{2}\;:=\;\max_{i}\left\lVert\bm{a}_{i}\right\rVert^{2}\;=\;\max_{i}\left\lVert\bm{k}_{i}\right\rVert^{2}\left\lVert\bm{v}_{i}\right\rVert^{2}\,,\qquad\kappa\;:=\;\beta\,A_{\max}^{2}\;\in\;(0,2)\,, (A101)

the last inclusion being the step-size condition (A45). Then the energy identity

𝒔LS⊤​𝑨¯​𝒔LS=E⁡[c2]−E⁡[ρ2]\bm{s}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}\top}\bar{\bm{A}}\,\bm{s}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}\;=\;\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[c^{2}]\,-\,\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\rho^{2}] (A102)

holds, hence the least-squares memory is pinned on both sides,

E⁡[c2]−E⁡[ρ2]λmax​(𝑨¯)≤‖𝑺LS‖F2≤E⁡[c2]−E⁡[ρ2]λmin​(𝑨¯),\frac{\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[c^{2}]-\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\rho^{2}]}{\lambda_{\max}(\bar{\bm{A}})}\;\leq\;\left\lVert\bm{S}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}\;\leq\;\frac{\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[c^{2}]-\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\rho^{2}]}{\lambda_{\min}(\bar{\bm{A}})}\,, (A103)

and the steady-state memory itself satisfies

Eπβ​[‖𝑺‖F2]=‖𝑺LS‖F2+tr⁡𝑽β,tr⁡𝑽β≤β​E​[ρ2​‖𝒂‖2](2−κ)​λmin​(𝑨¯).\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}_{\pi_{\beta}}\big[\left\lVert\bm{S}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}\big]\;=\;\left\lVert\bm{S}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}\;+\;\tr\bm{V}_{\beta}\,,\qquad\tr\bm{V}_{\beta}\;\leq\;\frac{\beta\,\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[\rho^{2}\left\lVert\bm{a}\right\rVert^{2}\big]}{\big(2-\kappa\big)\,\lambda_{\min}(\bar{\bm{A}})}\,. (A104)

The fluctuation term admits the exact decomposition

tr⁡(𝑨¯​𝑽β)\displaystyle\tr\big(\bar{\bm{A}}\bm{V}_{\beta}\big)\; =β2​σ2+Rβ,\displaystyle=\;\frac{\beta}{2}\,\sigma^{2}\;+\;R_{\beta}\,, (A105)

For κ≤1\kappa\leq 1 that coefficient is ≤0\leq 0, so dropping the E⁡[ρ2]\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\rho^{2}] term gives (A107); for κ>1\kappa>1, using E⁡[ρ2]≤E⁡[c2]\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\rho^{2}]\leq\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[c^{2}] gives the factor 1+2​(κ−1)/(2−κ)=κ/(2−κ)1+2(\kappa-1)/(2-\kappa)=\kappa/(2-\kappa). ∎

Residuals lower the bound. The E⁡[ρ2]\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\rho^{2}] term in (A106) enters with a negative sign throughout the non-expansive regime κ≤1\kappa\leq 1: overload shrinks the bound but does not inflate it, because residual energy is energy the bilinear features cannot explain and therefore cannot store. The two effects of ρ\rho are less memory content (A103) and more steady-state jitter (A104). They cancel exactly at κ=1\kappa=1 and the content term dominates below it. This is why the constant in (A107) is 11 rather than the 3/23/2 or 22 obtained by bounding the two contributions separately.

𝒲2​(μ0,πβ)2=Eπβ​[‖𝑺−𝑺0‖F2]=‖𝑺0−𝑺LS‖F2+tr⁡𝑽β,\mathcal{W}_{2}(\mu_{0},\pi_{\beta})^{2}\;=\;\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}_{\pi_{\beta}}\big[\left\lVert\bm{S}-\bm{S}_{0}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}\big]\;=\;\left\lVert\bm{S}_{0}-\bm{S}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}\;+\;\tr\bm{V}_{\beta}\,, (A115)

the second equality being the bias–variance split around the stationary mean 𝑺LS\bm{S}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}} (Theorem A7 (i)). E​[‖𝑺t‖F2]1/2≤(1+qβt/2)​Bβ,\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[\left\lVert\bm{S}_{t}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}\big]^{1/2}\;\leq\;\big(1+q_{\beta}^{\,t/2}\big)\,B_{\beta}\,, (A116)

Squaring preserves the inequality since both sides are nonnegative. Finally qβt/2≤1q_{\beta}^{\,t/2}\leq 1 bounds the transient factor by 44. The general-κ\kappa variant replaces Bβ2B_{\beta}^{2} by the bound of (A106), and the general-𝑺0\bm{S}_{0} variant (A113) keeps 𝒲2​(μ0,πβ)\mathcal{W}_{2}(\mu_{0},\pi_{\beta}) in the form (A115) instead of collapsing it. ∎

Summary.

The least-squares memory satisfies the exact energy identity (𝒔LS)⊤​𝑨¯​𝒔LS=E⁡[c2]−E⁡[ρ2](\bm{s}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}})^{\top}\bar{\bm{A}}\,\bm{s}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}=\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[c^{2}]-\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\rho^{2}], which sandwiches its Frobenius norm between (E⁡[c2]−E⁡[ρ2])/λmax(\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[c^{2}]-\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\rho^{2}])/\lambda_{\max} and (E⁡[c2]−E⁡[ρ2])/λmin(\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[c^{2}]-\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\rho^{2}])/\lambda_{\min}. This is the explained target energy divided by the extreme feature-covariance eigenvalues. The bound is an equality for isotropic designs, reproduces ∑ici2\sum_{i}c_{i}^{2} in the orthonormal design, extends to the running iterates with an additive O⁡(β)O(\beta) fluctuation term, shrinks under overload since the residual energy is subtracted.

Appendix A4 DeltaNet Steady-State Norm Bound

A4.1  Overview

The DeltaNet steady-state norm bound can be derived essentially verbatim to kronLSTM. DeltaNet’s update is affine in 𝑺t\bm{S}_{t} and acts on each row of the memory independently; each row obeys exactly the scalar delta-rule recursion analyzed for KronLSTM, with the association direction 𝒂t=𝒌t⊗𝒗t\bm{a}_{t}=\bm{k}_{t}\otimes\bm{v}_{t} replaced by the key 𝒌t\bm{k}_{t} and the scalar target ctc_{t} replaced by the value coordinate vt,jv_{t,j}. Every step of the argument — the energy identity, the two-sided bound, the exact stationary covariance bound, and the Wasserstein contraction that carries all of it to the running memory — therefore transfers, and yields Eπβ​[‖𝑺‖F2]≤2​E​[‖𝒗‖2]/λmin​(𝑲¯)\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}_{\pi_{\beta}}[\left\lVert\bm{S}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}]\leq 2\,\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\left\lVert\bm{v}\right\rVert^{2}]/\lambda_{\min}(\bar{\bm{K}}) with 𝑲¯=E⁡[𝒌​𝒌⊤]\bar{\bm{K}}=\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\bm{k}\bm{k}^{\top}]. The practical consequence is a scoping correction: a length-independent steady-state bound is a property of the delta-rule mechanism, shared by KronLSTM and DeltaNet, which separates both from mLSTM and from any stability argument resting on a forget gate. We also record where the two genuinely differ: in the step-size condition, in what the bound is a bound on, and in the conditioning constant that sets its scale.

A4.2  DeltaNet Affine Recursion

DeltaNet’s update is

𝑺t+1=𝑺t−βt​(𝑺t​𝒌t−𝒗t)​𝒌t⊤=𝑺t​(𝑰−βt​𝒌t​𝒌t⊤)+βt​𝒗t​𝒌t⊤,\bm{S}_{t+1}\;=\;\bm{S}_{t}\;-\;\beta_{t}\big(\bm{S}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}-\bm{v}_{t}\big)\bm{k}_{t}^{\top}\;=\;\bm{S}_{t}\big(\bm{I}-\beta_{t}\bm{k}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top}\big)\;+\;\beta_{t}\,\bm{v}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top}\,, (A117)

and Gated DeltaNet’s is the same with 𝑺t\bm{S}_{t} replaced by ft​𝑺t\mathrm{f}_{t}\bm{S}_{t} in the first term. Two features are immediate. First, (A117) is affine in 𝑺t\bm{S}_{t}, so the pair (memory, random input) generates a Markov chain of exactly the type analyzed for the Kronecker Delta Rule. Second, and decisively, the memory is acted on from the right only, so the rows of 𝑺\bm{S} do not mix. Transposing (A117),

𝑺t+1⊤=(𝑰−βt​𝒌t​𝒌t⊤)​𝑺t⊤+βt​𝒌t​𝒗t⊤,\bm{S}_{t+1}^{\top}\;=\;\big(\bm{I}-\beta_{t}\bm{k}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top}\big)\bm{S}_{t}^{\top}\;+\;\beta_{t}\,\bm{k}_{t}\bm{v}_{t}^{\top}\,, (A118)

and reading off the jj-th column, i.e. the jj-th row 𝒔(j):=𝑺⊤​𝒆j\bm{s}^{(j)}:=\bm{S}^{\top}\bm{e}_{j} of 𝑺\bm{S},

𝒔t+1(j)=(𝑰−βt𝒌t𝒌t⊤)𝒔t(j)+βtvt,j𝒌t,j=1,…,d.\bm{s}^{(j)}_{t+1}\;=\;\big(\bm{I}-\beta_{t}\bm{k}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top}\big)\,\bm{s}^{(j)}_{t}\;+\;\beta_{t}\,v_{t,j}\,\bm{k}_{t}\,,\qquad j=1,\dots,d\,. (A119)
The structural correspondence.

Equation (A119) is identical to the vectorized KronLSTM recursion 𝒔t+1=(𝑰−β​𝒂t​𝒂t⊤)​𝒔t+β​ct​𝒂t\bm{s}_{t+1}=(\bm{I}-\beta\bm{a}_{t}\bm{a}_{t}^{\top})\bm{s}_{t}+\beta c_{t}\bm{a}_{t} under the substitution

𝒂t=𝒌t⊗𝒗t⟼𝒌t,ct⟼vt,j,ℝd2⟼ℝd.\bm{a}_{t}\;=\;\bm{k}_{t}\otimes\bm{v}_{t}\;\;\longmapsto\;\;\bm{k}_{t}\,,\qquad c_{t}\;\;\longmapsto\;\;v_{t,j}\,,\qquad\mathbb{R}^{d^{2}}\;\;\longmapsto\;\;\mathbb{R}^{d}\,. (A120)

DeltaNet is thus dd independent copies of the same scalar delta rule all driven by a common key 𝒌t\bm{k}_{t} and differing only in their scalar targets vt,jv_{t,j}. KronLSTM is a single copy of that rule on a d2d^{2}-dimensional state with the richer direction 𝒌t⊗𝒗t\bm{k}_{t}\otimes\bm{v}_{t}. Neither is a generalization of the other; both are Kaczmarz/LMS iterations, which is why the same theory covers both.

A4.3  Steady-State Norm Bound

Model the stream as i.i.d. triples (𝒌t,𝒗t,βt)∼p(\bm{k}_{t},\bm{v}_{t},\beta_{t})\sim p and put

𝑲¯\displaystyle\bar{\bm{K}}\; :=E⁡[𝒌​𝒌⊤]≻ 0,𝑺LS:=E⁡[𝒗​𝒌⊤]​𝑲¯−1=argmin𝑺E⁡[‖𝑺​𝒌−𝒗‖2],\displaystyle:=\;\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[\bm{k}\bm{k}^{\top}\big]\;\succ\;\bm{0}\,,\qquad\bm{S}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}\;:=\;\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[\bm{v}\bm{k}^{\top}\big]\,\bar{\bm{K}}^{-1}\;=\;\mathop{\mathrm{argmin}\,}_{\bm{S}}\;\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[\left\lVert\bm{S}\bm{k}-\bm{v}\right\rVert^{2}\big]\,, (A121)
𝝆\displaystyle\bm{\rho}\; :=𝒗−𝑺LS​𝒌,\displaystyle:=\;\bm{v}-\bm{S}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}}\bm{k}\,,

so that E⁡[𝝆​𝒌⊤]=𝟎\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\bm{\rho}\bm{k}^{\top}]=\bm{0}. With a random, input-dependent βt\beta_{t} the same statements hold with 𝑲¯\bar{\bm{K}} replaced by the β\beta-weighted second moment E⁡[β​𝒌​𝒌⊤]\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\beta\bm{k}\bm{k}^{\top}] and 𝑺LS\bm{S}^{\mathrm{L}\mathrm{S}} by the correspondingly weighted least-squares solution; nothing else changes. Assume the step size satisfies βt​‖𝒌t‖2≤1\beta_{t}\left\lVert\bm{k}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}\leq 1, which for Gated DeltaNet’s sigmoid-bounded βt∈(0,1)\beta_{t}\in(0,1) and unit-norm keys holds by construction.

Let πβ\pi_{\beta} be the steady-state law of (A117) and 𝚺β\bm{\Sigma}_{\beta} the covariance of vec⁡(𝐒)\vecop(\bm{S}) under it. Then the energy identity

A4.4  Relation to the KronLSTM Bound

The bound is a consequence of the delta rule being a relaxed projection that is a correction proportional to a residual that shrinks as the memory improves. Both models have that structure, therefore separates the delta-rule family from mLSTM, whose Hebbian write is uncorrected and has no fixed point to contract toward. It separates the steady-state argument from the non-expansiveness argument, whose forget-gate bound β​C​Amax/(1−f)\beta CA_{\max}/(1-\mathrm{f}) is Ω⁡(T)\Omega(T) once f→1\mathrm{f}\to 1 as long contexts require.

The constants are not comparable.

The two bounds read

KronLSTM:E⁡[c2]λmin​(𝑨¯),DeltaNet:2​E​[‖𝒗‖2]λmin​(𝑲¯),𝑨¯=E[𝒂𝒂⊤]∈ℝd2×d2,𝑲¯∈ℝd×d.\text{KronLSTM:}\;\;\frac{\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[c^{2}]}{\lambda_{\min}(\bar{\bm{A}})}\,,\qquad\text{DeltaNet:}\;\;\frac{2\,\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\left\lVert\bm{v}\right\rVert^{2}]}{\lambda_{\min}(\bar{\bm{K}})}\,,\qquad\bar{\bm{A}}=\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\big[\bm{a}\bm{a}^{\top}\big]\in\mathbb{R}^{d^{2}\times d^{2}},\;\;\bar{\bm{K}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\,. (A129)

These are bounds on the same object, ‖𝑺‖F\left\lVert\bm{S}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}, but they are not bounds for the same task: KronLSTM’s stream carries one scalar ctc_{t} per step, DeltaNet’s a dd-vector 𝒗t\bm{v}_{t}, so E⁡[c2]\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[c^{2}] and E​‖𝒗‖2\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}\left\lVert\bm{v}\right\rVert^{2} measure different amounts of information being written. The denominators also differ structurally: 𝑲¯≻𝟎\bar{\bm{K}}\succ\bm{0} requires only that the keys span ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, whereas 𝑨¯≻𝟎\bar{\bm{A}}\succ\bm{0} requires the 𝒂i=𝒌i⊗𝒗i\bm{a}_{i}=\bm{k}_{i}\otimes\bm{v}_{i} to span ℝd2\mathbb{R}^{d^{2}}, and λmin​(𝑨¯)\lambda_{\min}(\bar{\bm{A}}) is typically the smaller of the two. The reason is that for independent isotropic keys and values, 𝑨¯=E⁡[𝒌​𝒌⊤]⊗E⁡[𝒗​𝒗⊤]\bar{\bm{A}}=\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\bm{k}\bm{k}^{\top}]\otimes\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\bm{v}\bm{v}^{\top}] gives λmin​(𝑨¯)=λmin​(𝑲¯)​λmin​(E⁡[𝒗​𝒗⊤])\lambda_{\min}(\bar{\bm{A}})=\lambda_{\min}(\bar{\bm{K}})\,\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf{\mathrm{E}}[\bm{v}\bm{v}^{\top}]), a product of two small numbers. On the other hand the constant 2 appears in the bound of the DeltaNet. Which constant is smaller in a given setting is an empirical question, not a structural one.

DeltaNet has a smaller bound.

The step-size condition is milder. KronLSTM requires β​‖𝒌t‖2​‖𝒗t‖2≤1\beta\left\lVert\bm{k}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}\left\lVert\bm{v}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}\leq 1, so a large value norm eats directly into the admissible step size and hence into the contraction rate β​λmin​(𝑨¯)\beta\lambda_{\min}(\bar{\bm{A}}); DeltaNet requires only βt​‖𝒌t‖2≤1\beta_{t}\left\lVert\bm{k}_{t}\right\rVert^{2}\leq 1, in which 𝒗t\bm{v}_{t} does not appear at all. It enters the drive but never the stability condition.

KronLSTM has advantages.

d2d^{2} rather than dd exactly satisfiable associations per scalar slot, interference gated by the product of key and value overlap rather than key overlap alone, an update direction 𝒗t​𝒌t⊤\bm{v}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top} fixed by the input pair rather than the state-dependent 𝒖t​𝒌t⊤\bm{u}_{t}\bm{k}_{t}^{\top} so that a write’s footprint on unrelated memories does not compound with context length, single-binding write/rewrite/erase, and linearity of the memory in the target sequence. None of these follow from, or are affected by, the steady-state bound.
